Base58 encoding of bytes

ALPHABET = '123456789ABCDEFGHJKLMNPQRSTUVWXYZabcdefghijkmnopqrstuvwxyz'
def b58(data):
    n = int.from_bytes(data, 'big')
    out = ''
    while n:
        n, r = divmod(n, 58)
        out = ALPHABET[r] + out
    zeros = len(data) - len(data.lstrip(b'\x00'))
    return '1' * zeros + out

title: Bitcoin Core, the reference implementation: chapter 3 of the 3rd edition checked against release 31.1

nodes.label: Node
nodes.body: A node is a computer that runs Bitcoin software and takes part in the peer-to-peer network, and this first branch of the chapter is about the most complete kind of node, the full verification node. The chapter opens with the reason such a node exists. People accept money in exchange for their goods and services only if they believe that they will be able to spend that money later, and money that is counterfeit or unexpectedly debased may not be spendable later, so every person who accepts bitcoins has a strong incentive to verify the integrity of what they receive (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The software that performs this verification is the subject of the whole chapter, and the program most operators use for it is Bitcoin Core.

paras.text: A node is a computer that runs Bitcoin software and takes part in the peer-to-peer network, and this first branch of the chapter is about the most complete kind of node, the full verification node. The chapter opens with the reason such a node exists. People accept money in exchange for their goods and services only if they believe that they will be able to spend that money later, and money that is counterfeit or unexpectedly debased may not be spendable later, so every person who accepts bitcoins has a strong incentive to verify the integrity of what they receive (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The software that performs this verification is the subject of the whole chapter, and the program most operators use for it is Bitcoin Core.

The branch matters because it decides whom a user has to trust. The book explains that Bitcoin was designed so that software running entirely on your own computer can prevent counterfeiting, debasement and several other critical problems, and that the data such a node reports is authoritative not because a powerful entity designated it as such but because the node independently verified it (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Every later chapter of the course examines transactions, blocks and mining, and it does so through the data that a node of this kind provides, so the branch is the practical foundation for everything that follows.

You meet nodes whenever someone checks a payment or reads the blockchain. Bitcoin Core is the implementation that most full node operators have used since the beginning of the network, and the book uses it throughout the rest of its chapters to create and examine data about the blockchain and the network (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Businesses that build on Bitcoin run nodes as well: the book notes that Bitcoin software companies typically run several of them, and the bitcoin.org page on full nodes adds that most full nodes also serve lightweight clients, which are wallets that do not verify everything themselves (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Bitcoin.org, 2026).

The branch has four groups of concepts. The verification group explains what a full node is, why Bitcoin Core is called the reference implementation, how proposals for changes are documented in Bitcoin Improvement Proposals, and how a soft fork changes the rules without splitting the network. The project group explains that Bitcoin Core is open-source software created by Satoshi Nakamoto and now maintained by a community. The resource group describes what a node costs in disk space, time and connections, and what it keeps in memory and on disk. The remaining branches of the chapter then follow the order of the book: building the software, operating it, calling its interface, reading its data, and checking the ecosystem around it.

A full node is a choice with costs, and it should not be confused with other roles. It is not a miner, because it does not need to produce blocks; it is not necessarily a wallet, although Bitcoin Core includes one; and it is not the only implementation of the protocol, as the last branches of the chapter show. Running a node also does not remove every kind of trust, because a user still has to trust the software that was downloaded, which is why the ecosystem branch returns to the verification of releases.

nodes.label: Verification
nodes.body: Verification is the second level of the node branch and gathers four ideas: the full node itself, the reference implementation, the Bitcoin Improvement Proposals and the soft fork. Together they answer one question, which is how a participant can be sure that what the software enforces is what the Bitcoin system actually requires. The first concept names the program that checks the rules, the second names the program that serves as the model of how to check them, and the last two explain how the written rules are documented and how they are changed (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: Verification is the second level of the node branch and gathers four ideas: the full node itself, the reference implementation, the Bitcoin Improvement Proposals and the soft fork. Together they answer one question, which is how a participant can be sure that what the software enforces is what the Bitcoin system actually requires. The first concept names the program that checks the rules, the second names the program that serves as the model of how to check them, and the last two explain how the written rules are documented and how they are changed (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

Checking rules is only meaningful if everyone checks the same rules. A node that accepted a payment which the others rejected would be living on a different version of the money. For that reason the group does not stop at describing a program; it also describes the documents, the Bitcoin Improvement Proposals, in which the design of each major part of the system is written down, and the mechanism, the soft fork, by which the rules can be tightened while old and new nodes stay on the same chain.

Verification works by re-doing the work rather than by trusting a report of it. When a block reaches a node, the node does not ask another participant whether the block is good; it recomputes the block's identifier from the eighty bytes of its header, checks that the identifier is numerically below the target the header itself declares, rebuilds the Merkle root - the single hash that commits to every transaction in the block - from the transactions it was sent, and compares that root with the one in the header. Only then does it apply the spending rules to each transaction: that every input names an output which exists and has not already been spent, that the conditions on that output are satisfied, and that the outputs created do not add up to more than the inputs consumed. Because each of those steps is a computation over data the node already holds, two honest nodes given the same block reach the same verdict without communicating, and that is what makes a verdict worth having (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The reader meets this group the moment a node is started, because verification is what the first hours of a node's life consist of. The start-up log of release 31.1, saved with this chapter's evidence, shows the node loading the block index and then working forward through the chain; the answer to the first status question a new owner asks names the number of blocks verified so far and how far that is from the chain's tip. The same group is met again whenever a disagreement is reported, because the first question an engineer asks about a disputed transaction is which rule it is said to break and which program enforced that rule (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

Two cautions belong here. The first is that the word reference, in reference implementation, describes a service the program performs for other programmers and not an authority it holds: the rules of Bitcoin are whatever the nodes that carry the economic weight of the network will accept, and Bitcoin Core is authoritative only for as long as those nodes run it or agree with it. The second is that verification is not validation of intent. A node can tell a learner that a transaction obeys every rule; it cannot tell them that the payment was wise, that the recipient was the one intended, or that the key which signed it was in the right hands. Those questions belong to the chapters on keys and on wallets, and no amount of rule checking answers them (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

nodes.label: Full node
nodes.body: A full node, which the chapter introduces as a full verification node, is software that verifies every confirmed Bitcoin transaction against every rule in the system (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The bitcoin.org page on running a node puts it in one sentence: a full node is a program that fully validates transactions and blocks, and almost all full nodes also help the network by accepting transactions and blocks from other full nodes, validating them and relaying them to further full nodes (Bitcoin.org, 2026). The adjective full distinguishes this node from a lightweight client, the kind of wallet described in chapter 1 that asks other computers for answers and checks only a small part of them.

paras.text: A full node, which the chapter introduces as a full verification node, is software that verifies every confirmed Bitcoin transaction against every rule in the system (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The bitcoin.org page on running a node puts it in one sentence: a full node is a program that fully validates transactions and blocks, and almost all full nodes also help the network by accepting transactions and blocks from other full nodes, validating them and relaying them to further full nodes (Bitcoin.org, 2026). The adjective full distinguishes this node from a lightweight client, the kind of wallet described in chapter 1 that asks other computers for answers and checks only a small part of them.

The reason for verifying everything is trust. The book states that the Bitcoin system was designed so that software on your own computer can perfectly prevent counterfeiting and debasement, and it describes the data that your own node returns as authoritative because your node independently verified it, whatever any powerful entity may say (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). A user who relies on someone else's server to say that a payment has arrived has to trust that server. A user who relies on a full node has only to trust the software and the rules, and the rules are public.

The chapter gives the common reasons for running one: not wanting to rely on any third party to validate the transactions you receive, not wanting to disclose to third parties which transactions belong to your wallet, developing Bitcoin software that needs programmable access to the network and the blockchain, building applications that must validate transactions according to the consensus rules, and supporting the network, which becomes more robust when more nodes validate (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The book concludes that a reader who is interested in strong security, superior privacy or developing Bitcoin software should be running their own node.

A full node receives blocks and transactions from its peers and checks each of them against the consensus rules, which chapter 2 listed for transactions: the syntax and data structure must be correct, the lists of inputs and outputs must not be empty, the amounts must be within the allowed range, the outputs being spent must exist and be unspent, the inputs must cover the outputs, and the scripts must validate (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Only what passes is kept and relayed. The start-up log of Bitcoin Core shows the machinery that does this work, with a cache for signatures and a number of additional threads for script verification; the book's example log reports a signature cache of 16 MiB and 3 additional threads (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

Verifying every rule has a price that the chapter states openly: processing more than 500 GB of data at first and about 400 MB of new transactions a day, in the book's figures for 2023 (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). A full node also does not make a user's money safe by itself, because the wallet that holds the keys is a separate function, and it does not make a user a miner. Finally, the word full is not a promise about storage: a pruned node, described in the resource group, still verifies the whole chain but keeps only the most recent blocks.

nodes.example: a node that verifies every rule
nodes.definition: A full verification node checks every confirmed transaction against every rule of the system, so that what it reports is authoritative because it was independently verified.

nodes.label: Reference implementation
nodes.body: A reference implementation is a program that serves as the model of how a specification should be realised. The book calls Bitcoin Core the reference implementation of the Bitcoin system, meaning that it provides a reference for how each part of the technology should be implemented, and it lists what Bitcoin Core implements: wallets, a transaction and block validation engine, tools for block construction, and all modern parts of the peer-to-peer communication (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The project's own readme describes it more briefly: it connects to the Bitcoin peer-to-peer network to download and fully validate blocks and transactions, and it includes a wallet and a graphical user interface that can optionally be built (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

paras.text: A reference implementation is a program that serves as the model of how a specification should be realised. The book calls Bitcoin Core the reference implementation of the Bitcoin system, meaning that it provides a reference for how each part of the technology should be implemented, and it lists what Bitcoin Core implements: wallets, a transaction and block validation engine, tools for block construction, and all modern parts of the peer-to-peer communication (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The project's own readme describes it more briefly: it connects to the Bitcoin peer-to-peer network to download and fully validate blocks and transactions, and it includes a wallet and a graphical user interface that can optionally be built (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

A decentralized network needs participants who agree exactly on what is valid, and agreement is easier when a complete, running program exists that others can compare themselves with. The point is made by the source code itself: the constant that limits the total amount of money is annotated in Bitcoin Core with the remark that its exact value is consensus critical (Bitcoin Core, 2026). If two implementations differed even slightly on a rule of this kind, a block that one accepted could be rejected by the other, which is why the implementation that most nodes run carries so much weight.

The history explains the word. When Satoshi Nakamoto created Bitcoin, the software was mostly completed before the whitepaper was published, because Nakamoto wanted to be sure that the implementation worked before publishing a paper about it. That first implementation, then known simply as Bitcoin, has been heavily modified and improved and has evolved into Bitcoin Core, named to differentiate it from other implementations (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The continuity is still visible in the source: the first line of Bitcoin Core's file for the proof-of-work rules carries a copyright notice for 2009 to 2010 in the name of Satoshi Nakamoto (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

The book includes a figure of the architecture of Bitcoin Core, credited to Eric Lombrozo, beside this list of parts: the wallet, the validation engine, block construction and the peer-to-peer layer belong to one program (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). In practice a user meets the program as a small set of executables: a node daemon, a command-line client, a graphical client and tools for transactions and wallets, which the build and operation branches describe. Each version is released under a number, and the project marks stable versions with a release tag in its source repository.

Reference does not mean that the code is the specification. The book points out that the whitepaper describes several early parts of the system and that most major parts since 2011 are documented in Bitcoin Improvement Proposals, so the written documents and the code together describe the rules (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). It also does not mean that Bitcoin Core is the only implementation: the final section of the chapter lists libraries, toolkits and full-node implementations in many languages, and the book's chapter on the network says that the most common implementation is Bitcoin Core, run by more than 95 per cent of the full nodes, which makes it dominant but not unique (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). A learner should treat Bitcoin Core as the most widely used model and not as the only possible one.

nodes.definition: Bitcoin Core is the reference implementation: it provides a reference for how each part of the technology should be implemented.

nodes.label: Bitcoin Improvement Proposal
nodes.body: A Bitcoin Improvement Proposal, abbreviated BIP, is a design document providing information to the Bitcoin community or describing a new feature for Bitcoin or its processes or environment, in the words of the process document that governed BIPs from 2016 (Dashjr, 2016). The chapter explains that most major parts of the system since 2011 have been documented in a set of BIPs and that the book refers to them by number: BIP9, for example, describes a mechanism used for several major upgrades (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Chapter 2 already used the term for the BIP that defines the payment URI, and this chapter shows where such documents sit among the other sources of the system.

paras.text: A Bitcoin Improvement Proposal, abbreviated BIP, is a design document providing information to the Bitcoin community or describing a new feature for Bitcoin or its processes or environment, in the words of the process document that governed BIPs from 2016 (Dashjr, 2016). The chapter explains that most major parts of the system since 2011 have been documented in a set of BIPs and that the book refers to them by number: BIP9, for example, describes a mechanism used for several major upgrades (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Chapter 2 already used the term for the BIP that defines the payment URI, and this chapter shows where such documents sit among the other sources of the system.

The documents make the design of a decentralized system discussable. The process document says that BIPs are intended as the primary mechanisms for proposing new features, for collecting community input on an issue, and for documenting the design decisions that have gone into Bitcoin, and that the author is responsible for building consensus within the community and documenting dissenting opinions (Dashjr, 2016). Because the documents are text files in a versioned repository, their revision history is the historical record of the proposal. Without such a record, a rule would exist only as a line in somebody's code.

A reader meets BIPs in three places. The book cites them by number in its text and lists the ones that Bitcoin Core has implemented in an appendix (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Bitcoin Core keeps a list in its own documentation that names, for each BIP, the version since which it is implemented; for BIP 9 the list says that multiple soft forks can be deployed in parallel since version 0.12.1 (Bitcoin Core, 2026). And the BIPs repository itself holds the documents, and the process is now described by BIP 3, assigned in 2025, which replaces BIP 2 with a streamlined process (Murch, 2025).

A proposal begins with an idea that a champion discusses publicly, usually on the Bitcoin development mailing list; a draft is then submitted to the BIPs git repository as a pull request, and a BIP editor assigns the number, because authors must not assign numbers to themselves (Dashjr, 2016). Under BIP 3 each document has a preamble of headers, among them the status, which is one of Draft, Complete, Deployed or Closed, and the type, which is Specification, Informational or Process; BIP 9, for example, carries the status Deployed (Murch, 2025) (Wuille et al., 2015). A specification document should be detailed enough to enable any Bitcoin project to create an interoperable implementation (Murch, 2025).

A BIP is a recommendation, not a decree. BIP 3 says in so many words that BIPs do not define what Bitcoin is: individual BIPs do not represent community consensus or a general recommendation for implementation, some may never be adopted, and no formal or informal decision body governs Bitcoin development or decides adoption (Murch, 2025). A document with the status Deployed has been implemented and activated; a document that exists in the repository has only been published. When the course cites a BIP, it cites it for the description of a mechanism, and the number is the stable name by which any reader can find the same text.

nodes.definition: Most major parts of the system since 2011 are documented in Bitcoin Improvement Proposals, referred to by number.
