nodes.label: Soft fork
nodes.body: A soft fork is a change to the consensus rules that is backward compatible. The book defines the property precisely: full nodes implementing the change must not accept any blocks that full nodes without the change would consider invalid, so newer nodes may reject blocks that older nodes would accept, which allows them to enforce new rules, but never the other way round (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). A change that does not have this property would be a hard fork, which the book describes as a change to the consensus rules that is not compatible with older full nodes. Segregated witness, discussed in the transaction group, was introduced as a soft fork (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: A soft fork is a change to the consensus rules that is backward compatible. The book defines the property precisely: full nodes implementing the change must not accept any blocks that full nodes without the change would consider invalid, so newer nodes may reject blocks that older nodes would accept, which allows them to enforce new rules, but never the other way round (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). A change that does not have this property would be a hard fork, which the book describes as a change to the consensus rules that is not compatible with older full nodes. Segregated witness, discussed in the transaction group, was introduced as a soft fork (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The advantage is that the network can be upgraded without splitting. Because older nodes still accept everything that newer nodes accept, an upgrade does not force every participant to move on the same day. The cost is coordination: the miners who produce the blocks and the nodes that enforce the rules have to agree when the new rule applies. The earlier methods of signalling support in the block version, as BIP 90 recounts, used thresholds of 75 and 95 per cent of the last 1000 blocks (Daftuar, 2016), and they allowed only one change to be rolled out at a time (Wuille et al., 2015).

The chapter mentions the mechanism by name when it introduces BIPs: BIP9 describes a mechanism used for several major upgrades (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Bitcoin Core's own list of implemented BIPs says that the changes allowing multiple soft forks to be deployed in parallel have been implemented since version 0.12.1, and that some deployments have since been replaced by fixed activation heights, which BIP 90 calls burying (Bitcoin Core, 2026) (Daftuar, 2016). The block explorer output of chapter 3 shows the field involved, the block version, with the value 1 for the old block 123456.

BIP 9 reinterprets the version field of a block as a bit vector in which each bit can track an independent change. Each deployment has a name, a bit chosen from 0 to 28, a start time and a timeout, both measured in median time past; its state moves from DEFINED to STARTED, then to LOCKED_IN once enough blocks of one retarget period signal the bit, and finally to ACTIVE, or to FAILED if the timeout passes first (Wuille et al., 2015). Blocks that signal have the top three bits of the version set to 001, so their version lies between 0x20000000 and 0x3FFFFFFF; shifting a signalling version such as 0x20000002 right by 29 bits leaves the value 1, which is the binary 001 (Wuille et al., 2015).

A soft fork is backward compatible only for nodes that do not need to understand the new rule. Older nodes keep accepting blocks, but they no longer verify the new rule themselves, so a user who wants the full protection has to upgrade. The mechanism of signalling is also not a vote of the users: BIP 9 tallies the blocks that miners produce, and the nodes that enforce the rule decide which chain they will accept. The details of how a rule change is chosen and activated belong to the later chapters on mining and on the network.

nodes.example: version bits in the block header
nodes.definition: A soft fork tightens the consensus rules in a backward-compatible way; BIP 9 lets several be deployed in parallel by signalling in the block version.

nodes.label: The Bitcoin Core project
nodes.body: The project group describes where Bitcoin Core comes from and who maintains it. It contains two concepts: open-source software, which is the legal and social form in which the program is published, and Satoshi Nakamoto, the name under which the system was first described and its first software written. Both belong to the first section of the chapter, From Bitcoin to Bitcoin Core, which explains why the program is called what it is (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: The project group describes where Bitcoin Core comes from and who maintains it. It contains two concepts: open-source software, which is the legal and social form in which the program is published, and Satoshi Nakamoto, the name under which the system was first described and its first software written. Both belong to the first section of the chapter, From Bitcoin to Bitcoin Core, which explains why the program is called what it is (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

A student who meets the term full node soon asks who decides what the node software does. The answer given by the chapter is that nobody owns it in the ordinary sense. The source code is available under an open license, it is developed by an open community of volunteers, and it began as the work of a single person. Knowing this explains why the chapter can invite the reader to download the code, build it and even contribute to it, and why the book can treat the program as a public reference and not as a product.

The project works as a review process with no owner at its centre. A change is written as a patch against the public repository, published for anyone to read, argued over in public, and merged only when maintainers are satisfied and nobody with standing objects; the maintainers can merge but cannot compel anyone to run what they merged, because a release only matters once node operators choose to install it. The licence is what makes this arrangement stable rather than fragile: because the MIT licence permits anyone to take the source, change it and distribute the result, a disagreement that cannot be settled by argument can be settled by forking the code, and the knowledge that it can be is itself a restraint on whoever holds the commit rights (Open Source Initiative, 2026) (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

A student meets the project, rather than just the program, the first time they want a question answered that the documentation does not cover: the answer is in the repository's own history, in the discussion attached to the change that introduced the behaviour, and in the release notes that announced it. The same material is what makes the chapter's invitation to build the program from source more than a gesture, since the text a reader compiles is the text they can also read and argue with (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The openness is easy to overstate in two directions. It does not mean that anyone's change is accepted, and a learner who reads open community as unmoderated will be surprised by how conservative the review of a consensus-critical change is; the cost of a mistake there is other people's money. Nor does it mean that the absence of a named author leaves nothing to trust: a reader still has to decide whether to trust the maintainers' review, the reproducibility of the published binaries, or their own reading of the code, and this chapter's own section on assurance exists because that decision has to be made explicitly rather than assumed away (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

nodes.label: Open-source software
nodes.body: Open-source software is software whose source code is available to everyone under a license that allows use, modification and redistribution. The Open Source Initiative, whose definition is widely used, says that open source does not just mean access to the source code: the distribution terms must also allow free redistribution, must include the source code, and must allow modifications and derived works (Open Source Initiative, 2026). The book describes Bitcoin in these terms: it is an open-source project whose source code is available under an open license, the MIT license, free to download and use for any purpose (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: Open-source software is software whose source code is available to everyone under a license that allows use, modification and redistribution. The Open Source Initiative, whose definition is widely used, says that open source does not just mean access to the source code: the distribution terms must also allow free redistribution, must include the source code, and must allow modifications and derived works (Open Source Initiative, 2026). The book describes Bitcoin in these terms: it is an open-source project whose source code is available under an open license, the MIT license, free to download and use for any purpose (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

Openness is what makes it reasonable to trust a program that guards money without trusting its authors. Anyone can read the code, compile it and test it, and the project's own readme asks for exactly that: testing and code review are the bottleneck of development, and because this is a security-critical project, a mistake might cost people lots of money, so changes should be tested by somebody other than the developer who wrote them (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The book also draws a social consequence. Bitcoin is developed by an open community of volunteers, which by 2023 had more than 1,000 contributors, about a dozen developers working on the code almost full time and several dozen more part time, and it adds that anyone can contribute, including the reader (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The source files of Bitcoin Core that were read for this chapter state their terms in the header, with the sentence that the file is distributed under the MIT software license, and the readme repeats that Bitcoin Core is released under the terms of the MIT license (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The license text itself is short. It grants permission, free of charge, to any person obtaining a copy of the software to deal in it without restriction, including to use, copy, modify, merge, publish, distribute, sublicense and sell copies, on the conditions that the copyright notice is included and that the software is provided as is, without warranty of any kind (Open Source Initiative, 2026).

The project's development process shows how the open model works in practice. The master branch is regularly built and tested, but it is not guaranteed to be completely stable; official stable versions are marked by tags created from release branches, a mechanism that the source group of the build branch explains. Developers are strongly encouraged to write unit tests for new code, regression and integration tests written in Python exist as well, and continuous integration systems check that every pull request is tested on Windows, Linux and macOS before it is merged (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

Open source does not mean that the code has no defects, or that no one is in charge of releases. The license says plainly that the software is provided as is, and the readme warns that the master branch is not guaranteed to be stable (Open Source Initiative, 2026) (Bitcoin Core, 2026). Openness of the source also does not by itself prove that a downloaded program was built from that source. For that reason the ecosystem branch of this chapter explains how a release is checked by its checksums and signatures and why some builds are made reproducible.

nodes.definition: Open-source software is published with its source code under a license that lets anyone use, change and distribute it; Bitcoin Core uses the MIT license.

nodes.label: Satoshi Nakamoto
nodes.body: Satoshi Nakamoto is the name used by the person or people who designed Bitcoin and created its original reference implementation. The glossary of the book adds that, as part of that implementation, they also devised the first blockchain database and were the first to solve the double-spending problem for digital currency, and that their real identity remains unknown (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The chapter on the history of Bitcoin says that the system was first described in 2008 in a paper written under the alias of Satoshi Nakamoto (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The name is therefore a pseudonym, and it must not be confused with the unit satoshi of chapter 2, which was named after it.

paras.text: Satoshi Nakamoto is the name used by the person or people who designed Bitcoin and created its original reference implementation. The glossary of the book adds that, as part of that implementation, they also devised the first blockchain database and were the first to solve the double-spending problem for digital currency, and that their real identity remains unknown (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The chapter on the history of Bitcoin says that the system was first described in 2008 in a paper written under the alias of Satoshi Nakamoto (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The name is therefore a pseudonym, and it must not be confused with the unit satoshi of chapter 2, which was named after it.

The paper is the starting point of the technology. Its abstract proposes a solution to the double-spending problem using a peer-to-peer network, in which the network timestamps transactions by hashing them into an ongoing chain of hash-based proof of work, forming a record that cannot be changed without redoing the proof of work (Nakamoto, 2008). The chapter adds a fact about the order of events: the software was mostly completed before the whitepaper was published, because Nakamoto wanted to make sure that the implementation worked before publishing a paper about it (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The name appears in several places. The paper is reproduced in an appendix of the book and is available at bitcoin.org (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Nakamoto, 2008). The first block of the blockchain carries the Unix time 1231006505, which the worked example converts to the third of January 2009; a fresh node of release 31.1, in the evidence files of this chapter, reports exactly that number as the time of its only block (Bitcoin Core, 2026). Nakamoto's name is also in the subversion string of the node: the book's output of the network information command shows /Satoshi:24.0.1/, and the book explains that more than 95 per cent of full nodes run versions of Bitcoin Core, which is identified as Satoshi in this string (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The chapter on the history of Bitcoin explains what Nakamoto combined: several prior inventions, such as digital signatures and Hashcash, into a completely decentralized electronic cash system that does not rely on a central authority for currency issuance or for the settlement and validation of transactions. A key innovation was to use a distributed computation system, the proof-of-work algorithm, to conduct a global lottery about every 10 minutes, which lets the decentralized network arrive at consensus about the state of transactions (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The Bitcoin network started in 2009 with a reference implementation published by Nakamoto and since revised by many other programmers (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

Two points should not be overstated. The first is authority: the book states that Nakamoto withdrew from the public in April 2011, leaving the development of the code and the network to a group of volunteers, and that neither Nakamoto nor anyone else exerts individual control over the system, which operates on transparent mathematical principles, open-source code and consensus among participants (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The second is identity: nothing in the sources of this course identifies the person or people behind the name, and a claim about the identity would need evidence that this course cannot give.

nodes.definition: Satoshi Nakamoto is the name under which Bitcoin was described in 2008 and its first software released; the identity of the person or people behind the name is unknown.

io.code: __import__('datetime').datetime.fromtimestamp(1231006505, __import__('datetime').timezone.utc).date().isoformat()

nodes.label: Node resources
nodes.body: Node resources are the things that a node consumes in order to do its work: time and bandwidth to download the chain, disk space to store it, memory to keep the data it needs often, and network connections to other nodes. The section Running a Bitcoin Core Node of the chapter lists the costs openly before it explains why a reader might still want to bear them, and this group collects the concepts needed to understand those costs (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: Node resources are the things that a node consumes in order to do its work: time and bandwidth to download the chain, disk space to store it, memory to keep the data it needs often, and network connections to other nodes. The section Running a Bitcoin Core Node of the chapter lists the costs openly before it explains why a reader might still want to bear them, and this group collects the concepts needed to understand those costs (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The costs decide who can run a node, and therefore how widely the verification of the rules is spread. The book's figures for 2023 are over 500 GB of data to download and process at first, about 400 MB of transactions per day, at least 1 TB of disk if all transactions are indexed and the full copy is kept for several years, and upload bandwidth that a metered connection may not afford (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The current download page of Bitcoin Core states a one-time download of about 600 GB plus a further 5 to 10 GB per month, and says that with pruning a node can store as little as 10 GB (Bitcoin Core, 2026). Every option that lowers these costs, such as pruning, is a trade between cost and what the node can offer to others.

The costs follow from one design decision, which is that a node believes nothing it has not checked itself. To check a transaction the node must know whether the output it spends still exists, so it has to have processed every block that came before; that is why the first synchronization reads the whole chain from the beginning rather than starting at today. Once the chain is processed, what the node needs in order to keep working is not the chain itself but the set of outputs that can still be spent, and that set is far smaller than the history which produced it. Pruning is exactly this observation turned into an option: the node verifies every block as it arrives and then discards the old ones, keeping the compact record of spendable outputs. The saving is large and the price is precise - a pruned node cannot serve old blocks to a peer that is synchronizing, and cannot answer a question about a transaction whose block it has thrown away (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

Two warnings about the figures themselves. They are measurements with a date, not constants: the chain grows every day, so a download size quoted for one year is a floor for the next, and this course therefore reads every such number against the date of the source that gave it rather than memorising it. And the figure that catches people out is not disk but upload: a node that has finished synchronizing spends most of its bandwidth serving others, which is the point of running one, and that is the cost a metered or capped connection cannot absorb. A learner who has only the cost of disk in mind will choose the wrong machine (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

The reader meets these costs twice, and in opposite moods. The first time is on the project's own download page, which states them plainly before offering the software, and in the book's own section on running a node, which does the same: both treat the costs as the price of an independent verdict rather than as a drawback to be minimised. The second time is on the machine itself, where the costs appear as the hours the first synchronization takes, as the growth of the data directory that this chapter's evidence captured from a real run, and as the choice of whether to prune, which is the first configuration decision whose consequences a learner can feel (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

nodes.label: Initial download
nodes.body: The initial download is the first synchronization of a new node with the network, in which it fetches the whole chain of blocks from its peers and validates every transaction in them. The chapter's tip says that Bitcoin Core keeps a full copy of the blockchain by default, with nearly every transaction confirmed since the start of the network in 2009, and that the node will not be able to process transactions or update account balances until the full dataset has been downloaded (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The status data of a node has a field for this phase: the flag initialblockdownload tells whether the node is still in it, and the explanation in Bitcoin Core's source calls it a debug-information estimate (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

paras.text: The initial download is the first synchronization of a new node with the network, in which it fetches the whole chain of blocks from its peers and validates every transaction in them. The chapter's tip says that Bitcoin Core keeps a full copy of the blockchain by default, with nearly every transaction confirmed since the start of the network in 2009, and that the node will not be able to process transactions or update account balances until the full dataset has been downloaded (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The status data of a node has a field for this phase: the flag initialblockdownload tells whether the node is still in it, and the explanation in Bitcoin Core's source calls it a debug-information estimate (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

The download is what turns the claim that a node verifies everything into a fact about a particular computer. Until the node has processed every block, it cannot know the current set of unspent outputs, so it cannot tell whether a payment is valid. The cost is substantial, and the book says it will take some time, perhaps more than a day, for the program to catch up to the current height, with almost a billion transactions to validate at the time of writing (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). That is the reason the chapter asks readers to make sure they have enough disk space, bandwidth and time before they begin.

A reader meets the phase in the output of the status command. The book's example of a node that has just been started shows a chain of 0 blocks and 83,999 headers, and explains that the node first fetches the block headers from its peers to find the chain with the most proof of work and afterwards continues to download the full blocks, validating them as it goes (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The same data from a fresh node of the current release, in the evidence files of this chapter, shows 0 blocks, 0 headers and a verification progress near zero (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

The same arithmetic applies after any interruption. Bitcoin Core must fetch whatever it missed while it was off: at the book's rate of about 400 MB a day, closing the program for ten days means 400 * 10 = 4000 MB, which is the 4 GB the book names (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The rate itself is not constant. The book's figure corresponds to about 12 GB a month, whereas the current download page speaks of 5 to 10 GB per month, and the bitcoin.org page of about 20 GB a month plus about 740 GB for the first start (Bitcoin Core, 2026) (Bitcoin.org, 2026). The numbers differ because they were measured at different times and under different definitions.

The download is only the first of two jobs: the node must also validate what it fetches, and on slow hardware validation, not bandwidth, can be the bottleneck. Bitcoin Core's own documentation warns that when the system starts swapping memory pages to disk continuously, a node can slow to a crawl, especially during the initial synchronization, and that a lower database cache makes the initial synchronization much longer (Bitcoin Core, 2026). A learner should therefore treat the figures in the book as a snapshot of 2023 and not as a promise, and should check the current ones on the download page before planning a node.

nodes.definition: A new node downloads and validates the whole chain before it can process transactions, and a node that was off for ten days downloads about four gigabytes at 400 megabytes a day.

nodes.label: Pruned node
nodes.body: A pruned node is a full node that deletes old block files after it has verified them, so that it needs far less disk space. The chapter describes the option prune as a way to reduce the disk requirements of the blockchain to a given number of megabytes by deleting old blocks, for use on a resource-constrained node, and it stresses that other parts of the system use disk space that cannot currently be pruned, so the minimum space of the data directory is still needed (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The tip of the same section adds that Bitcoin Core can be configured to discard old blocks but still downloads the entire dataset (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: A pruned node is a full node that deletes old block files after it has verified them, so that it needs far less disk space. The chapter describes the option prune as a way to reduce the disk requirements of the blockchain to a given number of megabytes by deleting old blocks, for use on a resource-constrained node, and it stresses that other parts of the system use disk space that cannot currently be pruned, so the minimum space of the data directory is still needed (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The tip of the same section adds that Bitcoin Core can be configured to discard old blocks but still downloads the entire dataset (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

Pruning allows a verifying node on a small machine. The current download page says that with pruning enabled a node can store as little as 10 GB in total without sacrificing any security (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The reason is that verification needs the current state of the chain and a recent stretch of blocks, not every old block: the node checked the old blocks when it first received them and keeps the compact record of unspent outputs, which is the basis for checking new ones. The price is that the node can no longer hand old blocks to other nodes.

The option is given as -prune=<n> on the command line or prune=<n> in the configuration file. In the book's sample for a resource-constrained node it is prune=5000. Bitcoin Core's help text defines the values: 0 disables pruning, 1 allows manual pruning through a remote procedure call, and any number of at least 550 means that block files are deleted automatically to keep under that target size in MiB (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The constant behind the 550 is MIN_DISK_SPACE_FOR_BLOCK_FILES in the source, and the constant MIN_BLOCKS_TO_KEEP, 288, protects the files that hold the most recent blocks (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

Bitcoin Core stores blocks in numbered files of 128 MiB each and deletes whole files until the stored blocks fit under the target, never touching the files that hold the 288 most recent blocks; the block index and the chain state are separate databases and stay (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The node also tells other nodes what it can offer. An unpruned node sets the service bit NODE_NETWORK, which says that it can serve all historical blocks, whereas BIP 159 defines the bit NODE_NETWORK_LIMITED, bit 10, for pruned peers, which must be capable of serving at least the last 288 blocks, about two days of blocks (Bitcoin Core, 2026) (Schnelli, 2017). Because the index of all transactions needs the old blocks, the program refuses to start when both options are given and prints the message that prune mode is incompatible with -txindex (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

Pruning cannot be undone cheaply. The help text warns that reverting the setting requires re-downloading the entire blockchain, and that wallets and indexes should be kept active while pruning is enabled so they stay synchronized before old block data is deleted (Bitcoin Core, 2026). A pruned node also cannot look up an old transaction or block that it has deleted, so the tools of this chapter, such as retrieving an arbitrary transaction by its identifier, work only for data that is still stored or that is part of the wallet. For a learner the safe rule is that pruning saves disk space and nothing else: it neither weakens verification nor makes the node faster.

nodes.example: a node that deletes old blocks
nodes.definition: A pruned node deletes old blocks to reduce disk use while still downloading and verifying the whole chain; automatic pruning needs a target of at least 550 MiB.

nodes.label: Peer and connection
nodes.body: A peer is another node of the Bitcoin network to which a node keeps a connection in order to exchange blocks and transactions. The chapter introduces the word when it says that, by default, Bitcoin nodes transmit transactions and blocks to other nodes, called peers, which consumes upload bandwidth (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The network information of a node counts the connections: the book's example shows 10 connections, none incoming and 10 outgoing, and the keys connections_in and connections_out give the two numbers (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: A peer is another node of the Bitcoin network to which a node keeps a connection in order to exchange blocks and transactions. The chapter introduces the word when it says that, by default, Bitcoin nodes transmit transactions and blocks to other nodes, called peers, which consumes upload bandwidth (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The network information of a node counts the connections: the book's example shows 10 connections, none incoming and 10 outgoing, and the keys connections_in and connections_out give the two numbers (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

Peers are how a node learns about the world. It has no central server to ask, so every block and every unconfirmed transaction reaches it from a peer, and every block that it has verified is passed on in the same way. Chapter 2 described this spreading of data as gossiping. For the operator, peers are also a cost, since each active connection takes some memory and bandwidth, and a node on a metered connection may want to limit how much it uploads (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

The start-up log of a node states the limit it works with: the book's log says Using at most 125 automatic connections, and the same line appears in the log of release 31.1 in the evidence files, whereas the source tree consulted for this chapter defines the default as 200 (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Bitcoin Core, 2026). Bitcoin Core's guide to reducing memory explains the structure: if inbound connections are enabled, the option maxconnections sets the maximum; otherwise the number of connections is not more than 11, of which 8 are full-relay connections, 2 are block-relay-only connections, and occasionally 1 is a short-lived feeler connection (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

A node finds peers from a stored list: the log of the book says that it loaded 63866 addresses from the file peers.dat, and the data directory of a node holds that file next to a list of banned addresses (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Bitcoin Core, 2026). It then opens outgoing connections to some of them and accepts incoming ones, if it is listening. Connections added by hand with the addnode option have a separate limit of 8 and do not count against the maximum (Bitcoin Core, 2026). Eight full-relay and two block-relay-only connections make 8 + 2 = 10 regular outgoing connections, and the 11th is the feeler or an extra block-relay-only connection.

A peer is not a trusted party. Everything it sends is checked by the receiving node against the rules, which is why a node can connect to strangers at all. The number of connections is also not a measure of quality: the node in the evidence files, started with its connections disabled, reports connections 0 and still holds a correct chain of one block (Bitcoin Core, 2026). Finally, the value of the default maximum differs between the release the book printed, release 31.1 and the newest source tree, so a configuration that depends on it should state the number explicitly.

nodes.example: a node connected to my node
nodes.definition: A peer is another node with which a node keeps a connection to exchange blocks and transactions; a node limits how many it keeps.

nodes.label: Set of unspent outputs
nodes.body: The set of unspent outputs, in the chapter often called the UTXO set, is the collection of all transaction outputs that have been created and not yet spent. Chapter 2 explained the unspent transaction output as the unit that a payment spends, and Bitcoin Core's documentation describes the database in which it keeps them, called the chain state, as a compact representation of all currently unspent transaction outputs and metadata about the transactions they are from (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The chapter refers to it when it describes the option dbcache as the size of the UTXO cache (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: The set of unspent outputs, in the chapter often called the UTXO set, is the collection of all transaction outputs that have been created and not yet spent. Chapter 2 explained the unspent transaction output as the unit that a payment spends, and Bitcoin Core's documentation describes the database in which it keeps them, called the chain state, as a compact representation of all currently unspent transaction outputs and metadata about the transactions they are from (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The chapter refers to it when it describes the option dbcache as the size of the UTXO cache (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The set is what makes verification fast. To decide whether a new transaction is valid, a node does not need to search the whole history: it needs to know whether each output being spent is in the set. The chapter's checklist for transactions says that the outputs being spent must match outputs in the memory pool or unspent outputs in a block of the main branch (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The set is much smaller than the chain of blocks, because every spent output has left it.

A reader meets it in three places: as a directory called chainstate in the data directory of the node, as the thing that the dbcache option keeps in memory, and as the thing that a reorganization changes. The evidence files of a fresh node of release 31.1 list the entry chainstate next to blocks, and Bitcoin Core's file documentation names it as a LevelDB database (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The book explains that when a node switches to a chain with more work it reorganizes its view of confirmed transactions and available UTXOs (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

Each block changes the set in the same way as the transaction of the example: the outputs that its transactions spend leave, and the new outputs enter. Alice's transaction spent one output of an earlier transaction and created two, the payment to Bob and the change, so verifying it removes one entry and adds two. The worked example shows the operation on a set of outpoint names, each written as a transaction and an output number: removing the spent outpoint 4ac5:1 and adding 4662:0 and 4662:1 leaves the unrelated entry and two new ones.

The set is derived data, not part of any block, and every node builds it for itself by verifying the chain; two honest nodes get the same set only because they apply the same rules. It is also not a list of balances: the set holds outputs, and the amount a wallet owns is the sum of the outputs it can spend. Finally, the size of the set affects the memory a node needs, which is why the chapter lists the database cache among the options that a resource-constrained node should lower.

nodes.definition: The set of unspent transaction outputs is the compact record of everything that can still be spent; a node updates it for every block and it is the data that the database cache holds.

nodes.label: Build
nodes.body: The build branch is about turning the text of Bitcoin Core into a program that can run. The book calls this part of the chapter the Bitcoin development environment: the tools, libraries and support software a developer needs for writing Bitcoin applications, which the chapter walks through step by step. It announces that the chapter is highly technical and that a reader who is not actually setting up a development environment may skip to the next chapter, which is less technical (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The branch follows the sections of the book: obtaining the source code, selecting a release, configuring the build and building the executables.

paras.text: The build branch is about turning the text of Bitcoin Core into a program that can run. The book calls this part of the chapter the Bitcoin development environment: the tools, libraries and support software a developer needs for writing Bitcoin applications, which the chapter walks through step by step. It announces that the chapter is highly technical and that a reader who is not actually setting up a development environment may skip to the next chapter, which is less technical (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The branch follows the sections of the book: obtaining the source code, selecting a release, configuring the build and building the executables.

Building from source is the most direct way to know what a node is made of. The source code of Bitcoin Core is public, so a reader who builds it has a program that corresponds to a particular version of the text that anyone can inspect, and can switch features on or off during the build, for example by leaving out the wallet. For a course on software engineering the branch also shows how a large, long-lived project organizes its work: a version control system, numbered releases, a build system that discovers what a computer provides, and an automatic test suite (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

The steps appear in the project's own documentation, which has separate build notes for each platform: the book names Android, FreeBSD, NetBSD, OpenBSD, macOS, Unix and Windows, and the current tree has files such as doc/build-unix.md for the platform that the chapter uses (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Bitcoin Core, 2026). Most users never build the program, because the project publishes ready-made releases for download, and the ecosystem branch explains how such a download is verified. The branch is nevertheless the reason the course can say what the executables are, where they come from and which options shaped them.

A build moves through four stages. First the source code is obtained and a particular release is selected. Then the build is configured, which means that the build system looks at the computer, checks that the needed libraries are present and records the chosen options. Next the compiler translates the source files into executables, and the project's tests are run to check them. Finally the executables are installed in a directory where the operating system can find them. The book describes these stages for the Autotools build system that Bitcoin Core used at the time of writing; the current project uses CMake with the same stages.

The most important caution is that the commands of the printed chapter belong to a build system that has been replaced: release 29.0 migrated the build from Autotools to CMake, and the current tree has a top-level CMakeLists.txt and no autogen.sh (Bitcoin Core, 2026). A student who follows the book literally on a current source tree fails at the first command. The second caution is that compiling it yourself does not prove that the program is trustworthy; it shows only that a program was built from the text you chose, and the choice of that text is made by selecting a release tag.

nodes.label: Source
nodes.body: The source group contains the concepts needed to obtain the right text of the program: the source code itself, the Git repository in which the project keeps it, the release tag that names a particular stable version, and the release candidate that precedes it. The book teaches these in its sections on compiling Bitcoin Core from the source code and on selecting a release (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: The source group contains the concepts needed to obtain the right text of the program: the source code itself, the Git repository in which the project keeps it, the release tag that names a particular stable version, and the release candidate that precedes it. The book teaches these in its sections on compiling Bitcoin Core from the source code and on selecting a release (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The program changes every day, and not every day's version is safe to run. The book explains that by default the local copy of the repository is synchronized with the most recent code, which might be an unstable or beta version of Bitcoin (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The concepts of the group give a learner the means to say exactly which version is meant: a repository holds every version, a tag names one of them, and a suffix tells whether it is meant for testing.

Choosing the right text works through two mechanisms that are easy to confuse. The first is the repository, which is a complete record of every version the project has ever had, so that cloning it gives a learner not one program but the whole history of the program; by default the copy sits at the most recent development state, which is why a fresh clone is not yet a release. The second is the tag, a name attached to one exact point in that history, which is how a release is identified: checking out a tag moves the working copy to the text that was released under that name, and because the tag is tied to the content rather than to a date, two people who check out the same tag get byte-for-byte the same text. The release-candidate suffix is a convention layered on top of this, and it is only a convention - the software cannot tell a learner that a tag is meant for testing, the name does (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Chacon and Straub, 2014).

A reader meets this group at the second command of the chapter's build sequence and again every time they update. The repository is met as a directory that appears after the clone; the tags are met as a long list printed by the command that asks the project's server which names exist, a list this chapter saved from the real repository so that the shape of the names can be studied offline; and the release candidate is met as the handful of names in that list which end in a testing suffix and which a production node should not run (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Git project, 2026).

The caution is that having the right text is not the same as having trustworthy text. A clone proves only that the bytes came from the address that was asked; it says nothing about whether that address is the project's. The repository's own signed tags, and the signed checksums published with the binary releases, are what close that gap, and they are the subject of this chapter's assurance section. A learner who checks out the correct tag from the wrong repository has built the wrong program carefully (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

nodes.label: Release tag
nodes.body: A release tag is a name that the developers attach to one specific snapshot of the code repository in order to mark a release by its version number (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The documentation of Git describes the command that creates such names: git tag adds a tag reference, and annotated tag objects are meant for releases, while lightweight tags are meant for private or temporary object labels (Git project, 2026). In Bitcoin Core a tag has the form v24.0.1, a letter v followed by the major, minor and revision numbers.

paras.text: A release tag is a name that the developers attach to one specific snapshot of the code repository in order to mark a release by its version number (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The documentation of Git describes the command that creates such names: git tag adds a tag reference, and annotated tag objects are meant for releases, while lightweight tags are meant for private or temporary object labels (Git project, 2026). In Bitcoin Core a tag has the form v24.0.1, a letter v followed by the major, minor and revision numbers.

Tags solve the problem of the moving target. The project's readme explains that the master branch is regularly built and tested but is not guaranteed to be completely stable, and that tags are created regularly from release branches to indicate new official, stable release versions (Bitcoin Core, 2026). A tag therefore lets two people on different continents talk about exactly the same code, and a book can say which version its screenshots belong to.

The chapter shows the three commands in sequence. The command git tag lists all tags, from v0.1.5 and v0.1.6test1 through v0.10.0 and v0.11.2 to the release candidates of version 0.12; the command git checkout v24.0.1 synchronizes the local copy with the highest release at the time of writing; and git status confirms that HEAD is detached at v24.0.1 (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The list of tags of the public repository, read for this chapter on 2026-10-02, now ends with v31.1 for the newest stable release and v32.0rc3 for the next candidate (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

The tag names a commit, the repository's own identifier of a snapshot. After the checkout the book shows the message that HEAD is now at b3f866a8d, a shortened commit identifier with the text of the merge that completed version 24.0.1 (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The version number in the tag is the same number that the running program reports: the program computes its client version as 10000 times the major number plus 100 times the minor number plus the build number, and for v24.0.1 that is 240001, which is the value of the field version in the book's network information (Bitcoin Core, 2026) (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

A tag is a label, not a guarantee. Checking out a tag gives the code that the maintainers tagged, but it does not by itself show that the label was placed by them, and the book's state message warns that the user is now in a detached HEAD state, where changes belong to no branch (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The tag list also contains names that follow no release scheme, such as noversion and v0.1.6test1. Trust in a release comes from the signatures and the reproducible builds described in the ecosystem branch.

nodes.definition: A release tag marks a snapshot of the source by version number; release candidates carry the suffix rc and stable releases none.

io.code: 'v24.0.1'.lstrip('v').split('.')

nodes.label: Source code
nodes.body: Source code is the text in which a program is written, in a programming language that a person can read, before it is translated into the form that a computer executes. The book says that Bitcoin Core's source code can be downloaded as an archive or by cloning the source repository from GitHub (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The project's own documentation shows what the text consists of: the main program is written in C++, which the notes on the build call a language whose compilers are memory-hungry, and its regression and integration tests are written in Python (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

paras.text: Source code is the text in which a program is written, in a programming language that a person can read, before it is translated into the form that a computer executes. The book says that Bitcoin Core's source code can be downloaded as an archive or by cloning the source repository from GitHub (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The project's own documentation shows what the text consists of: the main program is written in C++, which the notes on the build call a language whose compilers are memory-hungry, and its regression and integration tests are written in Python (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

The source is the only complete and exact description of the rules that the node enforces. The whitepaper describes several early parts of the system and the proposals describe later ones, but a question such as how much new money a block may create is answered finally by reading the code. The function GetBlockSubsidy in the file validation.cpp is a short example: it divides the block height by the halving interval, returns zero when the shift would be undefined, and otherwise starts from 50 coins and shifts the amount right by the number of halvings (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

A reader meets source code in the repository, whose top level holds the build files, the documentation folder, the source folder and the test folder, and in the documentation that the book tells the reader to review before compiling: the main readme in the repository and the build notes for the platform in the doc directory (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The genesis block, which every node knows from the beginning, is encoded in the source file for chain parameters, and the book points to that file for anyone who wants to see it (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

From the text to the program takes the steps of the build branch: a compiler translates each source file, a linker combines the results with libraries, and the build system orchestrates the order. A version of the source is identified by its place in the repository, either by a tag for a release or by a commit identifier for any other state. The block subsidy function can be checked by anyone: starting from 50 coins in the smallest unit, which is 5,000,000,000, a right shift by one per 210,000 blocks gives the amounts of the successive eras.

Reading the source requires care. The master branch holds work in progress, and a source file read at one commit can differ from the behavior of the release that a user runs, so a statement about the software should name the version it refers to. Also, a program that is open to reading is not thereby correct: the project's readme says that testing and review are the bottleneck and that every mistake might cost people lots of money, which is the reason the project asks for review by someone other than the author (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

nodes.definition: Source code is the human-readable text of a program, mainly C++ in Bitcoin Core, from which the executables are built; it can be read and audited by anyone.

nodes.label: Git repository
nodes.body: Git is a distributed version control system, and a repository is the database in which it keeps a project and all of its history. The book calls Git the most widely used distributed version control system and an essential part of the toolkit of every software developer (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The Pro Git book explains the main idea: Git thinks of its data more like a series of snapshots of a miniature filesystem, taking a picture of what all the files look like each time a project is committed, and everything in Git is checksummed before it is stored and is then referred to by that checksum (Chacon and Straub, 2014).

paras.text: Git is a distributed version control system, and a repository is the database in which it keeps a project and all of its history. The book calls Git the most widely used distributed version control system and an essential part of the toolkit of every software developer (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The Pro Git book explains the main idea: Git thinks of its data more like a series of snapshots of a miniature filesystem, taking a picture of what all the files look like each time a project is committed, and everything in Git is checksummed before it is stored and is then referred to by that checksum (Chacon and Straub, 2014).

A repository gives a project a memory and a way to share it. Because every copy contains the whole history, anyone can work offline, compare any two versions and verify that a given version is the one that the maintainers named. The chapter uses exactly this: the command git clone makes a complete local copy of the repository from GitHub, after which the command git tag shows the available release names, and the book's example output counts 245,912 objects received, about 217.74 MiB of data (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The Bitcoin Core repository is hosted on GitHub, and the project's readme says that stable releases are tagged from release branches while the master branch is the integration tree (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The documentation of Git describes the clone command in a sentence: it clones a repository into a newly created directory, creates remote-tracking branches for each branch of the cloned repository, and creates and checks out an initial branch forked from the cloned repository's currently active branch (Git project, 2026). The command git tag creates, lists, deletes or verifies tags (Git project, 2026).

Git names each snapshot, called a commit, by a hash computed from its content. The full name of the commit that the source tree consulted for this chapter is 05bc2f53ce0cb239c17dbdd6b261bd2db7d2a940, forty hexadecimal characters, and the book's output of the checkout command abbreviates its commit to nine characters, b3f866a8d. Chapter 2 explained hash functions and hexadecimal notation, and a commit identifier is an application of both: if the content changed in any way, the name would change as well. A tag is a second name for a commit, and a checkout makes the working files equal to that commit.

Two misunderstandings are common. A repository is not the same as a hosting service: GitHub stores a copy, and the clone on a user's machine is as complete as the original. And a clone is a snapshot of one moment, not a live view: the highest release at the time of writing was v24.0.1, whereas the public repository now holds the releases up to v31.1 and hundreds of tags in all, so a reader who cloned in 2023 does not see the later releases without updating the clone. The detached HEAD state that the book prints after checking out a tag is normal for reading a release and is a warning only for those who intend to commit changes.

nodes.definition: Git is a distributed version control system; cloning copies the whole repository with its history and a commit is named by a long hash.

io.code: len('05bc2f53ce0cb239c17dbdd6b261bd2db7d2a940')

nodes.label: Release candidate
nodes.body: A release candidate is a version that the developers believe could become the next stable release, published so that it can be tested first. The book gives the naming convention in one sentence: by convention, release candidates, which are intended for testing, have the suffix rc, and stable releases that can be run on production systems have no suffix (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The tag v0.12.0rc2 is therefore the second candidate of version 0.12.0, and v0.12.0 itself would be the release.

paras.text: A release candidate is a version that the developers believe could become the next stable release, published so that it can be tested first. The book gives the naming convention in one sentence: by convention, release candidates, which are intended for testing, have the suffix rc, and stable releases that can be run on production systems have no suffix (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The tag v0.12.0rc2 is therefore the second candidate of version 0.12.0, and v0.12.0 itself would be the release.

The two-step method lets the project find problems before ordinary users depend on the software. For a program that guards money, the cost of a defect is high, and the project's readme stresses the need for testing by people other than the developers (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The book's rule for readers follows: when selecting a release for compilation, choose the highest version without a suffix, because that is the one meant for production (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The tag list of the book already shows candidates next to releases: v0.11.2 and v0.11.2rc1, and v0.12.0rc1 and v0.12.0rc2 (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The list of tags of the public repository read for this chapter on 2026-10-02 contains many more; its newest entries at the time of reading were the stable v31.1 and the candidates v32.0rc1, v32.0rc2 and v32.0rc3, so a reader who checked out the very last tag in an alphabetical or chronological list would have received a candidate and not a release (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

Candidates are numbered in the order in which they are published: rc1, then rc2, rc3 and so on until a candidate is accepted and the same code is tagged without a suffix. The program itself knows whether it is a release: the start-up log of release 31.1 begins with the text Bitcoin Core version v31.1.0 (release build), and the source defines the client version from a major, minor and build number together with a flag that says whether it is a release (Bitcoin Core, 2026). A script can tell candidates from releases by the suffix alone, as the worked example does.

The suffix is a convention and not a guarantee, and not every unusual tag is a candidate: the first entries of the list include v0.1.6test1, which uses a different suffix. A candidate may also change before the final release, so results that a student obtains from a candidate need not hold for the release. The book itself recommends the plain tag, and a production system should follow that advice.

nodes.definition: Release candidates, intended for testing, carry the suffix rc; stable releases that can run on production systems have no suffix.

io.code: [t for t in ['v0.11.2', 'v0.11.2rc1', 'v0.12.0rc2'] if 'rc' not in t]

nodes.label: Toolchain
nodes.body: The toolchain group gathers the programs and conventions that turn source code into running executables: the build system, which decides how, the compilation, which does the translation, the prerequisites, which must be present, and the executables, which are the result. The book describes the toolchain of its time, built on Autotools; the current project uses CMake; and release 30.0 added a new front door, the bitcoin command (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

paras.text: The toolchain group gathers the programs and conventions that turn source code into running executables: the build system, which decides how, the compilation, which does the translation, the prerequisites, which must be present, and the executables, which are the result. The book describes the toolchain of its time, built on Autotools; the current project uses CMake; and release 30.0 added a new front door, the bitcoin command (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

A build system exists because a large program is not compiled by one command. Bitcoin Core consists of many source files, depends on libraries that differ between computers, and offers options such as leaving out the wallet. The build system looks at the computer, records the choices, and runs the translation steps in the right order and, if interrupted, from where they stopped. Knowing the toolchain also explains why the same program can be obtained in several ways with the same result.

A build works in two stages, and both generations of build system have them. In the first stage the build system inspects the computer - which compiler it has, which libraries are installed and where, which optional features were asked for - and writes the answers down, so that the second stage has no decisions left to make. In the second stage the compiler translates each source file on its own into an object file, and the linker joins the object files and the libraries into an executable. Two properties of a learner's experience follow directly from that shape. Because each file is translated independently, the work can be divided between several processor cores and an interrupted build can resume from where it stopped rather than start again. And because the first stage recorded the inspection, a library installed after configuration fails is picked up by running the inspection again, not by reinstalling the toolchain (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Kitware, 2026).

The reader meets the toolchain as the longest wait in the chapter and as its most common source of failure. The current build notes of the project, fetched for this version and saved with this chapter's sources, reduce the whole second generation to two commands, one to configure a build directory and one to build it, and they state what the wait costs in memory: at least 1.5 GB should be available while compiling, which is per compiler process, so a build divided over four cores wants around 6.0 GB rather than 1.5 (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

Two things trip learners here. The first is that the book's commands and the project's current commands are different generations, not alternatives: following a printed Autotools sequence against a recent source tree fails at the first command, because the file it names is no longer there, and the failure says nothing about the reader's machine. The second is that a build which finishes is not a build which works; the project ships its own test programs for exactly this reason, and running them is the last step of the build rather than an optional extra (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

nodes.label: Autotools build
nodes.body: Autotools is the family of tools with which Bitcoin Core was built until release 29.0, and the build of the book follows its three typical commands. The first, the script autogen.sh, creates a set of automatic configuration scripts that interrogate the system to discover the correct settings and make sure that all the necessary libraries are present. The second, configure, applies them and creates a customized build script for the computer. The third, make, runs the build (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: Autotools is the family of tools with which Bitcoin Core was built until release 29.0, and the build of the book follows its three typical commands. The first, the script autogen.sh, creates a set of automatic configuration scripts that interrogate the system to discover the correct settings and make sure that all the necessary libraries are present. The second, configure, applies them and creates a customized build script for the computer. The third, make, runs the build (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The method was designed to make a program portable between operating systems without hand-editing. The script configure offers options that override the defaults, and the book lists four: --prefix, which overrides the installation location /usr/local, for example with $HOME on a computer where only the home directory is writable; --disable-wallet, which disables the reference wallet; --with-incompatible-bdb, which allows an incompatible version of the Berkeley DB library when building a wallet; and --with-gui=no, which leaves out the graphical interface that needs the Qt library (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The commands in the chapter are ./autogen.sh, ./configure --help, ./configure, make, make check and sudo make install, in this order, and the book shows output such as the lines beginning CXX that name the object file produced for each source file (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Readers meet the same tool in many older projects, and the release notes of Bitcoin Core 29.0 name the change that ended its use here: the build system has been migrated from Autotools to CMake (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

The configuration step creates the build scripts only if the computer passes the checks. The book says that if any library is missing or incompatible, configure terminates with an error instead of creating the build scripts, and that after installing the missing prerequisite one runs it again (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The following make step may take up to an hour depending on the speed of the processor and the available memory, and if it is interrupted it can be resumed by typing make again; the option -j followed by a number sets the number of parallel compile jobs (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The commands of this section no longer work on the current source. The top level of the current tree has no autogen.sh and no configure script, and the option --with-incompatible-bdb has lost its purpose since legacy BerkeleyDB wallets can no longer be created or loaded (Bitcoin Core, 2026). A learner should therefore read the Autotools section as an explanation of the structure of a build, with configure, compile, test and install, and use the CMake commands for any real work.

nodes.definition: The book builds bitcoind with autogen.sh, configure and make, options such as --disable-wallet and --with-gui=no shaping the build; Bitcoin Core replaced this with CMake.

io.code: (lambda old, new: (len(old), len(new)))(['./autogen.sh', './configure', 'make'], ['cmake -B build', 'cmake --build build'])

nodes.label: CMake build
nodes.body: CMake is the build system that Bitcoin Core has used since release 29.0. The manual of CMake explains its role: a buildsystem describes how to build a project's executables and libraries from its source code using a build tool to automate the process, and CMake lets a project describe its buildsystem abstractly in files written in the CMake language, from which it generates a preferred buildsystem for each user (Kitware, 2026). The release notes of version 29.0 state the change plainly, and the build notes of the project give the three commands: cmake -B build, then cmake --build build, then optionally cmake --install build (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

paras.text: CMake is the build system that Bitcoin Core has used since release 29.0. The manual of CMake explains its role: a buildsystem describes how to build a project's executables and libraries from its source code using a build tool to automate the process, and CMake lets a project describe its buildsystem abstractly in files written in the CMake language, from which it generates a preferred buildsystem for each user (Kitware, 2026). The release notes of version 29.0 state the change plainly, and the build notes of the project give the three commands: cmake -B build, then cmake --build build, then optionally cmake --install build (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

Moving the project to CMake replaced a collection of generated scripts by a description that works on the platforms the project supports. The release notes list what a user of the old method must change: the minimum required CMake version is 3.22, options are now given as CMake variables, and some defaults changed. For example, one now needs -DWITH_ZMQ=ON to build with the ZeroMQ messaging library and -DBUILD_GUI=ON to build the graphical client bitcoin-qt (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

A reader meets the commands in the file doc/build-unix.md, which also says that the command cmake -B build -LH shows the full list of available options and that the build command accepts -j N for N parallel jobs (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The book's options map onto the new ones: --disable-wallet corresponds to -DENABLE_WALLET=OFF, which also removes the dependency on SQLite, and the book's --with-gui=no describes what is now the default, because the graphical client is built only when asked for (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The CMake manual lists an --install-prefix option for choosing the installation directory (Kitware, 2026).

The build is divided into configuration and construction. The first command creates a build tree, the directory named after the -B option, in which CMake writes its cache with the chosen options. The second command builds the targets in that directory with whatever native tool is behind it. The release notes add that the default build type for single-configuration generators is RelWithDebInfo, in which the optimization flag -O2 is used instead of -O3, which has not been extensively tested with Bitcoin Core (Bitcoin Core, 2026). Building only the node is possible with cmake --build build --target bitcoind (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

Copying options from a book or a blog is the usual source of failure. The names are specific to the build system and the version: an option written for Autotools is silently useless to CMake, and the build notes warn that the memory requirement is at least 1.5 GB for compiling, with advice on reducing it for smaller machines (Bitcoin Core, 2026). Environment variables that the old build honored, such as CXXFLAGS, have corresponding CMake variables with other names, so a build that is configured in a script needs to be rewritten, not merely adapted (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

nodes.definition: A current build is cmake -B build, cmake --build build and cmake --install build, with options such as -DENABLE_WALLET=OFF and -DBUILD_GUI=ON.

io.code: {'--disable-wallet': '-DENABLE_WALLET=OFF'}['--disable-wallet']

nodes.label: The bitcoin command
nodes.body: The bitcoin command is a single program, introduced with release 30.0, through which the node and the other tools of Bitcoin Core are started. The installed-files table of the project describes it as the command-line tool for interacting with Bitcoin, which calls the other binaries (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The help text of the program lists its commands: node starts the node, equivalent to running bitcoind; rpc calls an RPC method, equivalent to bitcoin-cli -named; wallet and tx run the wallet tool and the transaction tool; and gui starts the graphical client (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

paras.text: The bitcoin command is a single program, introduced with release 30.0, through which the node and the other tools of Bitcoin Core are started. The installed-files table of the project describes it as the command-line tool for interacting with Bitcoin, which calls the other binaries (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The help text of the program lists its commands: node starts the node, equivalent to running bitcoind; rpc calls an RPC method, equivalent to bitcoin-cli -named; wallet and tx run the wallet tool and the transaction tool; and gui starts the graphical client (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

The command exists to hide a change in the structure of the software. The project plans to split Bitcoin Core into separate processes for the node, the wallet and the graphical interface, so that each can run in its own address space for better isolation. A front door that chooses the binary spares users from learning new names for each stage of that change (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

In the book the user types bitcoind and bitcoin-cli. Those names still work in release 31.1, whose archive holds them in the folder bin together with bitcoin, bitcoin-qt, bitcoin-tx, bitcoin-util and bitcoin-wallet, and holds bitcoin-node, bitcoin-gui and test_bitcoin in a folder named libexec (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The release notes of 30.0 add that the new command makes an experimental interface for mining software available: when the node is started with bitcoin -m node -ipcbind=unix, it listens on a Unix socket for client connections (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

The option -m, also written --multiprocess, makes the command run the multiprocess binaries bitcoin-node and bitcoin-gui, instead of the monolithic binaries bitcoind and bitcoin-qt, which are the default behavior. The multiprocess documentation says the multiprocess binaries currently function the same as the monolithic ones except that they support an -ipcbind option, and that they should be started through the bitcoin command and not directly, because they may change or be renamed and are not installed in the path (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

A beginner can confuse the new command with the old name. The word bitcoin by itself starts no node; it needs a command such as node. The multiprocess mode is experimental and, in the words of the release notes, the option -m is currently required for the mining interface but will become optional (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The chapter's examples are written with the older names and are still valid for the monolithic binaries.

nodes.definition: The bitcoin command is a front door to the node and tools, and its -m option runs the multiprocess binaries instead of the monolithic ones.

io.code: {'node': 'bitcoind', 'rpc': 'bitcoin-cli -named', 'tx': 'bitcoin-tx'}['rpc']

nodes.label: Compilation
nodes.body: Compilation is the translation of source code into executable machine code by a program called a compiler. The CMake manual defines the neighbouring notion of the buildsystem as the description of how to build a project's executables and libraries from its source code (Kitware, 2026). In the chapter, the step is the one the reader starts by typing make, whose output is a long series of lines with the word CXX followed by names of the form bitcoind-bitcoind.o, one for each source file that is compiled (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: Compilation is the translation of source code into executable machine code by a program called a compiler. The CMake manual defines the neighbouring notion of the buildsystem as the description of how to build a project's executables and libraries from its source code (Kitware, 2026). In the chapter, the step is the one the reader starts by typing make, whose output is a long series of lines with the word CXX followed by names of the form bitcoind-bitcoind.o, one for each source file that is compiled (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The step takes a long time and a lot of memory because the program is large. The book says that the compilation can take up to an hour depending on the speed of the processor and the available memory, and the build notes of the project recommend at least 1.5 GB of memory, with advice on reducing the demand, because C++ compilers are memory-hungry (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Bitcoin Core, 2026). These facts matter to an operator who plans a build on a small computer and to a student who wonders why the step cannot be skipped.

The reader meets compilation after configuring the build. With the Autotools method the commands were make, then make check, then sudo make install; with CMake they are cmake --build build and cmake --install build, and the project's tests are run with ctest (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The unit tests, which the book asks the reader to run to ensure that the linked libraries are not broken in obvious ways, are run in the current tree with ctest, and the regression and integration tests of the project are written in Python (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

The work is spread over many small jobs. Each source file is compiled independently into an object file, and a final step links the object files and the libraries into an executable. For that reason the process can be interrupted and resumed, and the book notes that if an error occurs or the compilation is interrupted, it can be resumed any time by typing make again; on a computer with several processor cores the number of parallel jobs can be raised, as in make -j 2 or the option -j N of the CMake build command (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

A successful compilation shows that the program was built, not that it behaves correctly, which is why the book tells the reader to run the unit test suite before installing (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Installing needs administrative privileges in the book's example, because the default installation location is /usr/local/bin; the book mentions installing to the home directory as the alternative where the computer does not allow it (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

nodes.example: make and the lines that begin with CXX
nodes.definition: Compilation translates the source files into executable programs; it takes up to an hour, can be resumed, and is followed by the unit tests.
