nodes.label: Build prerequisite
nodes.body: A build prerequisite is a tool or library that must be installed on the computer before the program can be compiled. The book tells the reader to review the prerequisites, which it describes as the libraries that must be present on the system before the build can begin, in the first part of the build documentation, and adds that if they are missing the build process will fail with an error (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). A library, in this sense, is a collection of ready-made code that the program uses instead of containing it.

paras.text: A build prerequisite is a tool or library that must be installed on the computer before the program can be compiled. The book tells the reader to review the prerequisites, which it describes as the libraries that must be present on the system before the build can begin, in the first part of the build documentation, and adds that if they are missing the build process will fail with an error (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). A library, in this sense, is a collection of ready-made code that the program uses instead of containing it.

A large program is not written from nothing. Bitcoin Core relies on libraries for tasks such as storing the wallet in a database, drawing the graphical interface or sending messages to other programs, and each library has to be present in a version that fits. The documentation of dependencies exists so that a builder can see in advance what to install, and the book says that the build can be resumed from where it stopped after installing a missing prerequisite (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

In the current build notes, a table lists the required packages for each family of operating systems. For Debian and Ubuntu the required build dependencies are build-essential, cmake, python3 and libboost-dev; the packages for additional features are optional: libsqlite3-dev for the wallet, Cap'n Proto for interprocess communication, ZeroMQ for messaging, and the Qt packages with a QR-code library for the graphical client (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The book's equivalent concerns the Berkeley DB library for the wallet, which the wallet no longer uses.

Prerequisites are checked at configuration time. If a library is missing, the configuration command stops and says so; the user installs the library with the system's package manager and repeats the command. Optional features mean optional prerequisites: building without the wallet with -DENABLE_WALLET=OFF removes the need for SQLite, and building without the graphical interface, which is the default, removes the need for Qt (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

The prerequisites differ by platform and by release, so a list copied from a text about another system or version is likely to be wrong. The security perspective is that every library in the build is also part of the program that guards money, which is the reason the project documents the dependencies and offers a self-contained mechanism for building them, the depends system mentioned in its build notes (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

nodes.definition: The build prerequisites are the libraries and tools that must be present before compiling; a missing one makes configuration fail and can be installed afterwards.

io.code: (lambda req, wallet: (len(req.split()), len(wallet.split()), len((req + ' ' + wallet).split())))('build-essential cmake python3 libboost-dev', 'libsqlite3-dev')

nodes.label: Executable
nodes.body: An executable is a file that the operating system can run as a program. The book's installation step copies bitcoind, bitcoin-cli and bitcoin-tx into /usr/local/bin, and the command which asks the system for the path of an executable and confirms the installation (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The project's documentation describes the full set that a build installs: bitcoind as the node and wallet daemon, bitcoin-cli as the tool for making node and wallet calls, bitcoin-qt as the graphical node and wallet, bitcoin-tx for creating and modifying transactions, bitcoin-wallet as the wallet tool, bitcoin-util for miscellaneous utilities, and bitcoin as the command that calls the others (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

paras.text: An executable is a file that the operating system can run as a program. The book's installation step copies bitcoind, bitcoin-cli and bitcoin-tx into /usr/local/bin, and the command which asks the system for the path of an executable and confirms the installation (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The project's documentation describes the full set that a build installs: bitcoind as the node and wallet daemon, bitcoin-cli as the tool for making node and wallet calls, bitcoin-qt as the graphical node and wallet, bitcoin-tx for creating and modifying transactions, bitcoin-wallet as the wallet tool, bitcoin-util for miscellaneous utilities, and bitcoin as the command that calls the others (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

Each executable has a separate purpose, so that a user can run the part that is needed. A server needs the node without a graphical interface; an operator who sends commands uses the client; a developer who builds a transaction offline uses the transaction tool. The book chooses to build the daemon, the server version, because the chapter is about a node running in the background (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The project's plan for the multiprocess design is that node, wallet and interface code run in separate address spaces for better isolation (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

The release 31.1 archive that was downloaded and run for this chapter shows the layout: the folder bin holds bitcoin, bitcoin-cli, bitcoin-qt, bitcoin-tx, bitcoin-util, bitcoin-wallet and bitcoind, and the folder libexec holds bitcoin-gui, bitcoin-node and test_bitcoin (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The files of a source build depend on the options given: the italicized entries in the project's table, such as the library libbitcoinkernel and the benchmarking tool, are installed only when the relevant CMake options are enabled (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

Several executables share most of their code. The node and the wallet are in one program in the default, monolithic, arrangement, and the multiprocess binaries bitcoin-node and bitcoin-gui split the roles as the project moves toward separate processes (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The client bitcoin-cli does not contain the node: it connects to a running node over the network interface that the next branch of this chapter describes, and sends it commands.

The name of an executable is not an interface guarantee. Names and places have changed between versions: the unit-test program test_bitcoin was moved from the folder bin to libexec in release 30.0, and the project advises starting multiprocess binaries through the bitcoin command and not directly (Bitcoin Core, 2026). A script that relies on a path should therefore state the release for which it was written.

nodes.definition: The build produces several executables: bitcoind is the node, bitcoin-cli the command-line client, bitcoin-tx a transaction tool, and others for the wallet and the graphical interface.

nodes.label: Package manager
nodes.body: A package manager is the program of an operating system that installs, updates and removes software, together with the libraries each program needs, from a collection of packages. The build notes of Bitcoin Core say that the builder can either build from self-compiled dependencies or install the dependencies from the distribution's package manager (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The worked example takes the first column of the table of those notes, which names the system and its package manager, and finds the four package managers for which commands are given: apt for Debian and Ubuntu, dnf for Fedora, apk for Alpine and pacman for Arch.

paras.text: A package manager is the program of an operating system that installs, updates and removes software, together with the libraries each program needs, from a collection of packages. The build notes of Bitcoin Core say that the builder can either build from self-compiled dependencies or install the dependencies from the distribution's package manager (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The worked example takes the first column of the table of those notes, which names the system and its package manager, and finds the four package managers for which commands are given: apt for Debian and Ubuntu, dnf for Fedora, apk for Alpine and pacman for Arch.

Installing the prerequisites by hand would mean finding, downloading and compiling each library. A package manager does this with one command and resolves which other libraries are needed. The table of the build notes gives, for each system, the packages for the required build dependencies and then the optional ones for the wallet, the interprocess communication, the messaging and the graphical client, so that a builder chooses the columns that match the features wanted.

The first column of the table in the build notes is the package manager, and the second lists, for apt, the packages build-essential, cmake, python3 and libboost-dev (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The same word appears in the documentation of the reproducible builds, where the project says it achieves bootstrappability by using Guix as a functional package manager (Bitcoin Core, 2026). In that setting the package manager does not only install the tools but also builds them from source in a controlled way, so that the toolchain is reproducible.

A package manager keeps a list of packages with their versions and their dependencies, and installs a package by installing everything it depends on first. The packages are named differently on each system, which is why the build notes give a row for each: the library for the database of the wallet is libsqlite3-dev on Debian and sqlite-devel on Fedora. A package registry, as the ecosystem branch explains, plays a similar role for the libraries of a programming language.

A package manager trusts the collection it installs from. The software the builder obtains is the software the maintainers of the distribution packaged, in the version they chose. For a security-critical program like a node, the project therefore also offers a way to build the dependencies from source, called depends in its notes (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

nodes.example: four package managers in the build notes
nodes.definition: A package manager installs software and the libraries it depends on from a collection maintained for an operating system or a build.

nodes.label: Operation
nodes.body: Operation is the second large part of the chapter, and it is about what happens after the software has been built or downloaded: how a node is started, how it is configured, how its state is observed, and what kind of wallet comes with it. The book introduces it with the statement that the peer-to-peer network is composed of network nodes, run mostly by individuals and some of the businesses that provide Bitcoin services, and that those who run them have a direct and authoritative view of the blockchain, with a local copy of all the spendable bitcoins independently validated by their own system (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). A branch about operation therefore describes the daily practice of that independence.

paras.text: Operation is the second large part of the chapter, and it is about what happens after the software has been built or downloaded: how a node is started, how it is configured, how its state is observed, and what kind of wallet comes with it. The book introduces it with the statement that the peer-to-peer network is composed of network nodes, run mostly by individuals and some of the businesses that provide Bitcoin services, and that those who run them have a direct and authoritative view of the blockchain, with a local copy of all the spendable bitcoins independently validated by their own system (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). A branch about operation therefore describes the daily practice of that independence.

The branch matters because a node that is badly run gives little of what it promises. A node that is not given enough disk space cannot store the chain, a node whose cache is too small spends its time reading the disk, and a node whose settings nobody understands may expose services that were meant to stay private. The book lists the reasons for running a node in a short list: not relying on any third party to validate the transactions you receive, not disclosing to third parties which transactions belong to your wallet, having programmable access to the network and the blockchain, validating transactions according to the consensus rules in an application, and supporting the network (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Each of these reasons is only as good as the way the node is operated.

A reader meets operation in the configuration file that sits in the data directory, in the messages that the program prints when it starts, and in the answers of the status commands that the chapter calls just after starting the node. The evidence collected for this version comes from a real run of the release 31.1 as an offline node, whose start-up messages, data directory and answers are quoted in the concepts of this branch (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The book's own example is a node that holds the whole chain, keeps an index of all transactions on a very large disk and sends an e-mail when an alert is raised, together with a second example for a small server.

The branch has three groups. The configuration group explains the file and the options that shape the node: where the file and the data directory are found, how the database cache and the mempool limit divide the memory, what the transaction index is for, what blocks-only mode saves and how the alert command works. The running group explains how the node is started in the background, what it writes to its log when it starts, and how two status commands show where it stands in the chain and in the network. The wallet group explains the wallet that Bitcoin Core carries, the older kind that can no longer be created, and the descriptions of scripts on which the newer kind is built.

Two cautions apply to the whole branch. The first is that many of the book's figures belong to the release it printed: the default cache size, the wallet database and the first lines of the log differ in the current release, and the concepts of this branch give both values. The second is the warning in Bitcoin Core's own documentation, which tells users never to make configuration changes that they do not understand and to be wary of accepting any configuration changes provided to them by another source, even if they believe that they do understand them (Bitcoin Core, 2026). A copied configuration file is a set of instructions to a program that holds money-related data.

nodes.label: Configuration
nodes.body: Configuration is the group of concepts that describe how a user tells Bitcoin Core how to behave. The book says that the node looks for a configuration file in its data directory on every start, and that the program offers more than a hundred options that modify the behavior of the network node, the storage of the blockchain and many other aspects of its operation (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The group covers the file itself, the idea of an option and the order in which its sources are read, the directory that holds the data, and the options the book singles out as the most important.

paras.text: Configuration is the group of concepts that describe how a user tells Bitcoin Core how to behave. The book says that the node looks for a configuration file in its data directory on every start, and that the program offers more than a hundred options that modify the behavior of the network node, the storage of the blockchain and many other aspects of its operation (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The group covers the file itself, the idea of an option and the order in which its sources are read, the directory that holds the data, and the options the book singles out as the most important.

A node that runs on a default setting is usable, but the options are how it is adapted to the machine and to the purpose. The book's two sample files show the range: one is for a node that serves as the back end of a Bitcoin application and puts its data on a disk with a lot of room, the other is for a resource-constrained server and limits the cache, the mempool, the stored blocks and the traffic (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Knowing what each option does is what turns a copied example into a deliberate decision.

The options meet the reader in three forms: as lines of the configuration file, as parameters after the name of the program on the command line, and as entries in the help text, which the version 31.1 prints with 139 option entries, more than the hundred of the book (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The start-up messages of the node list the settings that it has actually read, so the log is the place where an option can be checked. The concepts that follow take the file, the option, the directory and then the individual settings.

The order of the concepts follows the order of the book. The file and its options come first because everything else is set there, followed by the data directory, the database cache, the transaction index, blocks-only mode, the mempool limit and the alert command. Four of them concern memory and disk, which are the resources the node consumes, one concerns bandwidth and one concerns a message to the owner. Each concept gives the book's value and the value that the current release shows.

nodes.label: Configuration file
nodes.body: The configuration file is a plain text file, named bitcoin.conf by default, in which the owner of a node writes the options that the program should use. Bitcoin Core's documentation describes its format: it consists of option=value entries, one per line, with the whitespace around them removed, an option is written without the leading hyphen that the command line needs, and a value is mandatory (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The book says that Bitcoin Core will look for a configuration file in its data directory on every start (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: The configuration file is a plain text file, named bitcoin.conf by default, in which the owner of a node writes the options that the program should use. Bitcoin Core's documentation describes its format: it consists of option=value entries, one per line, with the whitespace around them removed, an option is written without the leading hyphen that the command line needs, and a value is mandatory (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The book says that Bitcoin Core will look for a configuration file in its data directory on every start (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

A file is the practical way to keep a node's settings, because a node is meant to run for months and to restart after every power failure or update. The same options could be typed after the program name every time, but a file records them in one place that can be read, copied, compared and kept under control. It also keeps the settings out of the way of the start-up scripts that the book mentions in the end of the section, which only have to start the program (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The book shows how to find the file: run bitcoind -printtoconsole in a terminal and look at the first lines of the output, one of which begins with Config file followed by the path (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The log of the 31.1 release in the evidence shows the same line, together with one line for each setting that was read from the file, which is how the settings of that offline node (no connections, no seed lookup) were recorded (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The documentation lists the default places for the three common systems and says that the file is not created by the software and must be created by the user (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

The parser is simple. Blank lines are ignored, a comment starts with a number sign and runs to the end of the line, and a block with a name in square brackets, such as the one named main, holds options for one network only, which take precedence over options without a section (Bitcoin Core, 2026). An option can be negated with the prefix no, so that nofoo=1 turns off an option called foo, and a second file can be added with the option includeconf (Bitcoin Core, 2026). A small worked example splits the lines of a file at the first equals sign and gives a dictionary of option names and values, as the example shows for the data directory and the transaction index of the book's first sample.

Changes to the file take effect only after the node has been restarted, as the documentation states, so editing the file of a running node changes nothing until then (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The file is not a command language, and an option that the program does not know is not an error but shows up as a warning in the log, so a mistyped name can go unnoticed if nobody reads it. A last caution is that the file may hold secrets, for example the hashed credential of the interface, and should be readable only by the user who runs the node, which the init documentation also recommends for the file and the data directory (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

nodes.definition: Bitcoin Core reads bitcoin.conf from its data directory at every start; options can also be given on the command line, and bitcoind -printtoconsole shows where the file is looked for.

io.code: dict(l.split('=', 1) for l in 'datadir=/lotsofspace/bitcoin\ntxindex=1'.splitlines())

nodes.label: Configuration option
nodes.body: A configuration option is a named setting of the program, written in the book and in the help text with a leading hyphen, such as the setting that sets the size of the database cache. Most options take a value, some are switches that are off unless they are set, and almost all of them can be negated with the prefix no, which in general sets a boolean or numeric option to zero and a text option to an empty string, with some exceptions that the documentation names (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The book lists eight of them as the most important and says that Bitcoin Core offers more than 100 (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: A configuration option is a named setting of the program, written in the book and in the help text with a leading hyphen, such as the setting that sets the size of the database cache. Most options take a value, some are switches that are off unless they are set, and almost all of them can be negated with the prefix no, which in general sets a boolean or numeric option to zero and a text option to an empty string, with some exceptions that the documentation names (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The book lists eight of them as the most important and says that Bitcoin Core offers more than 100 (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The options are the program's interface for its owner, and the order in which their sources are read decides which value is used. The documentation states that all command-line options except the help, version and conf options may be specified in the configuration file, that all file options except the one that includes another file may also be given on the command line, and that command-line options override values set in the file (Bitcoin Core, 2026). A script that starts the node can therefore change one value for one run without editing the file.

A reader meets the options in the output of the help command of the program, which prints each option with its meaning and its default, such as the line for the database cache that gives a minimum of 4 and a default of 1024 in the current release (Bitcoin Core, 2026). They are also met in the log, where the start-up lines show whether a value came from the file or from the command line, and in the file named settings.json in the data directory, which holds values set at run time through the graphical client or the interface, and which the documentation ranks between the file and the command line (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

The precedence can be shown with two dictionaries. The file says 450 for the cache and 1 for the transaction index; the command line says 2048 for the cache. Merging the file's dictionary with the command line's, the second last, gives the cache of 2048 and keeps the index, which is what the example computes. Network-specific options add a second rule: an option in a section for one network, or prefixed with the network's name, takes precedence over the same option without it (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

The help text and the book must not be trusted blindly for the defaults, because defaults change from release to release: the book's value for the database cache is 450 and the current one is 1024 for machines with enough memory, and the minimum relay fee dropped in release 30.0 (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Bitcoin Core, 2026). Another common mistake is to put an option that is valid only on the command line, such as the one that names the file itself, into the file that it names, where it cannot work. A third is to forget that negation exists: a line written with the prefix no switches something off and is not a typing error.

nodes.example: dbcache on the command line and in the file
nodes.definition: An option has a name and a value and can come from the file, from the dynamic settings file or from the command line; the command line wins.

io.code: (lambda conf, cli: {**conf, **cli})({'dbcache': '450', 'txindex': '1'}, {'dbcache': '2048'})

nodes.label: Data directory
nodes.body: The data directory is the folder in which Bitcoin Core stores everything it has to remember between runs. The documentation describes it as the default location where the files of the program are stored, and gives the default place for each system: a folder named .bitcoin in the user's home directory on Linux, a folder called Bitcoin under Application Support on macOS, and a folder called Bitcoin under the local application data on Windows (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The book says the same for the .bitcoin folder, and that the option datadir selects the directory and filesystem in which to put all the blockchain data (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: The data directory is the folder in which Bitcoin Core stores everything it has to remember between runs. The documentation describes it as the default location where the files of the program are stored, and gives the default place for each system: a folder named .bitcoin in the user's home directory on Linux, a folder called Bitcoin under Application Support on macOS, and a folder called Bitcoin under the local application data on Windows (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The book says the same for the .bitcoin folder, and that the option datadir selects the directory and filesystem in which to put all the blockchain data (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The directory is the node's memory, so where it lives decides whether the node can run at all. The book says that, depending on the configuration, it can use from about 10 GB to almost 1 TB as of the writing, and that the maximum is expected to grow by several hundred gigabytes per year (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). For that reason the first sample file puts the directory on a separate disk with plenty of room, and a user who has a small system disk and a large second disk needs this option before the first start.

The evidence for this version shows what a young node keeps there. A freshly started release 31.1, with no peers, had in its directory a file for the banned addresses, the configuration file written for the run, the process identifier file, the folder of blocks, the folder of the unspent-output database called chainstate, the debug log, the folder of the wallet named demo, the fee estimates, the mempool dump, the peer address database and the settings file (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The documentation explains the others in the layout table: a LevelDB database holds the block index, the files blkNNNNN.dat hold the blocks in network format at 128 MiB per file, and the optional index folders appear when an index is switched on (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

All content of the directory except the configuration file is specific to one network. The main network uses the directory itself, and the others use subfolders: testnet3, testnet4, signet and regtest, as the lookup in the worked example shows for regtest (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The program keeps a lock file in the directory, writes its process identifier into a file while it runs and creates the cookie file there too, which is a reason why the access to the directory is a security matter.

A directory is not a place to copy files from one running node to another. The documentation warns that a wallet file must not be shared across different node instances, because that can result in key reuse and double spends, and that a backup of a wallet should be made with the backup call so that the file is locked while it is copied (Bitcoin Core, 2026). It also advises against the exFAT filesystem on macOS, because of reports of database corruption (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The cheapest mistake, however, is to fill the disk: a node that cannot write stops, and that is the reason to plan the space.

nodes.definition: The data directory is where Bitcoin Core keeps the blocks, the unspent-output database, the logs and the wallets; its default place depends on the system and its contents on the network.

nodes.label: Database cache (dbcache)
nodes.body: The database cache is a region of memory in which the node keeps part of the set of unspent outputs, so that it does not have to read the disk for every output it needs to check. The option that sizes it is called dbcache, and the book describes it as the size of the UTXO cache, with a default of 450 mebibytes, the advice being to increase it on high-end hardware to read and write the disk less often, or reduce it on low-end hardware to save memory at the expense of using the disk more frequently (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). A mebibyte is 1024 times 1024 bytes.

paras.text: The database cache is a region of memory in which the node keeps part of the set of unspent outputs, so that it does not have to read the disk for every output it needs to check. The option that sizes it is called dbcache, and the book describes it as the size of the UTXO cache, with a default of 450 mebibytes, the advice being to increase it on high-end hardware to read and write the disk less often, or reduce it on low-end hardware to save memory at the expense of using the disk more frequently (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). A mebibyte is 1024 times 1024 bytes.

The cache matters most while the node is catching up with the chain. The documentation on reducing memory says that a lower value makes the initial sync time much longer, and that after the first synchronization the effect is less pronounced for most uses, unless fast validation of blocks is important, such as for mining (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The same page warns that when the operating system starts swapping memory to disk continuously, the node can slow to a crawl, which is why a too-large value is also a mistake.

The current value differs from the book. Release 31.0 raised the default to 1024 MiB from 450 MiB on systems where at least 4096 MiB of RAM is detected, and the release notes say that to keep the previous behavior one sets dbcache to 450 (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The help of the release 31.1 states a minimum of 4 and a default of 1024, and the source shows the rule: the larger value is chosen only on a 64-bit system with the required memory, and the old 450 MiB remains the default in all other cases (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

The configured total is divided before it is used. The source gives the block index database up to 2 MiB, which is the smaller of that value and an eighth of the total, then the database of the chain state up to 8 MiB, which is the smaller of that value and half of what remains, and the rest goes to the cache of unspent outputs (Bitcoin Core, 2026). For 1024 MiB the worked example returns 2, 8 and 1014, which are the three numbers that the start-up log of the evidence prints for the block index, the chain state and the in-memory set of unspent outputs (Bitcoin Core, 2026). If the transaction index is on, ten percent of the total goes to it first.

The memory is shared with the mempool, which the log shows by saying that up to 286.1 MiB of unused mempool space can be added to the 1014 MiB, a figure that the mempool limit concept explains (Bitcoin Core, 2026). Setting the value larger than the memory that is really available is a mistake that containers make easy, because the detected RAM may exceed what the container may use, a case that the release notes mention, and the node may then run out of memory (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The node also logs a warning when it believes a value is too large for the detected memory.

nodes.definition: The dbcache option sizes the cache of the unspent-output set: 450 MiB by default in the book, 1024 MiB by default from Bitcoin Core 31.0 on machines with enough memory.

nodes.label: Transaction index (txindex)
nodes.body: The transaction index is an optional database that lets the node find any confirmed transaction by its identifier. The book explains that by default Bitcoin Core builds a database containing only the transactions related to the user's wallet, and that to access any transaction with commands like getrawtransaction one has to configure the node to build a complete index with the option txindex set to 1 (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The help of the release 31.1 describes it as a full transaction index used by the getrawtransaction call, off by default (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

paras.text: The transaction index is an optional database that lets the node find any confirmed transaction by its identifier. The book explains that by default Bitcoin Core builds a database containing only the transactions related to the user's wallet, and that to access any transaction with commands like getrawtransaction one has to configure the node to build a complete index with the option txindex set to 1 (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The help of the release 31.1 describes it as a full transaction index used by the getrawtransaction call, off by default (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

Without the index the node still has the whole chain, but it has no quick way from a transaction identifier to the block that holds it. The question matters to programs that look up arbitrary transactions, such as an explorer or the application back end of the book's first sample file. The book adds that if the option is not set at first and later set, one has to wait for the index to be rebuilt, and that the lookup works provided the block containing the transaction has not been pruned (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The index is met in the section that follows, where the book decodes Alice's transaction by asking for it by its identifier, and in the data directory, where the documentation says that it lives in a LevelDB database in a folder named indexes/txindex and exists only if the option is on (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Bitcoin Core, 2026). It is also met in the way the cache is split: when the index is enabled the source gives it ten percent of the total cache, up to one gibibyte, before the remainder goes to the set of unspent outputs; for 1024 MiB that is 102.4 MiB, as the example calculates (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

The source of the index describes it as written to a LevelDB database that records the block sequence number and the serialized block offset of each transaction by transaction hash (Bitcoin Core, 2026). A call such as getrawtransaction with an identifier looks the identifier up in the index, reads the block from the disk and returns the transaction. Building the first index means going through all the blocks, which explains the waiting time of the book. The index does not store the transactions again; it only stores where to find them, so its size is far smaller than the blocks themselves.

The index cannot be combined with pruning. The help text of the pruning option says the mode is incompatible with the transaction index, and the run of release 31.1 in the evidence confirms it: starting with both ends with the error that prune mode is incompatible with txindex (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The help of the current release is more exact than the book about what happens without the index: by default the call for a raw transaction returns a transaction only if it is in the mempool, and if the caller names a block, it returns the transaction when the block is available and contains it (Bitcoin Core, 2026). So a node without the index can still answer if it is told in which block to look, but not otherwise. Finally, the index is a convenience for the owner, and it is not part of the consensus rules.

nodes.definition: The txindex option builds an index of every transaction so that getrawtransaction can find any of them; it cannot be combined with pruning.

nodes.label: Blocks-only mode
nodes.body: Blocks-only mode is a setting in which the node does not take part in the relay of unconfirmed transactions. The book describes the option as a way to minimize bandwidth usage by only accepting blocks of confirmed transactions from the peers instead of relaying unconfirmed transactions (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The help text of release 31.1 is more exact: it rejects transactions from network peers, switches off the automatic broadcast and rebroadcast of transactions, unless the source peer has the forcerelay permission, and leaves transactions sent through the RPC interface unaffected (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

paras.text: Blocks-only mode is a setting in which the node does not take part in the relay of unconfirmed transactions. The book describes the option as a way to minimize bandwidth usage by only accepting blocks of confirmed transactions from the peers instead of relaying unconfirmed transactions (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The help text of release 31.1 is more exact: it rejects transactions from network peers, switches off the automatic broadcast and rebroadcast of transactions, unless the source peer has the forcerelay permission, and leaves transactions sent through the RPC interface unaffected (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

The mode exists because relaying every transaction is the largest continuing cost of a node after the first download. A node in this mode still downloads and validates every block, so it enforces the same rules and remains a full node, but it receives each transaction only once, inside a block, and it holds no pool of unconfirmed transactions. The documentation on reducing memory says that the mode reduces the default memory use of the mempool to 5 MB, and that the source defines the blocks-only default as 5, against 300 for a normal node (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

The book uses the option in its second sample file, together with pruning and small caches, for a node on a resource-constrained server (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). It is also useful where the owner pays for each gigabyte of upload, and the book recommends against running a node on a metered connection or running it in a way that constrains its bandwidth (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The documentation on reducing memory names it among the ways to use less memory (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

In normal operation a node announces and requests unconfirmed transactions from its peers and keeps them in its mempool, from where it can tell a miner or a wallet about them. In blocks-only mode it skips the request, so the mempool stays nearly empty, and the node learns of a payment only when the payment is confirmed in a block. The worked example divides the normal default of 300 megabytes by the blocks-only default of 5, which shows that the pool of a blocks-only node may be sixty times smaller.

The mode has a privacy cost that the documentation spells out: it must not be used when the node is also used to broadcast transactions, because any transaction sent will stick out like a sore thumb, and when it is combined with the wallet, the wallet should be told not to broadcast and not to spend unconfirmed change, and another mechanism for broadcasting should be used (Bitcoin Core, 2026). Because such a node does not receive transactions that are not yet in a block, a merchant who wants to see a payment before its confirmation cannot rely on it.

nodes.definition: In blocks-only mode a node accepts blocks from its peers but not unconfirmed transactions, which saves bandwidth and memory.

nodes.label: Mempool limit (maxmempool)
nodes.body: The mempool limit is the maximum size of the pool of unconfirmed transactions that the node holds, set by the option maxmempool. The book describes it as limiting the transaction memory pool to this many megabytes, and says to use it to reduce memory use on memory-constrained nodes; its second sample file sets it to 150 (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The help text of release 31.1 gives the default as 300 megabytes, and the documentation on reducing memory says the unit is the megabyte of 1000 bytes, not the mebibyte, and that the minimum is 5 (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

paras.text: The mempool limit is the maximum size of the pool of unconfirmed transactions that the node holds, set by the option maxmempool. The book describes it as limiting the transaction memory pool to this many megabytes, and says to use it to reduce memory use on memory-constrained nodes; its second sample file sets it to 150 (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The help text of release 31.1 gives the default as 300 megabytes, and the documentation on reducing memory says the unit is the megabyte of 1000 bytes, not the mebibyte, and that the minimum is 5 (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

A pool that has no limit would let any sender fill the memory of every node with unconfirmed transactions. The limit forces the node to decide which transactions to keep, and the documentation says that a lower maximum means that transactions will be evicted sooner, which affects any use of the node that processes unconfirmed transactions (Bitcoin Core, 2026). Chapter 2 explained that a transaction waits in the mempool until it is mined; this is the bound on how long and how many can wait.

A reader meets the figure in the start-up log. For the default of 300 megabytes, the log of the release 31.1 in the evidence says that the in-memory set of unspent outputs has 1014.0 MiB, plus up to 286.1 MiB of unused mempool space (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The source explains why: the limit in bytes is the number of megabytes times 1,000,000, and the unused part is lent to the cache of unspent outputs, so that the memory the node uses in total stays near the sum of the two settings (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

The conversion explains the odd-looking figure: 300 megabytes is 300 times 10 to the sixth bytes, and dividing by 2 to the twentieth bytes per mebibyte gives 286.1 mebibytes, as the worked example computes. The mempool and the cache therefore draw on one memory budget, which is why the documentation recommends limiting the mempool when trying to reduce the total memory use, and why the blocks-only mode, which needs only 5 MB, leaves more for the cache (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

The unit is the usual mistake: a number of megabytes of 1000 bytes is smaller than the same number of mebibytes, and the two options that look alike, the mempool limit and the database cache, use different units. A node with a small mempool also forgets low-fee transactions sooner, so a wallet that depends on the node may see its payment dropped from that node's pool while other nodes still hold it. Bitcoin Core also expires transactions after a number of hours, an option that the help lists, so the limit is not the only bound.

nodes.definition: The maxmempool option limits the memory used for unconfirmed transactions; the default is 300 megabytes, and unused mempool memory is lent to the database cache.

nodes.label: Alert notification (alertnotify)
nodes.body: The alert notification is a hook that lets a node tell its owner that something is wrong. The book describes the option as running a specified command or script to send emergency alerts to the owner of the node, and both its sample files set it to a script that sends an e-mail with the text Alert followed by the message (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The help text says that the command is executed when an alert is raised and that the symbol %s in the command is replaced by the message (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

paras.text: The alert notification is a hook that lets a node tell its owner that something is wrong. The book describes the option as running a specified command or script to send emergency alerts to the owner of the node, and both its sample files set it to a script that sends an e-mail with the text Alert followed by the message (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The help text says that the command is executed when an alert is raised and that the symbol %s in the command is replaced by the message (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

A node runs without anybody watching it, and some events need a person. Bitcoin Core's source shows two situations in which the node raises such a warning: when it finds an invalid chain with more work than its own best chain by more than six blocks of work, which could be due to database corruption or to consensus incompatibility with the peers, and when blocks signal new rules that this version of the software does not know, with the message that unknown new rules were activated and the number of the version bit (Bitcoin Core, 2026). Both are signs that the owner's software may be out of step with the network, a case that the soft fork concept explains.

The reader meets the option in the book's two sample files and in the help text. In practice it is a line that points to a script, which may send an e-mail, a message to a phone or an entry in a monitoring system. Since the script is the owner's, the node gives no idea of what is done with the message, and it does not wait for it: the source starts the command in a thread that runs free, so a slow script cannot hold up the node (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

When a warning is set, the node calls a function that reads the command from the option, takes the warning text, strips every character that is not a letter, a digit, a blank or one of the characters in the string .,;-_/:?@(), puts single quotes around the result and replaces each %s in the command with it (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The worked example copies these steps for a hostile message that tries to close the quote and add a command: the quote itself is removed, so the text stays inside one quoted word and the final command line is harmless. The rules of the shell for single quotes are the reason the technique works.

The cleaning protects against the message but not against the owner's own script. A script that passes its argument on without quoting it can still be abused, and the %s must be inside the quotes of the command, as the book's sample does. The option also depends on the system providing a command interpreter, since the source compiles the function only if the system has one, and on the script being executable by the user who runs the node (Bitcoin Core, 2026). Finally, the command runs only when a warning is newly set, because the source calls it only if the warning was not already present, so a script that sends e-mail should not be the only way to learn that the node is in trouble.

nodes.definition: The alertnotify option runs a command of the owner's choice when the node raises an alert, replacing %s with the message, which the node first cleans and puts in single quotes.

nodes.label: Running
nodes.body: Running is the group of concepts that describe a node while it is alive: how it is started so that it keeps going without a person, what it writes while it starts, and how its owner asks two short questions about its state. The book moves from the configuration to this stage with a test: the node is started in the foreground with the option that sends the log to the console, the owner reads the lines to see whether the right settings are loaded, and interrupts the program once satisfied. Then the node is run in the background as a process and queried with the command line client (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: Running is the group of concepts that describe a node while it is alive: how it is started so that it keeps going without a person, what it writes while it starts, and how its owner asks two short questions about its state. The book moves from the configuration to this stage with a test: the node is started in the foreground with the option that sends the log to the console, the owner reads the lines to see whether the right settings are loaded, and interrupts the program once satisfied. Then the node is run in the background as a process and queried with the command line client (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

A node is only useful when it runs continuously. The book ends the section with the advice to add Bitcoin Core to the start-up scripts of the operating system, so that it runs all the time and restarts when the operating system restarts, and it points to the examples in the folder contrib/init of the source (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The two status commands that follow tell the owner whether the node is synchronized with the chain and how it stands in the network, which are the two things that decide whether its answers can be relied on.

The reader meets this group the first time the program is started. The log printed to the console is the first thing seen, the data directory gains the log file and the files that mark a running process, and the owner types the first command to learn the state of the chain. The evidence of this version contains the real log of the release 31.1, the answers of its two status commands, and the directory it created, all from an offline node, which is a node that was told not to look for peers (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

Running works by separating the program from the terminal that started it. In the foreground the node writes its log to the console and dies with the shell, which is what makes the foreground useful for the one purpose the chapter puts it to - reading the first lines to confirm that the intended settings were loaded. As a daemon the program detaches from the terminal, keeps a file recording which process it is so that a second copy cannot be started by accident over the same data directory, and writes its log to a file instead of the screen. From then on the owner does not watch the node but questions it, and the two status questions of this section are the standard pair: one asks about the chain the node has verified, the other about the node's own position in the network. Together they answer the only question that matters before relying on any further answer, which is whether this node is actually caught up and connected (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The caution is that a node which is running is not necessarily a node which is ready. A freshly started node answers every question immediately and some of its answers are about a chain it has not finished verifying, which is precisely the state the book prints and the state this chapter's own evidence was captured in. The two status answers are what distinguish the cases, and a learner who skips them can take a confident answer from a node that has seen a fraction of the chain. The second caution is operational: adding the program to the system's start-up scripts, which the book recommends, makes the node survive a reboot but also means that a misconfiguration now restarts forever, so the foreground test earns its place (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

nodes.label: Daemon
nodes.body: A daemon is a program that runs in the background of the operating system, without a terminal and without a person typing to it, and waits for work. The installed-files table of Bitcoin Core describes the program bitcoind as the Bitcoin node and wallet daemon, and the book tells the reader how to make it one: to run Bitcoin Core in the background as a process, start it with the daemon option, as bitcoind -daemon (Bitcoin Core, 2026) (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The help of release 31.1 adds a second option, which makes the program wait for the initialization to be finished before it returns, and implies the first (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

paras.text: A daemon is a program that runs in the background of the operating system, without a terminal and without a person typing to it, and waits for work. The installed-files table of Bitcoin Core describes the program bitcoind as the Bitcoin node and wallet daemon, and the book tells the reader how to make it one: to run Bitcoin Core in the background as a process, start it with the daemon option, as bitcoind -daemon (Bitcoin Core, 2026) (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The help of release 31.1 adds a second option, which makes the program wait for the initialization to be finished before it returns, and implies the first (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

The daemon form exists because a node has to run for months, through the closing of terminals and the restarting of machines. A program that is attached to a terminal ends when the terminal ends. For this reason the book advises to add the node to the startup scripts of the operating system, and the documentation of the project says that running the program as a daemon does not need any manual configuration, because it creates its own credential for the interface when it starts (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

The project ships sample scripts and configuration files for systemd, Upstart, OpenRC, a SysV-style script for CentOS and a launch agent for macOS, all in the folder contrib/init, and the init documentation explains how to install each one: for systemd, copy the file to the services folder, reload the configuration, and start and enable the service with the systemctl command (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The data directory of a running node holds a file with its process identifier, which the evidence shows as a file called bitcoind.pid, created at start and deleted at shutdown (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

The systemd unit is a good example of what such a script does. Its start command calls bitcoind with the options for the process identifier file, the configuration file, the data directory, and two commands to run at start-up and before the shutdown, which tell systemd that the node is ready or that it is stopping; the unit does not pass the daemon option, because systemd itself keeps the program in the background (Bitcoin Core, 2026). It declares that the service sends notifications, asks that it be restarted on failure, allows ten minutes for stopping, and runs it as the user bitcoin with several restrictions of the system such as no new privileges and no access to the home directories of other users (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

The sample scripts assume paths that may have to be adjusted, such as /usr/bin/bitcoind, /etc/bitcoin/bitcoin.conf and /var/lib/bitcoind, and a user and group called bitcoin that must be created before use (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The init documentation also says that datadir cannot be overridden in the configuration file with the init files as they are, because the command-line options in those files take precedence, and the comment at the top of the unit file says the same of every option named in its start command (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The operating system keeping a program alive does not mean it is healthy: a node that was restarted a hundred times because of a bad setting is still a node with a bad setting, and its log is where to look.

nodes.definition: A daemon is a program that runs in the background; bitcoind -daemon detaches from the terminal, and init scripts such as the systemd unit start it at boot and restart it after a failure.

nodes.label: Start-up log
nodes.body: The start-up log is the stream of messages that the node writes while it starts, and afterwards as it runs. With the option that sends the log to the console it appears in the terminal, and otherwise it goes to a file called debug.log in the data directory, as the documentation of the data directory states (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The book prints the first lines of such a log twice, once to show where the configuration file is and once to show that the chosen settings are loaded, and it advises to interrupt the process once satisfied that the node is loading the correct settings and running as expected (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: The start-up log is the stream of messages that the node writes while it starts, and afterwards as it runs. With the option that sends the log to the console it appears in the terminal, and otherwise it goes to a file called debug.log in the data directory, as the documentation of the data directory states (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The book prints the first lines of such a log twice, once to show where the configuration file is and once to show that the chosen settings are loaded, and it advises to interrupt the process once satisfied that the node is loading the correct settings and running as expected (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

Reading the log is how an owner checks what the node is really doing. The documentation of the configuration file says that the values in use can be seen in the log and that options in the file that the program does not recognize appear there as warnings, so a mistyped option is visible only to someone who reads it (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The log also records the environment the node found: the machine instructions used for hashing, the sources of randomness, the limits on connections and the memory it assigned to each cache.

The evidence for this version holds the log of a real start of the release 31.1. It begins with the version, then lines about parameter interaction, since switching off listening switched off several related features, then the warning that the log may contain privacy-sensitive information and should be shared with care, and the choice of the implementation of the SHA-256 hash function that the processor supports (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The same pages show the data directory and the configuration file in use, one line for each setting read from the file, the limit of 125 automatic connections, and the opening of the interface on the local address 127.0.0.1, port 8332 (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

Several lines can be compared with the book's log of release 24.0.1. In the book the wallet check prints that BerkeleyDB version 4.8.30 is used, and in release 31.1 it prints that SQLite version 3.50.4 is used, which agrees with the removal of the older wallet format. The book prints that four threads were started for the interface, and the current log says that the server was started with 16 worker threads, the default of the option that sets that number, as the worked example reads from the log (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The authentication line is the same in both: the node generates a random cookie, which the interface concept explains. The log then lists the cache configuration, whose figures the database cache concept explains.

The log is not a stable interface: the wording and the order of lines change from release to release, and a program that parses them breaks. It is also sensitive: the node itself warns that the log may hold privacy-sensitive information, so an owner who pastes a log into a public forum to ask for help should read it first. A last caution is about size: the help of the release has an option that shrinks the file at start-up, which is on by default when no debugging categories are selected, so an owner who wants a long history has to keep copies of the file himself.

nodes.definition: While it starts, the node prints a log of what it is setting up: its version, the settings read, the connection limits, the interface it opens, the wallet database and the cache sizes.

nodes.label: Blockchain information (getblockchaininfo)
nodes.body: Blockchain information is the answer that the node gives to the call getblockchaininfo, the book's first example of monitoring a node: start it in daemon mode and then use the command bitcoin-cli getblockchaininfo to watch its progress and its status (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The answer is a JSON object. Its fields, as the source of the release describes them, include the name of the network, the height of the chain of most work that has been fully validated, the number of block headers the node has validated, the hash of the best block, the difficulty target, the median block time, an estimate of the progress of verification and the total work of the chain (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

paras.text: Blockchain information is the answer that the node gives to the call getblockchaininfo, the book's first example of monitoring a node: start it in daemon mode and then use the command bitcoin-cli getblockchaininfo to watch its progress and its status (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The answer is a JSON object. Its fields, as the source of the release describes them, include the name of the network, the height of the chain of most work that has been fully validated, the number of block headers the node has validated, the hash of the best block, the difficulty target, the median block time, an estimate of the progress of verification and the total work of the chain (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

The answer is the quickest way to learn whether a node can be trusted for a given purpose. A node whose blocks are far fewer than its headers is still downloading and validating, and the field that tells whether it is in the initial block download says so directly. The book explains what its own printout shows: a blockchain height of 0 blocks and 83,999 headers, because the node first fetches the block headers from its peers to find the blockchain with the most proof of work and then goes on to download the full blocks, validating them as it goes (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The reader meets the call as soon as the node runs. The printout of the book comes from a node that had just started its synchronization, and the evidence file of this version comes from the release 31.1 offline node that had only the first block, so its answer is also the beginning of the chain: the chain is the main network, there are 0 blocks and 0 headers, the best block hash is that of the first block ever mined, and the node reports that it is still in the initial download and is not pruned (Bitcoin Core, 2026). Two fields that the book's printout lacks, the compact target in the field bits and the full target, have been added to the current answer.

Some fields deserve a closer reading. The field with the work of the chain, written in hexadecimal, shows 100010001 at its end for the first block, as in the book's printout, which the chain work concept derives from the target. The median time of the first block equals its own time, since there are no earlier blocks, a point the median time concept explains. The size on disk was 89,087 in the book's printout and 293 in the evidence, because the node of the evidence has one block. And the field for warnings is an empty array, where the book's printout shows an empty string: release 28.0 made it an array of strings listing all active warnings, and the old behavior can be restored with a deprecated-option setting (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

The numbers are a snapshot, and a node that is receiving blocks changes them every few minutes. A height equal to the headers does not by itself prove that the node is caught up with the network, since both come from the node's peers, and the verification progress is an estimate between zero and one, not a measure. The field that says that the node is in the initial block download is described by the source as debug information and as an estimate. An owner who needs certainty compares the best block hash with a block explorer or with a second node.

nodes.label: Network information (getnetworkinfo)
nodes.body: Network information is the answer to the call getnetworkinfo, one of the commands that the book lists beside the call for the chain, the mempool and the wallet when it says how to get information on the status of the node (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Where the blockchain information describes the chain, this answer describes the node itself as a participant in the network: the version of the software, the version of the protocol, the services it offers to its peers, whether it relays transactions, how many connections it has and over which networks it can be reached (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

paras.text: Network information is the answer to the call getnetworkinfo, one of the commands that the book lists beside the call for the chain, the mempool and the wallet when it says how to get information on the status of the node (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Where the blockchain information describes the chain, this answer describes the node itself as a participant in the network: the version of the software, the version of the protocol, the services it offers to its peers, whether it relays transactions, how many connections it has and over which networks it can be reached (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

The answer tells the owner what the rest of the network sees. A node that offers fewer services than expected, or that has no connections, or that reports a network as not reachable, is not doing what its owner thinks. It also shows the settings that decide which transactions the node accepts, the minimum relay fee and the incremental fee, given in bitcoins per thousand virtual bytes, which is why the figure of 0.00001000 in the book's printout means one satoshi per virtual byte, and the figure of 0.000001 in the evidence means 0.1 satoshis per virtual byte, the value that the release notes of 30.0 give for the new default (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

The evidence file is from the offline node of release 31.1. It shows the version as 310100, the user-agent string as /Satoshi:31.1.0/, the protocol version as 70016, the local services as the hexadecimal number 0c09, which the list of names expands to network, witness, limited network and the new encrypted transport, no connections at all, and the two networks that are reachable, the internet protocols version 4 and version 6, while the privacy networks Tor, I2P and CJDNS are shown as limited and not reachable (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

The version number encodes three numbers: the source defines the client version as 10000 times the major number plus 100 times the minor number plus the build number, so release 31.1.0 is 310100 and the book's release 24.0.1 is 240001, and the user-agent string is built by writing the three numbers between the name Satoshi and slashes, following the specification in BIP 14 (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The services are a bit field: network is bit 0, which means value 1, witness is bit 3, value 8, limited network is bit 10, value 1024, and the encrypted transport of BIP 324 is bit 11, value 2048; their sum is 3081, or 0xc09 in hexadecimal, as the worked example reconstructs; the book's printout, from a node without the new transport, shows 0x409, the sum of the first three (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

Service bits are unauthenticated advertisements, as the source itself says, so a peer that claims a service may not provide it, and the code must be robust against that (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The protocol version of the evidence, 70016, is not the constant in the newest source tree, which is 70017, because the tree is newer than the release, so two figures from different dates should not be compared as if they were errors. A last caution is the name of the user agent: it says Satoshi for historical reasons and is not a claim about who runs the node.

nodes.label: Wallet
nodes.body: The wallet group collects the concepts about the wallet that comes with Bitcoin Core. Chapter 1 introduced the wallet as the application with which a user holds and spends bitcoin, and the book says here that the reference implementation includes wallets next to the validation engine and the tools for block construction (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). In this software the wallet is optional: the build can leave it out, as the book's option to disable the reference wallet implementation shows, and a node can run without one (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: The wallet group collects the concepts about the wallet that comes with Bitcoin Core. Chapter 1 introduced the wallet as the application with which a user holds and spends bitcoin, and the book says here that the reference implementation includes wallets next to the validation engine and the tools for block construction (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). In this software the wallet is optional: the build can leave it out, as the book's option to disable the reference wallet implementation shows, and a node can run without one (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The wallet is where a node meets money. Everything else in the node concerns the shared record, whereas the wallet concerns the outputs that belong to its owner and the keys that spend them. Its storage format therefore matters to users more than most settings: a format that is retired makes old files unusable until they are converted. The concepts in this group give the current format, the retired one and the language of descriptions that the current one is built on.

The reader meets the wallet in the log, which names the wallet directory and the database in use, in the data directory, where each named wallet has a folder, and in the calls that create and inspect it. The evidence of this version creates a wallet named demo on the real release 31.1 and asks for its information and its descriptions, and it tries to create a retired kind of wallet, which the release refuses with an error (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The documentation of the project adds that since version 0.21 Bitcoin Core no longer has a default wallet, so one is created on request (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

The three concepts follow the story of the format. The legacy wallet was the first kind, kept in a Berkeley DB file and described with keys alone. The descriptor wallet replaced it and is the only kind that can be created in the current release. The output descriptor is the language in which the descriptor wallet writes down which scripts belong to it, and in which the node answers when a transaction is decoded, as the later concept on decoding shows.

Two cautions apply. The first is that this chapter gives only what the node needs in order to run; the book treats keys and wallets in its later chapters. The second is that the file of a wallet holds what is needed to spend the owner's funds, and Bitcoin Core's documentation points out that the file is not encrypted by default and that it must be backed up with the call provided for it, not by copying the file of a running node (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

nodes.label: Descriptor wallet
nodes.body: A descriptor wallet is a wallet whose content is a set of output descriptions, each stating one family of scripts that the wallet can receive to and spend from. Bitcoin Core's documentation says that its code internally stores and operates on descriptors to reason about the sets of outputs that belong to the wallet (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The data are held in a file called wallet.dat that is a SQLite database, which the file documentation describes as a personal wallet with keys and transactions, and SQLite is a self-contained database engine that needs no server process and keeps a whole database in a single disk file (Bitcoin Core, 2026) (SQLite, 2026).

paras.text: A descriptor wallet is a wallet whose content is a set of output descriptions, each stating one family of scripts that the wallet can receive to and spend from. Bitcoin Core's documentation says that its code internally stores and operates on descriptors to reason about the sets of outputs that belong to the wallet (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The data are held in a file called wallet.dat that is a SQLite database, which the file documentation describes as a personal wallet with keys and transactions, and SQLite is a self-contained database engine that needs no server process and keeps a whole database in a single disk file (Bitcoin Core, 2026) (SQLite, 2026).

The descriptor wallet is the only kind that a current node can create. The release notes of 30.0 state that legacy wallets can no longer be created or loaded, and the run of release 31.1 in the evidence shows the consequence: asking for a wallet of the older kind fails with error code -4 and the message that the descriptors argument must be set to true because it is no longer possible to create a legacy wallet (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The change makes the wallet's behavior follow from descriptions that can be read, exported and checked, and no longer from a hidden list of keys.

In the evidence the call that creates a wallet named demo returns that name, and the call for the wallet's information returns the format sqlite, the value true for descriptors, 4000 for the number of keys in the pool of external keys and 4000 for the pool of internal ones, the value true for private keys enabled, and the flags that say a descriptor wallet is in use (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The log of the same release names the wallet directory and the version of SQLite, where the book's log of release 24.0.1 names Berkeley DB 4.8.30 (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

The list of descriptions of the demo wallet has eight entries: four kinds of script, the old pay-to-key-hash, the script-hash form that wraps a witness key hash, the witness key hash itself and the taproot form, and for each kind one entry for receiving and one for change, called internal. Each entry covers the range from 0 to 999 and is active. One thousand scripts in each of four kinds is the 4000 of the key pool for receiving, and the same count holds for change (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The wallet can therefore hand out addresses of any of the modern types.

The wallet file is not encrypted by default, and encrypting it needs a passphrase that cannot be recovered; the documentation warns that a lost passphrase loses the coins (Bitcoin Core, 2026). A copy or a backup should be taken with the backup call, not by copying a file that the running node is writing, and a wallet file must not be shared by two node instances (Bitcoin Core, 2026). Finally, a wallet made for the older format is not lost: it can be migrated to this one, as the concept of the legacy wallet explains.

nodes.definition: The current default wallet is a descriptor wallet stored in SQLite; legacy BerkeleyDB wallets can no longer be created or loaded and can only be migrated.

nodes.label: Legacy wallet
nodes.body: A legacy wallet is the kind of wallet that Bitcoin Core used before descriptors: a Berkeley DB database file holding the keys of the owner and the transactions that concern them. The file documentation still lists its parts under legacy files, a wallet.dat that is a Berkeley DB database, a folder with the logging files of the database, an error file called db.log and a lock file (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The book's log of release 24.0.1 shows the kind in use, with the line that BerkeleyDB version 4.8.30 is used, and the book's build options include one for building a wallet with an incompatible version of the Berkeley DB library (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: A legacy wallet is the kind of wallet that Bitcoin Core used before descriptors: a Berkeley DB database file holding the keys of the owner and the transactions that concern them. The file documentation still lists its parts under legacy files, a wallet.dat that is a Berkeley DB database, a folder with the logging files of the database, an error file called db.log and a lock file (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The book's log of release 24.0.1 shows the kind in use, with the line that BerkeleyDB version 4.8.30 is used, and the book's build options include one for building a wallet with an incompatible version of the Berkeley DB library (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The concept matters for two reasons. The first is historical: most of the books, articles and old backups that a learner will meet describe this wallet, with calls such as the ones for dumping or importing a private key. The second is practical: the release notes of 30.0 state that such wallets can no longer be created or loaded, and that they can be migrated to the descriptor format with the migratewallet call (Bitcoin Core, 2026). A user who owns an old file has to migrate it, because the node will not open it as it is.

The evidence shows the refusal. On the real release 31.1, a call to create a wallet with the descriptors argument set to false returns an error with code -4, and the text of the message says that the descriptors argument must be set to true because it is no longer possible to create a legacy wallet (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The worked example reads the code from that saved output. The same release notes list the legacy-only calls that were removed, among them the ones to add a multisignature address, to dump a private key, to dump or import a wallet, and to upgrade a wallet (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

The reason for the change lies in what a wallet must know. A legacy wallet stored keys and had to guess which scripts the keys might be used in, whereas a descriptor wallet stores the descriptions themselves, so a program that reads the wallet knows exactly which outputs are meant. Migration converts the old content into descriptions, and the release notes say that the wallet tool of the project lost the options that selected the older internal database and the legacy format (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

A learner should not treat a command from an older text as current, because commands that the book's era used for the legacy wallet may no longer exist: the release notes name eleven of them as removed (Bitcoin Core, 2026). A migration is a change to something that holds money, so a backup should be made before it, and a migration is not reversible by the node. Hardware or software that still expects a legacy file must be updated as well.

nodes.definition: The legacy wallet was stored in a Berkeley DB file and described by its keys; since Bitcoin Core 30.0 it can no longer be created or loaded, only migrated.
