nodes.label: Output descriptor
nodes.body: An output descriptor is a short piece of text in a simple language that describes a collection of output scripts. Bitcoin Core's documentation introduces it in exactly these words, and says that the wallet code uses descriptors internally to reason about the outputs that belong to the wallet (Bitcoin Core, 2026). A descriptor names the kind of script by a function, such as one for a pay-to-witness-public-key-hash script, one for a multisignature script, one for any type of address and one for raw hexadecimal script, and puts the keys inside it, as in the documented example of a witness key hash with a given public key (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

paras.text: An output descriptor is a short piece of text in a simple language that describes a collection of output scripts. Bitcoin Core's documentation introduces it in exactly these words, and says that the wallet code uses descriptors internally to reason about the outputs that belong to the wallet (Bitcoin Core, 2026). A descriptor names the kind of script by a function, such as one for a pay-to-witness-public-key-hash script, one for a multisignature script, one for any type of address and one for raw hexadecimal script, and puts the keys inside it, as in the documented example of a witness key hash with a given public key (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

Before descriptors, a wallet's backup contained keys and left the reader to guess which scripts they had been used for, and software of different makers could not agree on what a wallet contains. A descriptor states it completely, in a form that can be copied, printed and checked. The standard that defines the general syntax is BIP 380, and further BIPs define the individual expressions, which is why a descriptor written for one program can be read by another (Bitcoin Core, 2026) (Wuille and Chow, 2021).

The reader meets descriptors in several places. The call that decodes a transaction shows one for every output: in Alice's transaction, the second output is described as an address expression with the checksum qq404gts, and the first, which pays to a taproot output, as a raw taproot expression with the checksum 38d6v6ev (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The call to list the descriptors of the demo wallet returns eight descriptors, and the call that explains a descriptor, getdescriptorinfo, returns its checksum and says whether it can be solved and whether it has private keys, which for the documented witness key hash example are the checksum 8zl0zxma, the value true and the value false (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

The top level of a descriptor is a script expression, or the same followed by the number sign and a checksum of eight characters (Wuille and Chow, 2021). The checksum is an error-correcting code similar to the one of the address format called bech32, using its alphabet of 32 characters, and it can be generated from the BIP's reference code, which the worked example runs: it produces the checksum 8zl0zxma for the documented example, the one that Bitcoin Core 31.1 returned, and it reports false for a descriptor in which one character of the checksum or of the script was changed (Wuille and Chow, 2021) (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The documentation states how strong the code is: as long as the errors only replace characters of the basic set by others of it, up to four errors are always detected in descriptors of up to 501 characters, and for other errors there is roughly a one in a trillion chance of missing them (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

The checksum protects against accidents and not against attackers, since anybody can compute a valid one for any text, so it is no proof that a descriptor came from the person one thinks. Whether a checksum is required depends on the call: the BIP says it is optional for parsing and that applications may choose to reject descriptors without one, and Bitcoin Core requires it for only some calls, among them the one that derives addresses and the one that imports descriptors (Wuille and Chow, 2021) (Bitcoin Core, 2026). A descriptor that contains private keys is as secret as the keys, and one with only public keys reveals, to whoever reads it, every address of the wallet.

nodes.definition: An output descriptor is a short text that describes a set of output scripts, optionally followed by an 8-character checksum that detects typing and copying errors.

nodes.label: Output type
nodes.body: An output type is the form of the locking script of an output, which decides what the spender must show to spend it. Chapter 2 introduced the locking script, and the documentation of Bitcoin Core's output descriptors names the common forms. The expression pkh describes a P2PKH output, the pay-to-key-hash form, wpkh a P2WPKH output, the pay-to-witness-key-hash form, sh(wpkh) a P2SH-P2WPKH output, in which a witness key hash is wrapped in a script hash, and tr a P2TR output, the taproot form (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

paras.text: An output type is the form of the locking script of an output, which decides what the spender must show to spend it. Chapter 2 introduced the locking script, and the documentation of Bitcoin Core's output descriptors names the common forms. The expression pkh describes a P2PKH output, the pay-to-key-hash form, wpkh a P2WPKH output, the pay-to-witness-key-hash form, sh(wpkh) a P2SH-P2WPKH output, in which a witness key hash is wrapped in a script hash, and tr a P2TR output, the taproot form (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

The output type decides the address format and the cost of the payment. The older forms put all the data in the part of the transaction that counts fully towards its size, whereas the witness forms move the signature to the witness, which is discounted, as the weight concept explained. A descriptor wallet keeps one pair of descriptors for each type, one for receiving and one for change.

The demo wallet of the chapter's evidence has eight descriptors, and the worked example reads them and finds the four function names pkh, sh, tr and wpkh, each used once for receiving and once for change (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The names pkh and wpkh are the ones the documentation describes.

The descriptor of an output type is a function that takes a key, or several, and says how the locking script is built from it. A parser reading wpkh(KEY) knows that the script is a witness program of version 0 containing the hash of KEY, whereas tr(KEY) means a witness program of version 1. The checksum that ends the descriptor protects the expression as a whole, so a typing error in the type or the key is caught.

The abbreviations are easy to confuse. The lowercase function names of the descriptors, pkh, wpkh, sh and tr, and the uppercase names of the output types, P2PKH, P2WPKH, P2SH and P2TR, belong together but are not the same thing, and sh(wpkh) is one combined type and not two. The documentation's one-line descriptions are the reliable way to look up which is which.

nodes.label: Interface
nodes.body: The interface branch is about how other programs and people talk to a running node. A node that only validates and stores would be of little use if nothing could ask it a question, and so Bitcoin Core offers an application programming interface. The book introduces it as an interface that can be reached by a command-line helper, which lets a reader experiment interactively with the capabilities that are also available to programs, and then through code (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). This is the part of the chapter where the reader stops reading about the node and starts using it.

paras.text: The interface branch is about how other programs and people talk to a running node. A node that only validates and stores would be of little use if nothing could ask it a question, and so Bitcoin Core offers an application programming interface. The book introduces it as an interface that can be reached by a command-line helper, which lets a reader experiment interactively with the capabilities that are also available to programs, and then through code (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). This is the part of the chapter where the reader stops reading about the node and starts using it.

The interface is what turns a node into a platform. Wallets, explorers, payment processors and research tools get their information about the chain from a node they trust, and they ask it through this interface, which is also the reason why the book lists "programmable access to the network and the blockchain" as one of the reasons for running a node of one's own (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The same interface can also spend funds, change settings and read private data when a wallet is loaded, so the way it is protected is as important as the way it is used.

The reader meets the interface at the command line, where the helper program sends a request and prints the answer, in the examples of the chapter that decode a transaction and a block, and in the short Python programs that make the same calls through a library. The evidence of this version checks the printed examples against the real release 31.1, and it records what the release answers when asked for the list of commands, which in the current release has 151 entries in nine categories (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

The branch has two groups. The first group, the RPC interface, explains the idea of an interface, the remote procedure call protocol with its JSON messages and the HTTP requests that carry them, and the two ways in which Bitcoin Core decides who may call: a random cookie and hashed credentials. The second group, the clients, explains the command line, the helper program that builds the requests for a person, and the wrapper libraries that build them for a program.

The documentation of the project is blunt about the risk. The interface allows other programs to control Bitcoin Core, including spending funds from the wallets, affecting the verification of consensus rules, and reading private data; by default only a client on the same computer can reach it, and only with a valid credential, and the documentation says not to enable connections over the public Internet because the credentials are sent as clear text (Bitcoin Core, 2026). A reader who exposes the port to learn faster is taking the largest risk in the chapter.

nodes.label: RPC interface
nodes.body: The RPC interface is the group of concepts that describe the programmatic doorway of Bitcoin Core. It gathers the idea of an application programming interface, the protocol that Bitcoin Core uses for it, the data format and the transport on which that protocol rides, and the two mechanisms with which the node checks the identity of a caller. The book puts it in one sentence: Bitcoin Core's API is a JSON-RPC interface, where JSON is the way to present data and RPC means a remote procedure call over a network protocol, in this case HTTP (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: The RPC interface is the group of concepts that describe the programmatic doorway of Bitcoin Core. It gathers the idea of an application programming interface, the protocol that Bitcoin Core uses for it, the data format and the transport on which that protocol rides, and the two mechanisms with which the node checks the identity of a caller. The book puts it in one sentence: Bitcoin Core's API is a JSON-RPC interface, where JSON is the way to present data and RPC means a remote procedure call over a network protocol, in this case HTTP (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

Choosing an interface that rests on JSON and HTTP lets nearly every programming language use the node. The book remarks that any program that can make an HTTP request can call the interface, and that libraries in most popular programming languages wrap it so that the call looks like a function of the language (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The cost is that the node must decide whom to answer, and the group explains how it does so with a cookie that exists only while the node runs, or with credentials that are stored only in hashed form.

The first lines of the book's example are a call written for the command-line program curl, with the address 127.0.0.1, the default port 8332, a body that names the method, and a user name. The port is the node's own: the source gives 8332 for the main network, 18332 for the third test network, 48332 for the fourth and 38332 for the signet (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The log of the evidence node confirms that it bound to the address 127.0.0.1 and port 8332, after the attempt to bind the IPv6 address ::1 had failed (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

The concepts are taken from the outside inwards. The first is the interface in the general sense. Then come the protocol and the data format that define what a request looks like, and the HTTP exchange that carries it. The last two concepts describe the check that precedes any answer, the cookie, which needs no configuration, and the stored credential, which an owner must set up, and which a program that connects from another machine may need.

nodes.label: Application programming interface
nodes.body: An application programming interface, or API, is the defined way in which one program can use the functions of another. It names the requests that may be made, the information each request needs, and the form of the answer, and so it hides how the work is done behind a contract. The book states the purpose in a sentence: the whole point of an API is to access functions programmatically, while the helper that a person types is only useful for exploring the API and for testing functions (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The word application stands for any program that wants a service, and programming for the fact that the interface is meant for programs.

paras.text: An application programming interface, or API, is the defined way in which one program can use the functions of another. It names the requests that may be made, the information each request needs, and the form of the answer, and so it hides how the work is done behind a contract. The book states the purpose in a sentence: the whole point of an API is to access functions programmatically, while the helper that a person types is only useful for exploring the API and for testing functions (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The word application stands for any program that wants a service, and programming for the fact that the interface is meant for programs.

The API is the reason why one reference implementation can serve very different applications. A wallet, an exchange, a research script and a monitoring tool ask the same node different questions, and none of them needs to know how the node stores the blocks or checks the signatures. The book calls it programmable access to the network and the blockchain, and counts building applications that must validate transactions according to Bitcoin's consensus rules among the reasons for running one's own node (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

In Bitcoin Core the API is made of named methods, which the chapter calls RPC commands. The command help lists them in categories; in the real release 31.1 the list printed 151 entries in nine categories: blockchain, control, mining, network, raw transactions, signer, util, wallet and ZeroMQ (Bitcoin Core, 2026). A few of them appear in the rest of the chapter, among them one that returns the hash of a block at a given height, one that returns a block, and one that returns and one that decodes a transaction.

A method has a name and parameters, and it returns a result or an error. The help text for a method shows all three, and ends with two examples of how to call it, one with the helper program and one with the web client curl, as the book describes (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The documentation of the project adds that the interface may change from one major version to the next, so it is implicitly versioned by the major version of Bitcoin Core, and that a deprecated feature can usually be switched on again for one major version with a command-line option (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The worked example reads the result member of a typical answer.

An interface is a promise only for as long as its owner keeps it. The documentation gives the grace period of one major version for deprecated features, and the chapter's own examples show a change: the field of warnings was a string and became an array of strings in release 28.0 (Bitcoin Core, 2026). A program that depends on the exact text of an answer, as opposed to its documented fields, breaks sooner. Finally, an API gives access, not trust: an answer from a node one does not control is only as good as that node.

nodes.definition: An application programming interface is the set of requests that one program offers to other programs; Bitcoin Core's API lets a program ask the node about the chain, the mempool and the wallet.

nodes.label: JSON-RPC interface
nodes.body: JSON-RPC is a protocol for remote procedure calls whose messages are written in JSON. Its specification describes it as a stateless, light-weight remote procedure call protocol that defines a few data structures and the rules for processing them, independent of the transport, so that the same messages may travel within a process, over sockets or over HTTP (JSON-RPC Working Group, 2013). A call is a request object with a method name, parameters and an identifier chosen by the client, and the server replies with the same identifier, which lets the client match answers to calls (JSON-RPC Working Group, 2013).

paras.text: JSON-RPC is a protocol for remote procedure calls whose messages are written in JSON. Its specification describes it as a stateless, light-weight remote procedure call protocol that defines a few data structures and the rules for processing them, independent of the transport, so that the same messages may travel within a process, over sockets or over HTTP (JSON-RPC Working Group, 2013). A call is a request object with a method name, parameters and an identifier chosen by the client, and the server replies with the same identifier, which lets the client match answers to calls (JSON-RPC Working Group, 2013).

The protocol keeps the interface small. A client needs to know only the name of a method and its parameters, and the answer tells the result or the error. Because the identifier comes back unchanged, a client can send many requests and still know which answer belongs to which. A request without an identifier is a notification, to which the server must not reply, a feature that Bitcoin Core supports for the newer version of the protocol (JSON-RPC Working Group, 2013) (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

The book's example is a request in the older style: the body has the members jsonrpc with the value 1.0, id with the value curltest, method with the value getblockchaininfo and an empty list of parameters, sent by curl to the address 127.0.0.1 (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The documentation of the project says that the server also recognizes version 2.0 requests, identified by the member jsonrpc with the value 2.0, and otherwise follows the older protocol that was the only one available in release 27.0 and before (Bitcoin Core, 2026). Among the differences are that a version 2.0 reply carries either a result or an error and not both, and that HTTP status codes are always 200 unless the HTTP server itself failed (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

The two endpoints of the server are the root and a path for each wallet, and the documentation says that the second must be used for wallet requests when two or more wallets are loaded, as the helper does when it is given the name of a wallet (Bitcoin Core, 2026). Parameters may be passed by position or by name, as the specification allows; the helper offers the named form with an option, and the newer wrapper command bitcoin rpc is described as equivalent to the helper with that option (Bitcoin Core, 2026) (JSON-RPC Working Group, 2013). The worked example builds the book's request body and reads the method name back from it.

The name remote procedure call hides a danger: the call looks like a local function and behaves like a network request, so it can fail, be slow, or be answered by something else. The documentation warns that other programs on the same machine can try to provide an interface on the same port to trick a user into revealing the credentials, and that the interface does not guarantee escaping of data beyond what JSON needs, so the data of an answer, for example a decoded string, must be handled as untrusted (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The older style is also still accepted, so a program written for it keeps working, which may hide differences in the error behavior.

nodes.definition: Bitcoin Core's API is JSON-RPC over HTTP, by default to 127.0.0.1 on port 8332, so any program that can make an HTTP request can call it.

io.code: (lambda g: (exec("import json\nbody = json.dumps({'jsonrpc': '1.0', 'id': 'curltest', 'method': 'getblockchaininfo', 'params': []})\nresult = json.loads(body)['method']", g), g['result'])[1])({})

nodes.label: JSON data format
nodes.body: JSON, short for JavaScript Object Notation, is a text format for the serialization of structured data, which its standard describes as lightweight, text-based and independent of any language (Bray, 2017). It can represent four primitive types, namely strings, numbers, booleans and null, and two structured types, objects and arrays (Bray, 2017). An object is written between curly brackets and holds named members, and an array is a list of values; a value may itself be an object or an array, so a document can nest as deeply as it needs.

paras.text: JSON, short for JavaScript Object Notation, is a text format for the serialization of structured data, which its standard describes as lightweight, text-based and independent of any language (Bray, 2017). It can represent four primitive types, namely strings, numbers, booleans and null, and two structured types, objects and arrays (Bray, 2017). An object is written between curly brackets and holds named members, and an array is a list of values; a value may itself be an object or an array, so a document can nest as deeply as it needs.

The book calls JSON a very convenient way to present data that both humans and programs can easily read, and in the section on status information it says that the data is returned in JSON, a format that can easily be consumed by all programming languages while remaining quite human-readable (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). This is why the same answer can be read by a person at the terminal and parsed by a program, and why the rest of the book can show results as pieces of text.

Every answer in the chapter is JSON: the status of the chain, the status of the network, a decoded transaction, a block. The answer printed in the book for the call with the cookie contains an object with a member result that holds another object with the fields of the chain information, a member error with the value null and a member id with the value of the request (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The worked example parses that very text with the standard library and reads four of its values. The first member shows the string main, the block count is the number 799278, the error is null, which becomes None in Python, and the id is the string of the request.

A program turns the text into its own data structures, and back again, using a library; in Python the standard module json does both. Numbers are the delicate part. JSON makes no promise about their precision, and the value of an amount may be written with eight decimals, which a floating-point number cannot always hold exactly, so careful programs read amounts as decimal numbers or as integers of satoshis. Hexadecimal data are carried as strings, because JSON has no type for bytes, which is why the documentation recommends to show serialized data in hexadecimal form only (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

JSON is a data format, not a protocol, and by itself it says nothing about what a member means: the meaning of the member bits or of the member weight comes from the documentation of Bitcoin Core. The order of the members of an object has no meaning and should not be relied on. The format also has no comments and no way to say that a number is a hash or an amount, so a mistake in interpretation is not caught by the parser. The course returns to this point at the end of the chapter, where JSON is given a meaning by a context.

nodes.definition: JSON is a text format for structured data made of objects, arrays, strings, numbers, booleans and null; every answer of Bitcoin Core's API is written in it.

nodes.label: HTTP request
nodes.body: The Hypertext Transfer Protocol, HTTP, is the protocol on which the web is built. Its specification describes it as a family of stateless, application-level, request and response protocols: a client sends a request, the server sends a response, and the server keeps no memory between requests unless the client sends it again (Fielding et al., 2022). A request has a method, a target address, header fields and optionally a body, and a response has a status code, header fields and optionally a body. The status code 200 means that the request has succeeded (Fielding et al., 2022).

paras.text: The Hypertext Transfer Protocol, HTTP, is the protocol on which the web is built. Its specification describes it as a family of stateless, application-level, request and response protocols: a client sends a request, the server sends a response, and the server keeps no memory between requests unless the client sends it again (Fielding et al., 2022). A request has a method, a target address, header fields and optionally a body, and a response has a status code, header fields and optionally a body. The status code 200 means that the request has succeeded (Fielding et al., 2022).

Using HTTP as the carrier means that a call can be made by any of the tools that already speak it, from a browser to a library of any language. The book shows curl, the versatile command-line HTTP client, and says that a program may use a generic HTTP library to build the call, as the example with curl does (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The manual of curl describes it as a tool for transferring data from or to a server using URLs, with options for the user, for the data to be sent without change, and for header fields (Stenberg, 2026).

A reader sees the pieces of a request in the book's example: the option for the user supplies the credentials, the option for binary data supplies the body, the option for a header sets the content type to plain text, and the address gives the host 127.0.0.1 and the port 8332 (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The library python-bitcoinlib, version 0.12.2, builds the same exchange itself: it sends a POST request with a JSON body, with the member version set to 1.1, and the header field Content-type set to application/json, and it adds an Authorization field that holds the word Basic and the credentials encoded in base64 (Todd, 2023).

The POST method asks the target resource to process the representation enclosed in the request according to its own semantics, which is what a remote call needs, since the body names the method to run (Fielding et al., 2022). The Authorization header field lets the client prove who it is (Fielding et al., 2022). Bitcoin Core accepts the form that starts with the word Basic, decodes the rest from base64, splits it at the first colon into the user and the password, and then checks them, as the source shows; the worked example builds such a header value for the user alice and the password secret.

Base64 is an encoding, not encryption, so anybody who can read the request can read the credentials, and plain HTTP offers no protection on its way; the documentation of the project says that the interface uses authentication but no encryption (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The status codes are also an indication of a different kind from the errors of the call: with the older protocol a failed call returns an HTTP error status, and with the newer one it returns 200 with an error member, unless the failure was in the HTTP server itself (Bitcoin Core, 2026). A program that checks only the HTTP status will misjudge one of them.

nodes.definition: HTTP is the request-and-response protocol of the web; Bitcoin Core receives each JSON-RPC call as the body of an HTTP POST request and sends the answer as the body of the HTTP response.

nodes.label: Cookie authentication
nodes.body: Cookie authentication is the default way in which Bitcoin Core decides who may call its interface. The book says that Bitcoin Core will create a random password on each start and place it in the data directory under the name .cookie, and that the helper program can read this password file given the data directory (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). A program that can read the file can make calls, and one that cannot read it cannot. The documentation calls the file a session credential: it is created when the node starts and deleted when the node ends (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

paras.text: Cookie authentication is the default way in which Bitcoin Core decides who may call its interface. The book says that Bitcoin Core will create a random password on each start and place it in the data directory under the name .cookie, and that the helper program can read this password file given the data directory (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). A program that can read the file can make calls, and one that cannot read it cannot. The documentation calls the file a session credential: it is created when the node starts and deleted when the node ends (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

The method removes the need for the owner to invent and store a password. The init documentation says that a daemon run without any configuration uses a special cookie file for authentication, that the cookie is generated with random content when the daemon starts, and that read access to the file controls who can use the interface (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The project's security notes name this the preferred authentication method, because the secret is new at every start, never typed and never put into a configuration file (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

The book prints the content of the file: a user name, __cookie__, a colon, and 64 hexadecimal digits, and then passes the whole string to curl as the credential (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The log of the real node of release 31.1 shows the same events: it generated an authentication cookie in the data directory, used the permissions that allow only the owner to read and write it, and then announced that it was using random cookie authentication (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The option rpccookiefile can move the file and the option rpccookieperms can widen its permissions to the group or to all users (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

The source creates 32 random bytes with the node's random-number generator, writes them as 64 hexadecimal digits after the fixed user name __cookie__ and a colon, and renames the finished file into place (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The worked example takes the book's printed secret and shows that its 64 digits are 32 bytes. At start the node treats the cookie as a plaintext credential: it hashes the password with a random 16-byte salt, as it does for a configured user and password, and keeps only the user, the salt and the hash; a request is checked against them, so for a caller the cookie is an ordinary password whose value changes with every restart (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

Anyone who can read the cookie file controls the interface. The default file mode, owner only, is set by the process-wide file creation mask of 0077, and the documentation recommends that the data directory be readable only by the user and group of the node, with access to the interface controlled by group membership (Bitcoin Core, 2026). A cookie is also no solution for a client on another computer or a service that must survive restarts, because the secret changes each time; for these cases the stored credential of the next concept is used, as the book itself says by pointing to the helper script in the share folder (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

nodes.definition: By default Bitcoin Core creates a random credential on each start and stores it in the data directory as .cookie, which bitcoin-cli reads; rpcauth.py makes a static credential instead.

nodes.label: Hashed credentials (rpcauth)
nodes.body: The rpcauth option is the way to give the interface a fixed credential without storing the password in plain text. Its value has three parts: a user name, a salt, and a hash of the password computed with that salt, written as user:salt$hash. The book points to the helper script rpcauth.py in the share folder of the source for creating a static password (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The script prints the line to be appended to the configuration file, and the password that the client must use (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

paras.text: The rpcauth option is the way to give the interface a fixed credential without storing the password in plain text. Its value has three parts: a user name, a salt, and a hash of the password computed with that salt, written as user:salt$hash. The book points to the helper script rpcauth.py in the share folder of the source for creating a static password (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The script prints the line to be appended to the configuration file, and the password that the client must use (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

A stored password in a configuration file is a secret on a disk that is copied, backed up and sometimes shared. Storing only a salted hash means that a leaked file does not reveal the password. The source of the node logs a warning when the older options for user and password are used, saying that they are less secure because the credentials are configured in plain text, and recommends cookie-based authentication or hashed credentials instead; the project's security notes name the script as the way to generate static credentials and the plain user and password options as the last fallback (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

The script's output is a line starting with rpcauth= followed by the user, a colon, the salt, a dollar sign and the hash. For the user alice, the evidence file of this version records exactly this layout, with the salt and the hash replaced by placeholders so that no real secret is kept (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The init documentation mentions the option as the way to override the cookie behavior when the node runs as a daemon, noting that this password is mostly used as a fixed token that the node and the client programs read from the configuration file (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

The script makes a salt of 16 random bytes, written as 32 hexadecimal digits, and, if no password is given, a random password from 32 random bytes in a URL-safe text form; the hash is the keyed-hash message authentication code HMAC with SHA-256, using the salt as the key and the password as the message, written as 64 hexadecimal digits (Bitcoin Core, 2026). When a request arrives, the node finds the entry for the user name, computes the same HMAC from the password it was sent, and compares the two hash values in a time that does not depend on how many characters agree (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The worked example builds such a line and counts the parts: 5, 32 and 64 characters for alice, the salt and the hash.

The hash protects the file, not the connection: the client still sends the password itself in each request, and the interface does not encrypt, so the credential is only as safe as the path between client and node (Bitcoin Core, 2026). A hashed credential also does not limit what the caller may do; the option rpcwhitelist can restrict the methods a user may call, but the documentation says that such restrictions should not be seen as robust security boundaries, and recommends system-level isolation instead (Bitcoin Core, 2026). A weak password remains weak, even though the hash is not reversible: it can be guessed offline by anyone who has the line.

nodes.definition: The rpcauth option holds a user name, a random salt and the HMAC-SHA256 of the password under that salt, so the file never contains the password itself.

nodes.label: Salt
nodes.body: A salt is a random value that is stored next to a hashed password and mixed into the hash. The script rpcauth.py, which the book points to for creating credentials, draws a salt of 16 random bytes, writes it as 32 hexadecimal characters, computes the hash of the password using the salt as the key, and prints the three parts as user:salt$hash (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The worked example hashes the same password with two different salts and gets two unrelated values, e21e60d6 and d84d1ad6 at the start, and the same salt gives the same value every time.

paras.text: A salt is a random value that is stored next to a hashed password and mixed into the hash. The script rpcauth.py, which the book points to for creating credentials, draws a salt of 16 random bytes, writes it as 32 hexadecimal characters, computes the hash of the password using the salt as the key, and prints the three parts as user:salt$hash (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The worked example hashes the same password with two different salts and gets two unrelated values, e21e60d6 and d84d1ad6 at the start, and the same salt gives the same value every time.

The server must be able to check a password without keeping it. It keeps the user, the salt and the hash, and when a request comes it computes the hash of the supplied password with the stored salt and compares. The salt means that two users with the same password have different stored values, and that an attacker cannot use one prepared table of hashes against all users. The line in the configuration file therefore reveals neither the password nor whether two accounts share one.

The credential line of the evidence of this chapter has a user of 5 characters, a salt of 32 and a hash of 64, and the node's source reads the same three fields from the configuration, computes the hash of the supplied password with the salt, and compares the result with the stored hash by a function that takes the same time whatever the content (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The cookie, as the cookie concept explains, is treated in the same way at start: the node hashes it with a random salt and keeps only the result.

The salt does not need to be secret, since it is stored in the open, but it must be random and different for each credential. The hash function used is the keyed hash of the next concept, with the salt in the place of the key. Because the hash is one-way, the stored value cannot be turned back into the password; an attacker can only guess passwords and test them, and the salt makes each test specific to one credential.

A salt protects the stored value and not the password in transit. The password is still sent with each request, and over plain HTTP it is readable by anybody who can see the traffic, as the Base64 concept explains. A salt also does not make a weak password strong; it only prevents the reuse of work across credentials. That is why the helper script offers to generate a long random password, 32 bytes in text form, instead of leaving the choice to the user.

nodes.definition: A salt is a random value mixed into the hashing of a password, so that equal passwords give different stored values.

nodes.label: Keyed hash (HMAC)
nodes.body: An HMAC, the keyed-hash message authentication code, is a hash function used with a key. The standard that publishes the SHA algorithms also covers the HMACs based on them, and says that the algorithms are typically used with other cryptographic algorithms such as digital signature algorithms and keyed-hash authentication codes (Eastlake and Hansen, 2011). With SHA-256 the result is 32 bytes, 64 hexadecimal characters. The worked example computes the standard's own test, with the key Jefe and the message what do ya want for nothing?, and gets the value that the standard prints.

paras.text: An HMAC, the keyed-hash message authentication code, is a hash function used with a key. The standard that publishes the SHA algorithms also covers the HMACs based on them, and says that the algorithms are typically used with other cryptographic algorithms such as digital signature algorithms and keyed-hash authentication codes (Eastlake and Hansen, 2011). With SHA-256 the result is 32 bytes, 64 hexadecimal characters. The worked example computes the standard's own test, with the key Jefe and the message what do ya want for nothing?, and gets the value that the standard prints.

A plain hash proves nothing about who made it, because anybody can compute it. A keyed hash can be produced only with the key, so it is evidence that the holder of the key made it. Bitcoin Core uses this in a modest way, as the way to turn a password and a salt into a stored value. The same construction appears in other parts of the system, where a secret key is needed to derive other keys.

The script rpcauth.py calls the HMAC function of python with the salt as the key, the password as the message and SHA-256 as the hash, and the node's source does the same with its own implementation of the HMAC for SHA-256, writing the output in hexadecimal and comparing it with the stored hash (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The test value of the standard, 5BDCC146BF60754E6A042426089575C75A003F089D2739839DEC58B964EC3843, is reproduced exactly by the python library, which shows that the two implementations agree on a published case (Eastlake and Hansen, 2011).

The sample code of the standard states the construction in a comment: SHA(K XOR opad, SHA(K XOR ipad, text)), two nested hashes in which the key, combined with two fixed padding bytes, is mixed in at each level (Eastlake and Hansen, 2011). The details are in the standard and are not needed to use it. What matters is the interface: the key and the message go in and a value of the length of the hash comes out, and without the key the value cannot be reproduced or forged.

An HMAC authenticates data; it does not encrypt it. The message can be read by anybody who sees it, and the HMAC proves only that the sender knew the key. In the rpcauth credential the key is the salt, which is not secret, so the HMAC is used here as a one-way function with a per-credential parameter and not as a proof of the sender's identity. A reader should keep the two uses apart.

nodes.definition: An HMAC is a hash computed with a secret key, so that only someone who knows the key can produce or check the value.

nodes.label: Client
nodes.body: The client group collects the concepts about the programs that call the interface. A client is whatever makes a request to the node: a person at a terminal with the helper program, a script that builds the HTTP message itself, or an application that uses a library written for its language. The book goes through them in this order, starting with the help command of the helper, continuing with the curl command that the help prints, and ending with a Python library (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: The client group collects the concepts about the programs that call the interface. A client is whatever makes a request to the node: a person at a terminal with the helper program, a script that builds the HTTP message itself, or an application that uses a library written for its language. The book goes through them in this order, starting with the help command of the helper, continuing with the curl command that the help prints, and ending with a Python library (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The choice of client decides how much of the protocol a user has to know. At the terminal one needs only the name of a method and its parameters. With a generic HTTP tool one must also write the body and manage the credential. With a wrapper library one writes a function call, and the library does the rest. The book remarks that the helper is very useful for exploring the API and testing functions, and that the whole point of an API is to access functions programmatically (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

All three clients are met in the chapter. The helper is used for the first calls, to list the commands, to get help on one of them and to ask for the hash of block 1000, which the book prints as 00000000c937983704a73af28acdec37b049d214adbda81d7e2a3dd146f6ed09 (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The Python programs in the last part use the wrapper library, and in the evidence of this version the book's first program was run unchanged with the library at version 0.12.2 against the node of release 31.1 (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

Every client works the same way underneath, and the differences between them are only how much of that work the user does. A call is an HTTP request carrying a small document that names a method and lists its arguments, sent to the port the node listens on and answered by a document holding either a result or an error. The helper program of the project builds that document from what is typed, reads the credential out of the data directory so the user never handles it, and prints the answer; a generic transfer tool leaves the document and the credential to the user, which is why the chapter shows that form second, once the shape of the request is already familiar; a wrapper library turns a method into a function of the host language and the answer into one of that language's own data structures, which is what lets a program loop over results instead of reading them (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (JSON-RPC Working Group, 2013) (Fielding et al., 2022).

Two cautions. The credential is the whole of the node's security on this interface, so a request that carries it is as powerful as the node itself: the cookie file in the data directory exists so that a local client can authenticate without a password being written anywhere, and exposing the interface beyond the local machine turns a convenience into a liability. And a wrapper library is one more dependency with one more version: the program the book prints ran unchanged in this chapter's own evidence, but it ran against a stated library version and a stated node release, and a learner reporting that a printed program does not work should name both before concluding that the book is wrong (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

nodes.label: Command line
nodes.body: The command line is a way of using a computer by typing text commands in a terminal and reading the text that the programs print. A command is the name of a program followed by arguments, separated by spaces, and the program decides what to do with them. The books and the manuals of the chapter print a dollar sign as the prompt in front of what the user types, and print the lines under it as the output. The chapter uses this form throughout, starting with the commands that build and start the node (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: The command line is a way of using a computer by typing text commands in a terminal and reading the text that the programs print. A command is the name of a program followed by arguments, separated by spaces, and the program decides what to do with them. The books and the manuals of the chapter print a dollar sign as the prompt in front of what the user types, and print the lines under it as the output. The chapter uses this form throughout, starting with the commands that build and start the node (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The command line is the common ground of the people who run nodes: it works on a server without any graphical display, over a remote connection, and in scripts that can be repeated. It also leaves a record, because the text of a command can be copied into a document or a script, which is how the book can show an exact sequence of steps. The helper program of Bitcoin Core is made for it, as is the daemon with its options.

A reader meets the command line in every example of the chapter. The book's commands for starting the node, such as bitcoind with the option for the console, for reading the help, such as bitcoind with the help option, and for querying it, such as bitcoin-cli getblockchaininfo, are all typed this way (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The options of the programs follow the same conventions: a name with a leading hyphen, sometimes with an equals sign and a value, as the help text of the release shows for the options of the daemon (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

The shell splits what is typed into words, the first being the program and the others its arguments, which the worked example shows with the standard library's splitting function for the command that asks for the hash of block 1000: three words, the program, the method and the height as text. The program receives them as a list of text values, so a number such as 1000 arrives as text and the program converts it. Quotation marks keep a word with spaces together, which is why the book's alert command and the credentials of the interface are written inside quotes.

The command line is exact and unforgiving: a misplaced space or quote changes the meaning, and a command copied from a page may contain characters that look the same but are not, such as typographic quotation marks. Commands also run with the privileges of the user who types them, so a command copied from an unknown source can do harm, as the documentation says about configuration changes provided by others (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The history of the terminal may keep secrets typed as arguments, such as a password, which is a reason to use a prompt where one is offered.

nodes.definition: The command line is a text interface in which a person types the name of a program followed by arguments and reads the program's text output.

nodes.label: Command-line client (bitcoin-cli)
nodes.body: The command-line client is the program bitcoin-cli, which the installed-files table of Bitcoin Core describes as the tool for making node and wallet RPC calls (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The book calls it a helper and says that it allows experimenting interactively with the capabilities that are also available programmatically via the API (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Given a method name and its parameters, it builds the request, finds the credential, sends the request to the node and prints the answer.

paras.text: The command-line client is the program bitcoin-cli, which the installed-files table of Bitcoin Core describes as the tool for making node and wallet RPC calls (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The book calls it a helper and says that it allows experimenting interactively with the capabilities that are also available programmatically via the API (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Given a method name and its parameters, it builds the request, finds the credential, sends the request to the node and prints the answer.

The client lets a reader try the interface before writing any code. The book starts the section with the command help, which lists all RPC commands; adding the name of a command after help gives the description, the arguments, the result and two examples (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The first example in the book is bitcoin-cli getblockhash 1000, whose result, a block hash, shows that the node is running, accepting commands and holding the block, as the book puts it (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

In the evidence of this version the list of commands printed by release 31.1 has nine categories and 151 entries, and contains the commands that the chapter uses, among them the one for the block hash at a height, the one that returns a block, the one that returns a raw transaction and the one that decodes it (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The hash that the book prints for block 1000 is the double SHA-256 of that block's 80-byte header, which the check in the worked example confirms with the header data of a public explorer: the identifier of the block of height 1000 is 00000000c937983704a73af28acdec37b049d214adbda81d7e2a3dd146f6ed09 (Blockstream, 2026).

The client reads the data directory to find the cookie, or the configured credential, and sends an HTTP request to the local port. A named form passes parameters by name, and the documentation of the project describes the new command bitcoin rpc as a substitute for the helper with the option for named parameters; the help of the wrapper program says the same (Bitcoin Core, 2026). For a wallet request, the option that selects a wallet makes the client use the wallet-specific path of the interface, which the documentation says must be used when two or more wallets are loaded (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

The helper is a convenience and not a separate interface: everything it does is a call to the node, and a typing mistake becomes a request for the wrong thing. The positional form needs the parameters in the exact order, which for a method with many optional parameters is error-prone, and the named form is safer, as the documentation's example for creating a wallet shows (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The book's printed results are from a node at a given height, and a reader's results will differ; the chapter itself warns that the examples assume the node is at least at block 775,072 (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

nodes.definition: The bitcoin-cli helper sends the same calls the API offers, which makes it the way to experiment interactively; its help command lists the available RPC commands.

nodes.label: Wrapper library
nodes.body: A wrapper library is a package for a programming language that makes the node's interface look like ordinary functions of that language. The book explains that libraries exist in most popular programming languages that wrap the Bitcoin Core API in a way that makes the call a lot simpler, and it chooses python-bitcoinlib for its examples, noting that the library is not part of the Bitcoin Core project and must be installed in the usual way (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The program in the book creates a proxy object, calls getblockchaininfo on it as if it were a method, and prints one member of the result.

paras.text: A wrapper library is a package for a programming language that makes the node's interface look like ordinary functions of that language. The book explains that libraries exist in most popular programming languages that wrap the Bitcoin Core API in a way that makes the call a lot simpler, and it chooses python-bitcoinlib for its examples, noting that the library is not part of the Bitcoin Core project and must be installed in the usual way (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The program in the book creates a proxy object, calls getblockchaininfo on it as if it were a method, and prints one member of the result.

A wrapper takes away the work of building the request, finding the credentials, sending the message and decoding the answer, so that the programmer thinks in terms of the node's methods. The book contrasts it with the alternative of building the call with a generic HTTP library as shown with curl (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The price is a dependency: the wrapper must follow the changes of the node, and it is maintained by someone else. The documentation of python-bitcoinlib says that its interface should work with Bitcoin Core 24.0 or later, and the evidence of this version confirms that the book's first program runs with version 0.12.2 on Python 3.14.4 against the release 31.1 (Todd, 2023) (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

The book's three programs, which read the number of blocks, list the outputs of Alice's transaction and add up the outputs of a block, all use a proxy object of this kind (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). In the evidence of this version the first one was run unchanged against the offline node and printed 0, the number of blocks of that node, which agrees with the answer of the call for blockchain information (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The library's proxy also reads the data directory's cookie file when it is created without arguments (Todd, 2023).

The trick is in a special method of the Python class. When a program asks the proxy for an attribute that does not exist, such as getblockchaininfo, the class receives its name and returns a function; when that function is called, it builds a JSON message with the member version set to 1.1, the method name, the arguments as parameters and a counter as identifier, sends it as an HTTP POST with the authorization header, checks the error member and returns the result member (Todd, 2023). The worked example reproduces the idea with the standard library only, for the call that asks for the hash of block 1000: it returns the message that the real class would send.

A wrapper hides the protocol and so can hide failures: it raises an error of its own when the node reports one, it needs the node to be running and reachable, and it needs a credential that works, which is the usual cause of failure. A library that is not maintained may lack the newest methods or the newest fields. The version in the book's era, 0.12.2, dates from June 2023, a point the research record of this chapter checks against the package index. And a wrapper is only a client of the node: the quality of the answers is the quality of the node behind it.

nodes.definition: A wrapper library hides the HTTP call: python-bitcoinlib's RawProxy turns p.getblockchaininfo() into the JSON-RPC request and returns the decoded answer.

nodes.label: Data
nodes.body: The data branch is about what a node holds and what the interface shows of it: the transactions that move value, the blocks that gather them into the shared record, and the state of the chain that results. The section of the book on exploring transactions and blocks takes one payment, Alice's purchase from Bob's store, and follows it from a serialized hexadecimal string to a decoded structure, and then goes up a level to a block, which can be referenced either by its height or by its hash (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The chapter treats them as things to look at, and this branch explains what the fields mean.

paras.text: The data branch is about what a node holds and what the interface shows of it: the transactions that move value, the blocks that gather them into the shared record, and the state of the chain that results. The section of the book on exploring transactions and blocks takes one payment, Alice's purchase from Bob's store, and follows it from a serialized hexadecimal string to a decoded structure, and then goes up a level to a block, which can be referenced either by its height or by its hash (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The chapter treats them as things to look at, and this branch explains what the fields mean.

A student who understands the fields can check the node's answers, which is the point of running a node. The book says that a transaction ID is not authoritative before confirmation, that a block's confirmations tell its depth, and that the median time of the block is a time measurement harder for miners to manipulate (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Each of these statements is a claim about how the system is built, and each can be tested on data that anybody can fetch. The branch therefore pairs each field with a computation that reproduces it from the raw bytes.

The data are met whenever one asks the node about something that happened on the chain. The evidence of this version contains the real hexadecimal of Alice's transaction, the answer that release 31.1 gives when asked to decode it, the header and the list of transaction identifiers of block 123456, the times of the eleven blocks around it and the outputs of all 1,966 transactions of block 775072, taken from a public explorer, which is a third party's index and not the reader's own node (Blockstream, 2026) (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

The branch has three groups. The transaction group covers the serialized form, the decoded form, the witness, the identifiers and the weight. The block group covers the height and hash, the header, the weight, the Merkle root, the subsidy, the target and difficulty, and the median time. The chain state group covers the relations between blocks: the chain with the most work, the amount of work, the confirmations and the reorganization. The computations use only the Python standard library, so that every number printed in the text can be repeated by the reader.

Two cautions apply to the whole branch. The first is that the data in the book belong to a moment: the confirmations of a block grow with every new block, and the block of the later example is so old that its figures are history only. The second is that the book contains one printed result that does not match its script. The program that adds the outputs of block 775072 prints 10,322.07722534 BTC and explains it as including a reward of 25 BTC, but the reward at that height is 6.25 BTC, and the sum of all outputs of that block is 5,863.00566521 BTC, as the executed checks of this chapter show (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

nodes.label: Transaction
nodes.body: The transaction group collects the concepts about the objects that carry value. Chapter 2 introduced the transaction with its inputs, outputs and fee; this group looks at the same object as a node sees it, first as a string of bytes, then as a decoded structure with fields, with an identifier and with a cost in block space. The book's example is Alice's payment to Bob, retrieved by its identifier and decoded, in which the transaction used one input and generated two outputs, the payment to Bob and the change back to Alice (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: The transaction group collects the concepts about the objects that carry value. Chapter 2 introduced the transaction with its inputs, outputs and fee; this group looks at the same object as a node sees it, first as a string of bytes, then as a decoded structure with fields, with an identifier and with a cost in block space. The book's example is Alice's payment to Bob, retrieved by its identifier and decoded, in which the transaction used one input and generated two outputs, the payment to Bob and the change back to Alice (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

How a transaction is stored decides how it is identified and how much it costs. A change in the serialization introduced the witness, a part of the transaction that is not included in the old identifier, and with it a second identifier and a new measure of size. A reader who knows only the simple picture of inputs and outputs will not be able to explain why Alice's transaction has a size of 194 bytes and a virtual size of 143, or why it has two identifiers. This group explains why.

The group's concepts are met in the output of the two commands of the book: the first returns the serialized transaction in hexadecimal notation, and the second decodes it into the fields shown in the chapter (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). They are met again in every block explorer and every wallet, which show the same fields under other names. The evidence of this version decodes the book's hexadecimal with both the real release 31.1 and a short Python program, and the two agree on every field (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

The concepts follow the path from bytes to meaning. Serialization explains the layout of the bytes, decoding the structure that results, the witness the part that the old layout did not have, the identifiers the two hashes that name a transaction, the weight the way the cost is counted, and malleability the reason why an identifier cannot be relied on before the transaction is confirmed.

nodes.label: Transaction serialization
nodes.body: Serialization is the writing of a structured object as a sequence of bytes, so that it can be stored or sent. The book shows the result for Alice's transaction as 388 hexadecimal digits, which the command getrawtransaction returns when it is asked for the transaction by its identifier (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The same bytes travel between nodes, are stored in the block files and are hashed to produce identifiers. Hexadecimal notation, which chapter 2 explained, writes each byte as two digits.

paras.text: Serialization is the writing of a structured object as a sequence of bytes, so that it can be stored or sent. The book shows the result for Alice's transaction as 388 hexadecimal digits, which the command getrawtransaction returns when it is asked for the transaction by its identifier (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The same bytes travel between nodes, are stored in the block files and are hashed to produce identifiers. Hexadecimal notation, which chapter 2 explained, writes each byte as two digits.

A precise byte layout is what lets independent programs agree. The specification BIP 144 defines the layout with witness data: a four-byte version, a marker byte that must be zero, a flag byte that must be nonzero, the number of inputs, the inputs, the number of outputs, the outputs, the witnesses and a four-byte lock time (Lombrozo and Wuille, 2016). The marker is zero so that the layout is never mistaken for a valid transaction by a program that does not know about witnesses, because in the old layout a zero would mean a transaction with no inputs (Lombrozo and Wuille, 2016).

A reader can take the hexadecimal in the book and read it by eye. It starts with 01000000, the version 1 written with the least significant byte first, then 00 and 01, the marker and the flag, then 01 for one input, then the 32 bytes of the previous transaction identifier written in reverse order, the four bytes of the index 1, a zero for an empty signature script and ffffffff for the sequence. Then come 02 for two outputs, each with eight bytes of value and a script, and finally the witness and the four zero bytes of the lock time (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The worked example is a parser of about twenty lines that follows this layout. It reads the integers with the least significant byte first, uses a count of one byte for the numbers of inputs, outputs and witness items, and returns the version 1, the marker 0, the flag 1, one input, two outputs and the lock time 0. The values of the two outputs come out as 20000 and 75000 satoshis, and the single witness item has 65 bytes, as the other checks of this branch use. The count that precedes a list is a compact number of one byte when it is less than 253, and uses more bytes after that.

The layout has a short and a long form. A transaction with no witness is written without the marker and the flag, and that is the form that is hashed to get the old identifier, so one transaction has two serializations. A parser that assumes one of them will misread the other, which is the reason why the call that decodes a raw transaction has an option to tell whether the hexadecimal is in the witness form, and uses a heuristic when it is not told (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The numbers are also written the unexpected way round: byte order in identifiers is reversed between the display and the bytes that are hashed.

nodes.example: the hexadecimal string of Alice's transaction
nodes.definition: Serialization writes a transaction as a sequence of bytes, with a marker and a flag before the inputs when the transaction has witness data, shown in hexadecimal notation.
