nodes.label: Decoded transaction
nodes.body: A decoded transaction is the structure that results from reading the bytes of a serialized transaction and naming each field. The command decoderawtransaction takes the hexadecimal string and returns a JSON object (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The help text of the current release describes it as returning a JSON object representing the serialized, hex-encoded transaction (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The object has the identifiers, the sizes, the version and the lock time, a list of inputs under the key vin and a list of outputs under the key vout.

paras.text: A decoded transaction is the structure that results from reading the bytes of a serialized transaction and naming each field. The command decoderawtransaction takes the hexadecimal string and returns a JSON object (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The help text of the current release describes it as returning a JSON object representing the serialized, hex-encoded transaction (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The object has the identifiers, the sizes, the version and the lock time, a list of inputs under the key vin and a list of outputs under the key vout.

Decoding turns an opaque string into something a person can check. The book remarks that the decode shows all the components of the transaction, and that following the identifier of the input to the previous transaction lets a reader walk back through the chain of transactions as the coins pass from one owner to the next (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Anyone who distrusts a wallet or an explorer can run the same decoding on their own node, which is the independent check that the chapter advocates.

In Alice's transaction the input refers to output number 1 of the earlier transaction 4ac5...3aeb, has an empty signature script, one witness item and the sequence number 4294967295, which is ffffffff; the lock time is 0 and the version 1 (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The first output has the value 0.0002 BTC, 20000 satoshis, and a script of the type witness_v1_taproot; the second has 0.00075 BTC, 75000 satoshis, and a script of the type witness_v0_keyhash. The two outputs correspond to the payment to Bob and the change back to Alice (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The decoding code reads the bytes as the serialization concept describes and converts what it reads: the satoshi values become amounts in bitcoin by dividing by 100,000,000, the scripts are shown as assembly and as hexadecimal, the type of each script is recognized from its pattern, and for a known type an address is derived and shown. Each output script also has a descriptor, the field desc, whose checksum the output descriptor concept explains (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The worked example takes the number, the amount and the type of each output from the answer of release 31.1.

The decoder shows what the bytes say, not whether they are valid or confirmed. A transaction may be well formed and still spend an output that does not exist, or one that is already spent. The values are given as decimal fractions of a bitcoin, with eight decimals, which a floating-point program should not use for money arithmetic. And the book's example gives the address of an output only because the node was able to derive it from the script: an output whose script has no standard form has no address. The call that fetches a transaction by identifier only works for mempool transactions unless the transaction index is on, or the block is named (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

nodes.definition: Decoding the serialized hexadecimal of Alice's payment shows its one input, two outputs, addresses and script types, exactly as the chain holds them.

nodes.label: Segregated witness
nodes.body: Segregated witness, often written SegWit, is an upgrade that separates the data that prove a spending right, the signatures, from the rest of the transaction. The book's glossary describes it as a proposed upgrade that separates signature data from bitcoin transactions, and as a soft fork, a change that makes the protocol rules more restrictive (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). In a transaction the separated data form the witness, a list of items for each input, which BIP 144 writes after the outputs and before the lock time (Lombrozo and Wuille, 2016).

paras.text: Segregated witness, often written SegWit, is an upgrade that separates the data that prove a spending right, the signatures, from the rest of the transaction. The book's glossary describes it as a proposed upgrade that separates signature data from bitcoin transactions, and as a soft fork, a change that makes the protocol rules more restrictive (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). In a transaction the separated data form the witness, a list of items for each input, which BIP 144 writes after the outputs and before the lock time (Lombrozo and Wuille, 2016).

The upgrade solved two problems. It removed the witness from the data that the transaction identifier covers, so that a third party can no longer change an identifier by changing a signature, a point that the malleability concept develops. And it changed the way block space is measured: BIP 141 defines the weight of a block as the base size times three plus the total size, and limits it to 4,000,000, so witness bytes count one unit each while all the other bytes count four (Lombrozo et al., 2015). Witness data are therefore cheaper than other data.

Alice's transaction uses it. Its input has an empty signature script, and all of its proof is in the witness: one item of 65 bytes, a signature of 64 bytes followed by one byte for the way it was signed (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The decoded form shows the item under the key txinwitness. Of the 194 bytes of the transaction, 125 are the old layout and 69 are the marker, the flag, the number of items, the length of the item and the item itself. The output scripts show the two kinds that the upgrade created: a witness script of version 0 that pays to a key hash, and one of version 1, the taproot type.

Software that knows the upgrade finds a witness program in an output script: a version number followed by a short piece of data. For version 0 the program is either 20 bytes, a key hash, or 32 bytes, a script hash; versions 1 to 16 are reserved for future extensions (Lombrozo et al., 2015). The block commits to the witnesses of its transactions through a second tree built from the witness identifiers, and the witness identifier of the coinbase transaction is taken to be all zeros (Lombrozo et al., 2015). The worked example shows the byte accounting: 194 minus 125 is 69, which is the marker and flag, the count and the length, and the 65 bytes.

The upgrade was designed to be a soft fork: old nodes see an output script with a version and a program and consider anyone able to spend it, while upgraded nodes enforce the new rules, so old nodes keep accepting the chain without understanding the witness (Lombrozo et al., 2015). This also means that a node which does not understand witnesses cannot verify the signatures of such transactions, even though it accepts them, which is a reason to run current software. The upgrade was activated at height 481824 on the main network, a constant that Bitcoin Core's chain parameters record (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

nodes.definition: Segregated witness moves the signature data of a transaction out of the part that the identifier covers, into a witness that counts less toward the size limit.

nodes.label: Transaction weight
nodes.body: The weight of a transaction is a measure of the block space it uses, in weight units. BIP 141 defines it as the base transaction size times three plus the total transaction size, and defines the virtual size as the weight divided by four, rounded up to the next integer (Lombrozo et al., 2015). The base size is the size in bytes of the old serialization, without any witness data, and the total size is the size of the new one, with the witness. Equivalently, every byte outside the witness counts four units and every byte inside it counts one.

paras.text: The weight of a transaction is a measure of the block space it uses, in weight units. BIP 141 defines it as the base transaction size times three plus the total transaction size, and defines the virtual size as the weight divided by four, rounded up to the next integer (Lombrozo et al., 2015). The base size is the size in bytes of the old serialization, without any witness data, and the total size is the size of the new one, with the witness. Equivalently, every byte outside the witness counts four units and every byte inside it counts one.

Weight is the unit in which the limit of a block is set. The source of the consensus rules gives the maximum block weight as 4,000,000 and the witness scale factor as 4, so a block of only old-style bytes can contain 1,000,000 of them, and a block with witnesses can contain more (Bitcoin Core, 2026). Weight is also the basis of the fee rate that chapter 2 introduced: a fee rate in satoshis per virtual byte divides the fee by the weight over four, which is why the decoded answer shows both the size and the virtual size.

The decoded form of Alice's transaction shows size 194, vsize 143 and weight 569, the three numbers printed in the book and reproduced by release 31.1 (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The Python parser of this branch finds that the old layout is 125 bytes and the full one 194. The weight is then 3 times 125 plus 194, which is 569, and the virtual size is 569 divided by 4, which is 142.25, rounded up to 143. The worked example is the same arithmetic, written as four times the base size plus the witness bytes.

Weight units make the witness discount a precise rule. The 69 extra bytes of Alice's transaction, the marker, the flag and the witness, cost 69 units, whereas the 125 base bytes cost 500, so the witness is 35.6 percent of the bytes of the transaction but only 12.1 percent of its weight, which is 69 out of 569. The same transaction written without its witness would weigh 500. The rounding up is why the virtual size is a whole number, and why two transactions can have the same virtual size and different weights.

Virtual bytes are not bytes, and the discount does not reduce the data that nodes must store or send: a node still downloads and stores all 194 bytes. The limit on weight is a consensus rule, whereas the policy of which transactions a node relays has other limits, one of which is the minimum fee rate, so a transaction of valid weight may still not be relayed. A last point is that older material speaks of a block limit of one megabyte, a rule that the upgrade replaced by the limit of weight, and the figure quoted in the book for the block of the later example, 4179 bytes, is far below either.

nodes.definition: A transaction's weight counts its non-witness bytes four times and its witness bytes once, and its virtual size is the weight divided by four, rounded up.

nodes.label: Transaction identifier (txid and wtxid)
nodes.body: A transaction identifier is the name of a transaction: the double SHA-256 hash of its serialization, written with the bytes in reverse order. The transaction has two of them. BIP 141 leaves the definition of the txid unchanged, the double SHA-256 hash of the traditional serialization format, and defines a new witness identifier, the wtxid, as the double SHA-256 hash of the serialization with witness data (Lombrozo et al., 2015). In the decoded answer the first appears under txid and the second under hash.

paras.text: A transaction identifier is the name of a transaction: the double SHA-256 hash of its serialization, written with the bytes in reverse order. The transaction has two of them. BIP 141 leaves the definition of the txid unchanged, the double SHA-256 hash of the traditional serialization format, and defines a new witness identifier, the wtxid, as the double SHA-256 hash of the serialization with witness data (Lombrozo et al., 2015). In the decoded answer the first appears under txid and the second under hash.

Identifiers are how everything refers to a transaction: the inputs of later transactions, the lists in blocks, the Merkle tree, the requests to the node. Having a second identifier that covers the witness allows the network to commit to the signatures in the block without changing what the old identifier covers. If no input uses a witness, the two identifiers are equal (Lombrozo et al., 2015). The book's tip adds the warning that a txid is not authoritative, a point that the malleability concept develops (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The book gives the identifier of Alice's transaction as 466200308696215bbc949d5141a49a4138ecdfdfaa2a8029c1f9bcecd1f96177 and the node's decode shows the second one under the key hash as f7cdbc7cf8b910d35cc69962e791138624e4eae7901010a6da4c02e7d238cdac (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The Python parser of this branch computes both from the hexadecimal: it hashes the 125 bytes of the old layout twice with SHA-256 for the txid, and the 194 bytes of the full layout for the wtxid, and reverses the byte order of each result.

The reversal is the reason why identifiers, which are numbers, are written backwards: the 32-byte hash result is shown with its last byte first, the way the block hashes, which start with many zeros, are conventionally displayed. The Merkle tree of a block is built from txids, and BIP 141 adds a second tree built from wtxids, whose root is committed to in the coinbase transaction (Lombrozo et al., 2015). The coinbase transaction's wtxid is assumed to be 32 zero bytes (Lombrozo et al., 2015).

A txid can be looked up in the block files only with the transaction index or with the name of the block, as the earlier concepts explain, and the book warns that the absence of a txid from the blockchain does not mean the transaction was not processed (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The wtxid is the more specific name, and is the one used when transactions are announced to peers in current protocols. It is also not secret, and not an address: two parties who know the identifier know only which transaction is meant.

nodes.definition: The txid hashes the transaction without its witness and the hash includes it; a txid is not authoritative before confirmation because a transaction can be modified.

nodes.label: Transaction malleability
nodes.body: Transaction malleability is the possibility that a transaction can be changed by a third party before it is confirmed, so that its identifier changes while what it does stays the same. The book puts it in a tip: a transaction ID is not authoritative, the absence of a txid from the blockchain does not mean that the transaction was not processed, and this is known as transaction malleability because transactions can be modified before confirmation in a block, changing their txids (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The reason is that the identifier hashes data, such as signatures, that someone other than the sender may be able to alter.

paras.text: Transaction malleability is the possibility that a transaction can be changed by a third party before it is confirmed, so that its identifier changes while what it does stays the same. The book puts it in a tip: a transaction ID is not authoritative, the absence of a txid from the blockchain does not mean that the transaction was not processed, and this is known as transaction malleability because transactions can be modified before confirmation in a block, changing their txids (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The reason is that the identifier hashes data, such as signatures, that someone other than the sender may be able to alter.

A program that watches for a payment by its txid can be misled. If a transaction is changed in transit and the changed version is the one that is confirmed, the original identifier never appears in a block, and a program that waits for it would conclude that the payment failed although the money moved. The book's advice is to treat the txid as authoritative only after confirmation: after the transaction is included in a block, its txid cannot change unless a reorganization removes that block from the best chain, and reorganizations are rare after several confirmations (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The problem was met by exchanges and by protocols that build a chain of unconfirmed transactions, since the child names the parent by its txid and breaks if the parent's txid changes. Segregated witness addresses it for the transactions that use it: because the txid does not cover the witness, a change of the signature changes the wtxid but not the txid (Lombrozo et al., 2015). The worked example shows this on Alice's transaction: it flips one bit of the signature, which makes the transaction invalid but serves to show the identifiers. The wtxid changes, the txid does not, and all the bytes before the witness are unchanged.

The old identifier covers the version, the inputs, the outputs and the lock time. For inputs that spend a witness output the signature script is empty and the signature is in the witness, outside that hash; so no one can change what the txid covers without changing the transaction's meaning, since the signatures commit to those fields. For old-style inputs the signature script is covered, and the signature encoding could be altered, which is why the BIPs of the time tightened what is accepted. The wtxid covers everything and so does change.

Segregated witness does not make every transaction immune. A transaction that spends an old-style output still has its signature script in the txid, and a transaction can still be replaced by a conflicting one that spends the same inputs, which is a different matter from malleability, since it has different outputs or a different meaning. The wtxid, in turn, can still change with the witness. And the TIP of the book is still true for the careful programmer: use the transaction's confirmation, not only its identifier, to know that a payment was made.

nodes.example: changing a signature changes the wtxid but not the txid
nodes.definition: Malleability is the possibility that a transaction is modified before confirmation so that its identifier changes while its meaning does not; the witness separation removed it for the txid of witness spends.

nodes.label: Block
nodes.body: The block group collects the concepts about the unit in which transactions are recorded. A block holds a header, which is a small fixed-size summary, and a list of transactions, which makes up most of its size; the book of the chapter on the blockchain says that the header is 80 bytes while the transactions of a block can total much more (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). In the chapter on Bitcoin Core the block is explored with two commands: one finds a block's hash from its height, and the other returns the block as a JSON object.

paras.text: The block group collects the concepts about the unit in which transactions are recorded. A block holds a header, which is a small fixed-size summary, and a list of transactions, which makes up most of its size; the book of the chapter on the blockchain says that the header is 80 bytes while the transactions of a block can total much more (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). In the chapter on Bitcoin Core the block is explored with two commands: one finds a block's hash from its height, and the other returns the block as a JSON object.

Knowing the block's fields is knowing how the chain is held together. Each block names its parent by the hash of its header, so changing anything in a block changes its hash and breaks the link to the next. The header also commits to the transactions through the Merkle root, to the work that was spent through the target and the nonce, and to the time through the timestamp. The book says of the fields of the answer that some are used for security and proof of work: merkle root, nonce, bits, difficulty and chainwork (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The reader meets the group in the answer of the block command for block 123456 in the book: its hash, 13 transactions, a height, the number of confirmations, the version, the Merkle root, the time, the median time, the nonce, the bits, the difficulty, the chain work, the sizes and the list of transaction identifiers (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The evidence of this version confirms the hash of this block from its header, its Merkle root from its 13 identifiers, and its difficulty from its bits, using the public data of an explorer (Blockstream, 2026).

The concepts of the group go from the outside to the inside. The height and the hash name a block, the header holds what is hashed, the weight measures the size, the Merkle root summarizes the transactions, the subsidy is the new money it creates, the compact target and the difficulty say how hard it was to make, and the median time is the clock rule that bounds its timestamp.

nodes.label: Block height
nodes.body: The height of a block is its position in the chain: the number of blocks that precede it. The book says that the height tells how many blocks preceded the block, and the glossary of the chapter on the blockchain adds that the first block, the genesis block, is at height 0 (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The description in the source code is the same: the genesis block has height 0, and the field of the chain information called blocks gives the height of the chain of most work that has been fully validated (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

paras.text: The height of a block is its position in the chain: the number of blocks that precede it. The book says that the height tells how many blocks preceded the block, and the glossary of the chapter on the blockchain adds that the first block, the genesis block, is at height 0 (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The description in the source code is the same: the genesis block has height 0, and the field of the chain information called blocks gives the height of the chain of most work that has been fully validated (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

Heights give people a convenient name for a block, because they are short and ordered. A hash identifies a block without doubt, but it cannot be read or ordered; a height can be said aloud and compared. The book says that blocks can be referenced either by their height or by their hash, and the first command of the exploration, getblockhash, takes a height and returns the block header hash (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The consensus rules also use heights: they decide when the reward is halved and when an upgrade becomes active.

In the book the command getblockhash 123456 returns 0000000000002917ed80650c6174aac8dfc46f5fe36480aaef682ff6cd83c3ca (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). For block 1000 it returns 00000000c937983704a73af28acdec37b049d214adbda81d7e2a3dd146f6ed09, which the evidence of this version checks by hashing the block's header (Blockstream, 2026). In the source of Bitcoin Core the heights of the rule changes are constants of the main network, for example 227931 for the rule of BIP 34, 481824 for segregated witness, and 210000 as the interval between halvings of the subsidy (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

The height is not stored in the header and is not part of a block's identity: it is the length of the path to the genesis block, and the node counts it in its index. This also means that two blocks may have the same height, if there is a fork, though only one of them can be part of the best chain. The relation to depth is simple: the depth of a block is the height of the tip minus its height plus one. For block 123456, whose book printout says 651742 confirmations, the tip then has height 123456 + 651742 - 1 = 775197, as the worked example computes.

Height 0 is the first block and not the second, so the number of blocks in a chain is its height plus one. A height is also not a proof: the same height names different blocks on different chains, and BIP 34 made the height a part of the coinbase of each block precisely so that it is unambiguous (Andresen, 2012). The height of the tip changes every ten minutes or so, and any figure quoted in the book, such as the assumption that the node is at least at block 775,072, is a snapshot of that day (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

nodes.definition: A block is found by its height, how many blocks precede it, or by its header hash; its confirmations count the blocks built on top, itself included.

nodes.label: Block hash
nodes.body: The block hash is the identifier of a block. The book on the blockchain explains that the primary identifier of a block is its cryptographic hash, a commitment made by hashing the block header twice through the SHA-256 algorithm, and that the resulting 32-byte hash is called the block hash but is more accurately the block header hash, because only the header is used to compute it (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The first block of the chain has the hash 000000000019d6689c085ae165831e934ff763ae46a2a6c172b3f1b60a8ce26f, which the log and the chain information of the release 31.1 also show (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

paras.text: The block hash is the identifier of a block. The book on the blockchain explains that the primary identifier of a block is its cryptographic hash, a commitment made by hashing the block header twice through the SHA-256 algorithm, and that the resulting 32-byte hash is called the block hash but is more accurately the block header hash, because only the header is used to compute it (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The first block of the chain has the hash 000000000019d6689c085ae165831e934ff763ae46a2a6c172b3f1b60a8ce26f, which the log and the chain information of the release 31.1 also show (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

A single hash stands for the entire block, because the header contains the Merkle root of the transactions, and the next block's header contains this hash as the previous block hash. Anyone who knows the hash of the latest block can in principle check the whole chain behind it. The book says that the hash identifies a block uniquely and unambiguously and can be independently derived by any node by hashing the header (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The hashes in the chapter all begin with a long string of zeros: 0000000000002917... for block 123456 and 00000000c9379837... for block 1000. These zeros are the proof of work that the miners did, as chapter 2 explained: the hash of a header had to be below a target (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The worked example takes the header of block 123456 from the explorer's data, with the version, the previous hash, the Merkle root, the time, the bits and the nonce, hashes it, and compares the result with the printed hash; for block 1000 the check in the next concept does the same.

The header's fields are packed in a fixed order into 80 bytes: the version as four bytes with the least significant first, the 32 bytes of the previous block hash and 32 bytes of the Merkle root, both reversed from their display order, and the time, the bits and the nonce as four bytes each. The packed bytes are put through SHA-256 twice, and the 32-byte result is reversed to produce the familiar display. The book notes that the hash is not included in the block's data structure; each node computes it as the block arrives and may store it in a separate index (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

A hash is not an authority. It tells which block is meant, not whether the block is valid or part of the best chain; a block with a very small hash can still be invalid because of a transaction in it. The display order differs from the order used in computation, and a program that forgets to reverse the bytes gets a different value. And the explorer's data used here are a secondary source: the check confirms that the explorer's fields are consistent with each other, which is what the hash promises, not that the explorer is honest about the chain.

nodes.definition: The block hash is the double SHA-256 hash of the 80-byte block header, written backwards; it identifies a block uniquely and is not stored in the block.

nodes.label: Block header
nodes.body: The block header is the summary at the head of every block. The book's table lists its six fields and their sizes: the version, four bytes; the previous block hash, 32 bytes, a hash of the previous block in the chain; the Merkle root, 32 bytes, the root of the Merkle tree of the block's transactions; the timestamp, four bytes, the approximate creation time as Unix epoch time; the target, four bytes, a compact encoding of the proof-of-work target; and the nonce, four bytes, arbitrary data used for the proof-of-work algorithm (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The sum, 4 + 32 + 32 + 4 + 4 + 4, is 80 bytes.

paras.text: The block header is the summary at the head of every block. The book's table lists its six fields and their sizes: the version, four bytes; the previous block hash, 32 bytes, a hash of the previous block in the chain; the Merkle root, 32 bytes, the root of the Merkle tree of the block's transactions; the timestamp, four bytes, the approximate creation time as Unix epoch time; the target, four bytes, a compact encoding of the proof-of-work target; and the nonce, four bytes, arbitrary data used for the proof-of-work algorithm (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The sum, 4 + 32 + 32 + 4 + 4 + 4, is 80 bytes.

The header is small on purpose. Because it commits to everything else, a program that holds only the headers can follow the chain and its work without the transactions. This is what the node in the book does when it starts: it first fetches the block headers from its peers to find the blockchain with the most proof of work, and afterward continues to download the full blocks (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Nakamoto's paper made the same point about lighter programs: a user needs to keep only a copy of the block headers of the longest proof-of-work chain (Nakamoto, 2008).

The fields are found under the same names in the answer of the block command: version, merkleroot, time, nonce, bits and previousblockhash, together with the hash itself (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). For block 123456 the version is 1, the time 1305200806 and the nonce 2436437219; its header is the 80-byte string whose double hash is the block hash (Blockstream, 2026). The chain information of the node shows bits and target for the best block as well (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

Each field has a role in the chain. The previous block hash links the block to its parent. The Merkle root ties the transactions to the header. The target says how small the hash has to be, and the nonce is what the miner changes to try again, together with the timestamp and, indirectly, the contents of the coinbase transaction. The timestamp is a Unix time, a count of seconds since the first of January 1970, and it must obey the rules of the median time and of the two-hour limit (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The version field no longer means a version. The book's table says it was originally a version field and its use has evolved; the upgrade mechanism of BIP 9 uses its bits to signal readiness, as the soft fork concept explains (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Wuille et al., 2015). The header's time is set by the miner and is only roughly right. And the header does not contain the number of transactions, the block's height or its hash, which are all derived.

nodes.definition: The block header holds the version, the previous block hash, the Merkle root, the timestamp, the compact target and the nonce, in 80 bytes.

nodes.label: Block weight
nodes.body: The weight of a block is its size in weight units, calculated like the weight of a transaction: BIP 141 defines it as the base size times three plus the total size, where the base size is the size without witness data and the total size is the size with it (Lombrozo et al., 2015). The block command returns three measurements, which the book describes as the legacy stripped size, the full size, and the size in weight units (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The rule is that the block weight must not exceed 4,000,000 (Lombrozo et al., 2015).

paras.text: The weight of a block is its size in weight units, calculated like the weight of a transaction: BIP 141 defines it as the base size times three plus the total size, where the base size is the size without witness data and the total size is the size with it (Lombrozo et al., 2015). The block command returns three measurements, which the book describes as the legacy stripped size, the full size, and the size in weight units (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The rule is that the block weight must not exceed 4,000,000 (Lombrozo et al., 2015).

The limit decides how many transactions a block can hold, and so how much the network can do in ten minutes. It replaced the earlier limit of 1,000,000 bytes of total size with a combined measure, so that witness data, which is cheaper to verify and does not burden the set of unspent outputs, is charged less (Lombrozo et al., 2015). The limit is also a constant in the source: the maximum block weight is 4,000,000, and the witness scale factor is 4 (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

For block 123456, which was mined years before the upgrade, the book's answer shows a stripped size of 4179, a size of 4179 and a weight of 16716 (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). When a block has no witness data, the base size and the total size are the same, so the weight is 3 times 4179 plus 4179, or simply 4 times 4179, which is 16716, as the worked example computes. The explorer's data for the block agree: 13 transactions, size 4179 and weight 16716 (Blockstream, 2026).

The node computes the weight by serializing the block twice, once without and once with witness data, and combining the sizes; the source shows the three results being filled into the answer as strippedsize, size and weight (Bitcoin Core, 2026). A block with witness data has a total size larger than its stripped size, and a weight between four times the stripped size and the total size times 4, so a full block of heavy-witness transactions can have a total size well above one million bytes while staying below the limit in weight units.

Weight is not the same as size and the two should not be mixed. A tool that reports a block size in bytes and one that reports it in virtual bytes give different numbers for the same block, and a reader who compares them with the limit of 4,000,000 must use the weight. The limit is also a rule for miners, not for relay nodes, which means that a block over the limit is invalid, whereas a transaction is only rejected by policy before that.

nodes.definition: A block without witness data weighs four times its size in weight units, which the getblock result shows as size, strippedsize and weight.

nodes.label: Merkle root
nodes.body: The Merkle root is the single hash in a block header that stands for all the transactions of the block. The glossary of the book describes a Merkle tree as a tree constructed by hashing paired data, the leaves, then pairing and hashing the results until a single hash remains, the Merkle root; in Bitcoin the leaves are almost always the transactions of one block (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The root is a descendant of all the hashed pairs in the tree, and a block header must include a valid root for the transactions in the block (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: The Merkle root is the single hash in a block header that stands for all the transactions of the block. The glossary of the book describes a Merkle tree as a tree constructed by hashing paired data, the leaves, then pairing and hashing the results until a single hash remains, the Merkle root; in Bitcoin the leaves are almost always the transactions of one block (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The root is a descendant of all the hashed pairs in the tree, and a block header must include a valid root for the transactions in the block (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The root makes the header a commitment to the contents. Changing, adding, removing or reordering any transaction changes the root, which changes the header and so the block hash, and the proof of work would have to be redone. It also allows a short proof of membership: to show that one transaction is in a block, one needs only the hashes along the path from the transaction to the root, not the whole block, a property that Nakamoto's paper describes when it explains how payments can be verified without running a full node (Nakamoto, 2008).

The answer of the block command shows the root under merkleroot and lists the transaction identifiers under tx; for block 123456 it lists 13 (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The evidence of this version takes these 13 identifiers from the explorer, builds the tree and obtains 0e60651a9934e8f0decd1c5fde39309e48fca0cd1c84a21ddfde95033762d86c, which is the Merkle root in the header of the block and the one printed in the book (Blockstream, 2026) (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). In the header it occupies 32 bytes.

The tree is built from the bottom. The identifiers of the transactions are the leaves, taken in their bytes in the internal order, which is the reverse of the display order; each pair is joined and hashed twice with SHA-256, giving a level with half as many nodes; and the process repeats until one hash remains. When a level has an odd number of nodes, the last one is paired with itself. With 13 leaves the levels have 13, 7, 4, 2 and 1 nodes, because the lists of 13 and 7 are each extended by a copy of the last element before pairing, as the worked example does.

The rule of duplicating the last element has a known weakness: two different lists of transactions can give the same root if the later one repeats the last transaction, and for this reason a node must check a block's transactions for duplication in addition to the root. The root is also computed from txids, not wtxids, so it does not commit to the witnesses; the second tree of BIP 141 does (Lombrozo et al., 2015). And a root is not evidence of validity: it proves only that the listed transactions are those that the miner hashed.

nodes.example: the Merkle root of the block's transactions
nodes.definition: The Merkle root in a block header commits to every transaction of the block, and hashing the block's transaction identifiers pairwise up to one value reproduces it.

nodes.label: Block subsidy
nodes.body: The block subsidy is the amount of new bitcoin that a block creates, which the miner may claim in the first transaction of the block, the coinbase transaction. Bitcoin Core computes it in a short function: the number of halvings is the height divided by the halving interval of 210,000 blocks, the subsidy starts at 50 bitcoins, and it is shifted right once for each halving, which divides it by two each time (Bitcoin Core, 2026). Chapter 2 introduced the block reward, which is this subsidy plus the fees of the block's transactions.

paras.text: The block subsidy is the amount of new bitcoin that a block creates, which the miner may claim in the first transaction of the block, the coinbase transaction. Bitcoin Core computes it in a short function: the number of halvings is the height divided by the halving interval of 210,000 blocks, the subsidy starts at 50 bitcoins, and it is shifted right once for each halving, which divides it by two each time (Bitcoin Core, 2026). Chapter 2 introduced the block reward, which is this subsidy plus the fees of the block's transactions.

The schedule is what makes the supply of bitcoin finite and predictable. The amounts are counted in satoshis, 100,000,000 to a bitcoin, so each shift right halves an integer; the sum of all the subsidies over the 64 possible periods is 2,099,999,997,690,000 satoshis, which is slightly below 21 million bitcoins by 2,310,000 satoshis, because of the rounding in the shifts, as the worked checks of this branch compute (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The consensus constant for the maximum amount of money is 21,000,000 times the number of satoshis in a bitcoin (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

The book's program that adds the outputs of block 775072 says that the total includes a reward of 25 bitcoins (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The subsidy at that height is not 25: 775072 divided by 210000 is 3 with a remainder, so there have been three halvings and the subsidy is 50 shifted right three times, which is 6.25 bitcoins, or 625000000 satoshis, as the worked example computes. The coinbase transaction of that block in the explorer's data pays out 633799108 satoshis, which is 625000000 plus fees of 8799108, and the sum of the fees of the other 1,965 transactions is exactly that number (Blockstream, 2026).

The coinbase transaction cannot create more than the subsidy plus the fees of the block, and the amount is checked by every node. The function ends in zero for a height of 64 halvings or more, because a shift by 64 or more is undefined in the language of the program and the code returns zero instead (Bitcoin Core, 2026). A coinbase output also cannot be spent until it is 100 blocks deep, a constant named the coinbase maturity in the consensus source (Bitcoin Core, 2026). For block 775072 the numbers fit: 633,799,108 less 625,000,000 is 8,799,108.

The book's text mentions a reward of 25 BTC and 0.0909 BTC in fees for the block of its example, and the total of 10,322.07722534 BTC. Neither matches block 775072: its reward is 6.25 BTC, its fees are 0.08799108 BTC, and the sum of all its outputs is 5,863.00566521 BTC, so the printed result does not belong to that block, and a student who compares with an explorer, as the book suggests, will find the difference (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Blockstream, 2026). 25 BTC was the reward for blocks 420,000 to 629,999. The error shows why printed numbers should be checked.

nodes.definition: The subsidy starts at 50 bitcoins and is shifted right once for every 210,000 blocks, so it is 6.25 bitcoins at height 775072.

nodes.label: Compact target (bits)
nodes.body: The compact target is the way in which the header records the proof-of-work target in only four bytes. The target is a 256-bit number that the hash of a valid block must not exceed, as chapter 2 explained for the difficulty target, and a 256-bit number would need 32 bytes. The header's field, called bits, holds instead an exponent in the first byte and a mantissa in the other three. The book's table calls the field a compact encoding of the proof-of-work target (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: The compact target is the way in which the header records the proof-of-work target in only four bytes. The target is a 256-bit number that the hash of a valid block must not exceed, as chapter 2 explained for the difficulty target, and a 256-bit number would need 32 bytes. The header's field, called bits, holds instead an exponent in the first byte and a mantissa in the other three. The book's table calls the field a compact encoding of the proof-of-work target (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

Four bytes were enough because the target needs only a few digits of precision: it changes in small steps, and the lower digits would not matter. A compact form keeps the header at 80 bytes. The chain information of the current release shows both the compact form, in the field bits, and the target in full, which the book's printout of 2023 does not have (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The form also has a sign bit, a legacy of the number type it was borrowed from, which Bitcoin Core rejects as a target when it is set.

The block printed in the book has the bits 1a6a93b3, which is 443192243 in decimal and the value the explorer gives for block 123456 (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Blockstream, 2026). The first byte, 0x1a, is 26, and the other three bytes are 0x6a93b3. For the first block the value is 1d00ffff, and the chain information of the evidence node shows it together with the full target, 00000000ffff followed by zeros (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

The source decodes the field with two lines: the size is the value shifted right by 24 bits, the word is the value masked by 0x007fffff, and the target is the word shifted left by 8 times the size minus 3 bits, that is, by size minus three bytes (Bitcoin Core, 2026). For 0x1a6a93b3 this puts the three bytes 6a 93 b3 followed by 23 zero bytes, which written in 64 hexadecimal digits is 0000000000006a93b300...00, with 12 leading zero digits, as the worked example prints. The reverse conversion rounds a target down to three significant bytes, so not every number is the target of a block.

Because only three bytes of the target are kept, the true target that the hash is compared with is the decoded one, not the one the retargeting formula first computed, and a table of difficulties from a program that uses the full-precision number can differ by a tiny amount from one that uses bits. A second caution is the sign bit: the code reduces the mantissa and raises the size if the top bit of the three bytes is set, so values such as 0x1d00ffff and not 0x1d0100.. are seen in practice. And the header's field is named bits in the answer but target in the book's table (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

nodes.definition: The bits field is a four-byte compact form of the target: the first byte is the length in bytes and the next three are the leading digits, so the target is the digits shifted left by the length minus three bytes.

nodes.label: Difficulty
nodes.body: The difficulty is a number that tells how much harder it is to produce a valid block than it was at the start. The glossary of the book defines it as a network-wide setting that controls how much computation is required to produce a proof of work (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). It is defined relative to the easiest allowed target, that of the first block, so the first block has difficulty 1, as the chain information of the evidence node shows, and a block with a target a hundred times smaller has difficulty 100.

paras.text: The difficulty is a number that tells how much harder it is to produce a valid block than it was at the start. The glossary of the book defines it as a network-wide setting that controls how much computation is required to produce a proof of work (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). It is defined relative to the easiest allowed target, that of the first block, so the first block has difficulty 1, as the chain information of the evidence node shows, and a block with a target a hundred times smaller has difficulty 100.

The network keeps the time between blocks near ten minutes by changing the difficulty. The consensus parameters give a target spacing of 10 minutes and a target timespan of two weeks, which is 2016 blocks; after every 2016 blocks the target is multiplied by the time the last 2016 blocks actually took and divided by two weeks, and the change in one step is limited to a factor of four in either direction (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The book says that every node retargets independently, every 2,016 blocks, and notes a small bias of 0.05 percent toward higher difficulty because the calculation uses 2,015 intervals (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

For block 123456 the answer of the block command shows the difficulty 157416.4018436489 and the bits 1a6a93b3 (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The worked example computes the ratio of the two targets: 0xffff times 256 to the power 26 over 0x6a93b3 times 256 to the power 23, which is 157416.4018436489. The explorer gives the same value with one more digit, 157416.40184364893, since the book's printout is rounded to its sixteen significant digits (Blockstream, 2026). In the chain information of release 31.1 the first block has difficulty 1 (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

The program in Bitcoin Core computes it from the bits with floating-point arithmetic: it takes 0x0000ffff divided by the mantissa, and multiplies or divides by 256 until the exponent is 29, the value for the easiest target (Bitcoin Core, 2026). Written as an exact ratio the formula is the same as the example. The retargeting code in pow.cpp clamps the timespan to between a quarter and four times the target timespan, multiplies the old target by the timespan, divides by two weeks, and never allows a target above the proof-of-work limit (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

Difficulty is a result and not a setting that anyone chooses: it follows the hash rate of miners with a delay of up to two weeks, so a sudden fall in mining power slows blocks until the next adjustment. It is also relative: a difficulty of 157,416 at one time and one of 53,911,173,001,054 at another, the figure printed in the book's cookie example, say how the work grew, not how much work either was (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). A change in a test network may follow different rules, since the parameters allow a minimum-difficulty exception there (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

nodes.definition: A block's difficulty follows from its bits, the compact form of its target, as the ratio of the easiest target to this block's target.

nodes.label: Median time past
nodes.body: The median time past, often written MTP, is a clock that the chain defines for itself. For a block it is the median, the middle value in sorted order, of the timestamps of that block and the ten before it. Bitcoin Core's source states the number of blocks as the constant 11, sorts the times and returns the element in the middle (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The book of the chapter on mining says that no node will accept a block with a time less than or equal to the median time of the last 11 blocks, called the median time past (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: The median time past, often written MTP, is a clock that the chain defines for itself. For a block it is the median, the middle value in sorted order, of the timestamps of that block and the ten before it. Bitcoin Core's source states the number of blocks as the constant 11, sorts the times and returns the element in the middle (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The book of the chapter on mining says that no node will accept a block with a time less than or equal to the median time of the last 11 blocks, called the median time past (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The timestamps in headers are set by the miners, who have some latitude, and the book explains the danger: a miner could set the time in the future to lower the difficulty, or in the past to make it look as if blocks were slow, or to collect the fees of transactions with time locks that have not matured (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The median of eleven blocks is hard for one miner to move; BIP 113 made it the time that the checks on time locks use, so that the incentive to lie disappears (Kerin and Friedenbach, 2015).

The answer of the block command shows the median under mediantime. For block 123456 it is 1305197900, while the block's own timestamp is 1305200806, which is 2906 seconds later (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Blockstream, 2026). The chain information of the node shows the same field for the best block, and for the first block, which has no predecessors, the median equals its own time (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The source applies the median of the previous block to check a new block's time, with the error time-too-old (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

The worked example takes the times of blocks 123446 to 123456, the eleven blocks ending with block 123456, sorts them and picks the sixth, which is 1305197900, the time of block 123451. This is exactly the value the node reports. The time-lock rule works one block later: the median used when checking a new block is that of its parent, and a block whose time is not greater than it is rejected (Bitcoin Core, 2026) (Kerin and Friedenbach, 2015). The consensus time is thus usually about an hour behind the wall clock, as the book notes (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The book describes the field as the median time of the 11 blocks that precede the block, but the code includes the block itself. The eleven blocks that precede block 123456 are blocks 123445 to 123455, whose median is 1305195947, not the 1305197900 that the node prints, so the sentence of the chapter is slightly off, and the median of the chapter on mining is the one that the field shows (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Bitcoin Core, 2026). Timestamps are also not required to increase from block to block, only to exceed the median, so a sorted list of times can differ from the order of blocks.

nodes.definition: The median time past is the middle value of the timestamps of the last 11 blocks, which the consensus rules use as the clock for time limits because a single miner cannot move it.

nodes.label: Chain state
nodes.body: The chain state group collects the concepts that describe the blocks as a whole: which chain is the true one, how much work it represents, how deep a block is in it, and what happens when the node changes its mind. The word has a second meaning in Bitcoin Core, where the chain state is also the name of the database of unspent outputs, as the earlier concept on the set of unspent outputs explained; here the word means the shape of the chain (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

paras.text: The chain state group collects the concepts that describe the blocks as a whole: which chain is the true one, how much work it represents, how deep a block is in it, and what happens when the node changes its mind. The word has a second meaning in Bitcoin Core, where the chain state is also the name of the database of unspent outputs, as the earlier concept on the set of unspent outputs explained; here the word means the shape of the chain (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

A blockchain is not a single list but a tree, since two miners may find blocks at about the same time. The rule that resolves the tree is simple, and everything a user can trust depends on it. The book says that by selecting the greatest-cumulative-work valid chain all nodes eventually achieve network-wide consensus, and that temporary discrepancies between chains are resolved as more work is added (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The concepts of this group make that rule precise.

The group shows in the answers of the node: the chain work in the chain information and in the block data, the confirmations in the block data and the transaction data, and the reorganization only when the best chain changes, an event that the log records. The book's tip about transaction IDs refers to it, since a txid can change only if a reorganization removes the block that holds the transaction (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The rule works on accumulated work rather than on length or on arrival time. Each block's header declares the target its identifier had to fall below, and from that target the work the block must have cost can be computed; the work of a chain is the sum over its blocks. A node holds every valid chain it has heard of and treats the one with the greatest total work as the chain, which means a shorter chain of harder blocks beats a longer chain of easier ones. When a competing chain overtakes the current one, the node reorganizes: it undoes the blocks it had applied, returning their transactions to the waiting pool unless the new chain already contains them, and applies the blocks of the new chain instead. Nothing is voted on and no message is exchanged to settle it, because each node reaches the same conclusion from the same arithmetic (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Nakamoto, 2008).

The caution is that this makes confirmation a matter of degree rather than of kind. A transaction in the most recent block is in the chain only as long as that block stays in the chain, and a reorganization one block deep is an ordinary event rather than an attack. What depth is enough is therefore an economic question about the value at stake and not a technical constant, which is why the figure the book's glossary quotes is a convention rather than a rule a node enforces. A learner should also keep the two senses of the words chain state apart: in this section it means the shape of the chain, while in the software it also names the database of spendable outputs (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

nodes.label: Best chain
nodes.body: The best chain is the chain of valid blocks that a node regards as the true record. Nakamoto's paper states the rule as the longest proof-of-work chain, the one that represents the greatest effort (Nakamoto, 2008). The book of the chapter on mining restates it precisely as the greatest-cumulative-work valid chain (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The end of the best chain is called its tip, and the node's chain information reports the height of the most-work fully validated chain as the number of blocks (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

paras.text: The best chain is the chain of valid blocks that a node regards as the true record. Nakamoto's paper states the rule as the longest proof-of-work chain, the one that represents the greatest effort (Nakamoto, 2008). The book of the chapter on mining restates it precisely as the greatest-cumulative-work valid chain (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The end of the best chain is called its tip, and the node's chain information reports the height of the most-work fully validated chain as the number of blocks (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

Without such a rule nodes would not agree, and without agreement there would be no single record of who owns what. Because blocks are found by a random process, two miners sometimes find a block at nearly the same time, and the chain forks: the glossary of the book describes this accidental fork as the situation when two or more blocks have the same height (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The rule tells every node which branch to follow, and as the next block is found on one of them, that branch gains work and the other is abandoned.

A node applies the rule whenever a new block arrives. The book describes it: the node looks at the block's previous block hash and tries to find that parent in the existing blockchain; most of the time the parent is the tip of the best chain, and the new block extends it; sometimes it does not, and then the node attaches the header to a secondary chain and compares the work of the two (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The setting of the block header on a branch and the fields of the answer, such as confirmations equal to -1 for a block that is not on the main chain, show this to the user (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

Work, not length, decides. The chain work concept shows how to measure it: a block with a smaller target represents more expected hashes. The worked example compares an invented chain A of three blocks at the first block's target with an invented chain B of two blocks at a target four times smaller. Chain A has three units of work and chain B has two blocks of four units each, a ratio of 8 to 3, so B has about 2.67 times the work, although it is shorter, and a node would follow B. These numbers are made up for the illustration.

The best chain is a local judgment that nodes make with the same rule, not an announcement. At any moment two honest nodes can briefly hold different tips, and a payment in a block at the tip is not final. The longest-chain wording of the paper is a shorthand that was precise in a time when every block had the same difficulty, and the more exact wording is the one with the most work. Also, the rule applies only to valid blocks, and a chain with more work that contains an invalid block is not the best chain.

nodes.example: the chain with the most work
nodes.definition: The best chain is the valid chain with the most cumulative proof of work; it is not necessarily the one with the most blocks.

nodes.label: Chain work
nodes.body: The chain work is the total amount of proof of work behind a block, expressed as the expected number of hashes needed to produce the chain up to it. The help text of the block command defines it as the expected number of hashes required to produce the chain up to this block, in hexadecimal (Bitcoin Core, 2026). It is the sum, over all blocks from the first to this one, of the work of each block, and the work of a block is the expected number of hashes needed to find a hash below its target.

paras.text: The chain work is the total amount of proof of work behind a block, expressed as the expected number of hashes needed to produce the chain up to it. The help text of the block command defines it as the expected number of hashes required to produce the chain up to this block, in hexadecimal (Bitcoin Core, 2026). It is the sum, over all blocks from the first to this one, of the work of each block, and the work of a block is the expected number of hashes needed to find a hash below its target.

This is the quantity that nodes compare to choose the best chain. The source of Bitcoin Core stores it in the index entry of each block, described as the total amount of work, the expected number of hashes, in the chain up to and including that block (Bitcoin Core, 2026). Because it adds numbers that depend only on the targets in the headers, it is the same in every node, and a node can compute the work of a chain from its headers alone, before having any transactions, which is why the node of the book fetches headers first (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The chain information of the evidence node shows chainwork 0000...0100010001 for the first block, and the book's printout has the same ending for a node that had only the first block (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The block data of block 123456 in the book shows a much longer string ending in 541788211ac227bc, abbreviated in the printout (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The unit is hashes, so the value 0x100010001, which is 4295032833, means that about 4.3 billion hashes are expected to find the first block.

The work of one block is computed in the source as 2 to the power 256 divided by the target plus one, with a trick to avoid the number 2 to the power 256, which a 256-bit integer cannot hold: it computes the complement of the target divided by the target plus one, and adds one (Bitcoin Core, 2026). For the first block's target, 0xffff times 256 to the power 26, the result is 4295032833, which is hexadecimal 100010001, exactly the chain work in the node's answer, as the worked example and the checks show. The work of a block with a target of 0x6a93b3 shifted by 23 bytes is about 16.7 trillion hashes.

The chain work counts expected work and not work actually done: the miner of a block may have been lucky or unlucky. It is also not a measure of the value of the chain, only of its cost to reproduce. The number is large and is shown in hexadecimal with leading zeros, which makes it easy to misread; a comparison of two such strings is a comparison of numbers with the same number of digits. And it is a quantity that the node computes itself from the headers, so it is not something that a peer tells it.

nodes.definition: The work of a block is 2^256 divided by its target plus one, the expected number of hashes needed to find it, and the chain work is the sum of the work of all blocks up to it.

nodes.label: Confirmation
nodes.body: A confirmation is a block added at or above the block that contains a transaction. The glossary of the book says that once a transaction is included in a block it has one confirmation, as soon as another block is mined on the same blockchain it has two, and so on (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The block command shows the number under confirmations and the book explains that it tells the depth of the block, how many blocks have been built on top of it, indicating the difficulty of changing any of the transactions in it (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: A confirmation is a block added at or above the block that contains a transaction. The glossary of the book says that once a transaction is included in a block it has one confirmation, as soon as another block is mined on the same blockchain it has two, and so on (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The block command shows the number under confirmations and the book explains that it tells the depth of the block, how many blocks have been built on top of it, indicating the difficulty of changing any of the transactions in it (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

Confirmations are how a user decides when a payment is safe enough. A transaction in the mempool has none and can be replaced or dropped; one in a block at the tip has one and can still be undone by a reorganization; with each block on top, undoing it needs more work. The glossary says that six or more confirmations is considered sufficient proof that a transaction cannot be reversed, and the book's tip says that reorganizations are rare after a transaction has several confirmations (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). How many are enough depends on the value.

In the book the block 123456 has 651742 confirmations, and the source shows how the node computes the number: the height of the tip minus the height of the block plus one, or -1 if the block is not on the main chain (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The worked example reverses it: if the tip is at height 775197, the block at 123456 has 775197 - 123456 + 1 = 651742 confirmations, and the tip itself has one. The call for a raw transaction also reports confirmations for a transaction in a block (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

Each new block extends the chain that already contains the transaction, so the number grows by one with every block on the best chain. If a different branch overtakes the chain, the block that held the transaction leaves the best chain and its confirmations become -1 in the block data, until the transaction is included again in a block of the new chain. An attacker who wants to reverse a transaction with k confirmations has to produce a chain with more work than the honest chain from the block before it, which is the argument that Nakamoto's paper makes with probabilities (Nakamoto, 2008).

A confirmation is a count, not a guarantee; its meaning grows with the work of the blocks, and a confirmation in a low-difficulty chain is worth less. The conventional six is a convention of the book and of its era, not a rule of the protocol, and a large payment may warrant waiting for more. Another trap is that different programs count differently: some start from zero for a transaction in the tip block, while Bitcoin Core counts that block as the first confirmation (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

nodes.definition: A confirmation counts the blocks from a transaction's block to the tip, itself included; each one makes it harder to reverse the transaction.

nodes.label: Chain reorganization
nodes.body: A reorganization is the event in which a node changes which chain it regards as the best. The book of the chapter on mining describes it: when the new block does not extend the best chain, the node attaches its header to a secondary chain and compares the work; if the secondary chain is now the best chain, the node will reorganize its view of confirmed transactions and available UTXOs, and a miner will construct a candidate block extending the new chain (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The blocks that were on the old chain and are not on the new one leave the best chain.

paras.text: A reorganization is the event in which a node changes which chain it regards as the best. The book of the chapter on mining describes it: when the new block does not extend the best chain, the node attaches its header to a secondary chain and compares the work; if the secondary chain is now the best chain, the node will reorganize its view of confirmed transactions and available UTXOs, and a miner will construct a candidate block extending the new chain (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The blocks that were on the old chain and are not on the new one leave the best chain.

Reorganizations are the mechanism by which the network resolves forks without any authority. They matter to a user because they are the only way in which a confirmed transaction can become unconfirmed. The book's tip says the txid of a confirmed transaction cannot change unless there is a reorganization that removes the block from the best chain, and that such reorganizations are rare after a transaction has several confirmations (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Most reorganizations are only one block deep.

A reader meets the term in the book's discussion of identifiers and of mining, in the documentation of the node's log, which records the switch, and in wallets, which may show a payment as unconfirmed again. It is also the reason why a node keeps for each block data to undo it, the files called rev in the data directory, which Bitcoin Core's file documentation describes as block undo data (Bitcoin Core, 2026). And the alert command can be triggered by a related event, when the node finds an invalid chain with more work than its own (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

When the new chain has more work, the node disconnects the blocks of the old branch from the tip down to the point where the branches split, which restores the outputs those blocks spent and removes the ones they created in the set of unspent outputs, and then connects the blocks of the new branch. The transactions of the disconnected blocks that are not in the new blocks go back to the mempool, where they may be mined again. The worked example represents the two branches by invented sets of transactions: tx2 and tx3 lose their confirmation, tx4 gains one, and tx1 is confirmed in both, and so never changes.

A reorganization does not undo a payment by itself: the transaction usually returns to the pool and is confirmed again in a later block, unless it conflicts with a transaction in the new chain, for instance one that spent the same output. The dangerous case is a double spend, in which the sender pays twice and tries to make the second payment win, and this is the attack that the number of confirmations guards against. A last caution is the scale: after an attack, a deeper reorganization needs more work than the honest network, and the argument depends on no single party controlling most of it (Nakamoto, 2008).

nodes.example: switching to a branch with more work
nodes.definition: A reorganization occurs when a node switches to a different chain with more work: blocks leave the best chain, their transactions return to the mempool unless the new chain includes them, and the set of unspent outputs is updated.

io.code: (lambda g: (exec("a = {'tx1', 'tx2', 'tx3'}\nb = {'tx1', 'tx4'}\nresult = (sorted(a - b), sorted(b - a))", g), g['result'])[1])({})

nodes.label: Fork
nodes.body: A fork is a point where the chain of blocks divides into two branches. The glossary of the book defines the fork, also called an accidental fork, as the case in which two or more blocks have the same block height, forking the blockchain, which typically occurs when two or more miners find blocks at nearly the same time (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The worked example has a genesis block G with two children A1 and B1 at height 1 and a further block A2 on top of A1, so that the chain has two tips, A2 and B1, and the longer branch is the one that ends in A2.

paras.text: A fork is a point where the chain of blocks divides into two branches. The glossary of the book defines the fork, also called an accidental fork, as the case in which two or more blocks have the same block height, forking the blockchain, which typically occurs when two or more miners find blocks at nearly the same time (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The worked example has a genesis block G with two children A1 and B1 at height 1 and a further block A2 on top of A1, so that the chain has two tips, A2 and B1, and the longer branch is the one that ends in A2.

Forks are how a distributed network without a central clock behaves, and they are resolved by the rule that a node follows the branch with the most proof of work. The shorter branch is abandoned, its blocks become stale, and the transactions in them return to the pool, which is what a reorganization does. Understanding the accidental fork is what makes the advice about waiting for confirmations sensible, since the block that ends a payment's journey is safe only when a branch has grown on top of it.

The word is used in two other senses in the chapter. A soft fork is a change of the rules that tightens them, so that the nodes that have not upgraded still accept the blocks of those that have. A hard fork, in the glossary's words, is a permanent divergence in the blockchain, which commonly occurs when non-upgraded nodes cannot validate blocks created by upgraded nodes that follow newer consensus rules (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The glossary adds that it must not be confused with a software fork or a Git fork, the copy of a repository, which has nothing to do with the chain.

At a fork each node has seen the blocks in a different order and may have a different tip until one branch is extended. The node stores both branches in its block index and tracks the work of each, and when a branch overtakes the other it switches, as the concept of reorganization explains. In the permanent case, nodes on the two sides follow different rules, so that no branch can overtake the other from the point of view of the other side, and the chain stays divided.

Not every split is a fork of the chain. Two nodes can disagree for a moment about the tip because a block has not reached one of them yet, and this is normal, not a fork. And a software fork, in which somebody copies the code and changes it, creates a new program but not a new chain unless its rules are incompatible with the old ones and someone runs it on the same network.

nodes.definition: A fork is a split of the chain into two branches, accidental when two miners find blocks at about the same time, or permanent when rules change incompatibly.
