nodes.label: Ecosystem
nodes.body: The ecosystem branch is about the software around the reference implementation and about how a person can trust what they download. The last section of the chapter, on alternative clients, libraries and toolkits, says that there are many alternative clients, libraries, toolkits and even full-node implementations in the Bitcoin ecosystem, written in a variety of programming languages that offer programmers native interfaces in their preferred language (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The chapter ends by sending the reader back to their own running node, and this branch asks two questions that follow from that: how do I know that the program I run is the program the project published, and what else could I use to talk to Bitcoin if the reference implementation does not fit my work.

paras.text: The ecosystem branch is about the software around the reference implementation and about how a person can trust what they download. The last section of the chapter, on alternative clients, libraries and toolkits, says that there are many alternative clients, libraries, toolkits and even full-node implementations in the Bitcoin ecosystem, written in a variety of programming languages that offer programmers native interfaces in their preferred language (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The chapter ends by sending the reader back to their own running node, and this branch asks two questions that follow from that: how do I know that the program I run is the program the project published, and what else could I use to talk to Bitcoin if the reference implementation does not fit my work.

A node is only as trustworthy as the software it runs, because the node is the thing that checks the rules on the owner's behalf. If the program has been altered on its way to the computer, every answer it gives is worthless, however carefully the owner reads the output. The branch therefore treats the download as the first link of the chain of verification, before the first block is validated, and treats the choice of a library as a decision that can be examined with data rather than with taste.

The evidence for this branch comes from the real release 31.1 of Bitcoin Core: the file of checksums that the project publishes next to its programs, the file of signatures on it, and the documentation of the project's own tools for checking them (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The second kind of evidence is the data of the package registries on the toolkits that the book lists, which were queried on the day this chapter was prepared (Package registries, 2026). Both are saved in the repository of the course, so that the statements of the branch can be recomputed instead of believed.

The branch is organised in one group, assurance, with seven concepts. A checksum and an OpenPGP signature are the two mechanisms; the verification of a release combines them; a reproducible build is the project's way of letting several people arrive at the same files independently; a package registry is where the libraries of the ecosystem are published; and the alternative toolkits are the libraries themselves. Each concept is explained with a computation that anybody can run on the saved files.

nodes.label: Assurance
nodes.body: Assurance is the group of concepts that answer the question how do I know. In this chapter it covers the evidence one can gather about a program before trusting it, namely the checksum published for the download, the signatures on that checksum and the build that makes the files reproducible, and the evidence one can gather about a library before depending on it, namely its latest release in a package registry. The common feature is that each statement can be checked by a computation on saved files and does not depend on the reputation of whoever makes it.

paras.text: Assurance is the group of concepts that answer the question how do I know. In this chapter it covers the evidence one can gather about a program before trusting it, namely the checksum published for the download, the signatures on that checksum and the build that makes the files reproducible, and the evidence one can gather about a library before depending on it, namely its latest release in a package registry. The common feature is that each statement can be checked by a computation on saved files and does not depend on the reputation of whoever makes it.

The distinction between checking and trusting is the course's theme in miniature. The documentation of the build tooling of Bitcoin Core puts it as the wish to audit and reproduce the toolchain instead of blindly trusting binary downloads (Bitcoin Core, 2026). A reader who has taken this chapter's own advice and runs a node has made the same choice for the data: instead of trusting a block explorer, the reader verifies the chain. Assurance extends the choice to the software that does the verifying, and it also shows where the choice ends, since some trust always remains and the useful question is which trust is left.

The group is met when somebody downloads a release, when a project publishes one, and when a developer chooses a library. The saved check of release 31.1 recomputed the checksum of the Linux program archive and counted 11 good signatures on the file of checksums, using 38 builder keys taken from the signature repository of the project (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The registry data separates the toolkits of the book that published a release within a year of the query from those that did not (Package registries, 2026). These are small and concrete results, and the individual concepts of the group show how they are obtained and what they do not prove.

None of the results of this group is a proof of safety. A matching checksum shows that two files are the same, not that either is harmless, and a good signature shows that a key signed, not who holds the key. A recent release in a registry shows activity, not quality. The concepts below state the limit of each check next to the check.

nodes.label: Release verification
nodes.body: Release verification is the check of a downloaded program against what the project published, done before the program is run. The project publishes, for each release, a file named SHA256SUMS that lists a checksum for every file of the release, and next to it a file of signatures on that list (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The check has two steps: first that the list is genuine, which is decided by the signatures, and second that the downloaded file has the checksum listed for it. The book's chapter does not contain this step, since the name of the checksum file does not occur in it, so the material here comes from the documentation of the project.

paras.text: Release verification is the check of a downloaded program against what the project published, done before the program is run. The project publishes, for each release, a file named SHA256SUMS that lists a checksum for every file of the release, and next to it a file of signatures on that list (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The check has two steps: first that the list is genuine, which is decided by the signatures, and second that the downloaded file has the checksum listed for it. The book's chapter does not contain this step, since the name of the checksum file does not occur in it, so the material here comes from the documentation of the project.

A downloaded program runs with the rights of the person who starts it, so a file that was altered on the way is the most direct way to compromise a node. The documentation of the project explains that, as of version 22.0, releases are signed by a number of public keys on the basis of the signature repository, that the end user decides which of these keys to trust, and that the downloaded programs are then hashed and compared to the signed list of checksums (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The user, and not the web site that hosts the file, is the party who decides whom to believe, which is why the check protects against a web site or a mirror that has been tampered with.

The saved check of this chapter was made on release 31.1 and recomputed on the day of preparation. The file of checksums lists 28 files, from archives for several processor families and for Windows and macOS, to debug archives and the source archive, and the Linux archive for the common 64-bit processors is listed with the checksum b80d9c3e04da78fb6f0569685673418cf686fadba9042d926d13fb87ff503f9e. The file downloaded and hashed again has the same checksum and the size 90293352 bytes. The file of signatures holds 11 signature blocks, and the signature-checking program of the saved run reported 11 good signatures after importing 38 builder keys (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The worked example reads the saved files and prints the comparison.

The project ships a script for the whole procedure, which first checks whether the file of checksums is valid based upon a plurality of signatures and then downloads the files named in it and checks that their hashes are as expected (Bitcoin Core, 2026). It can be told to require a number of good signatures, for example at least 10 from a given set of trusted keys, and then the list is accepted only if enough of the people the user chose have signed the same list (Bitcoin Core, 2026). Done by hand, the procedure is the same in substance: compute the checksum of the archive, find its line in the list, and verify the signatures on the list.

The check has a limit that the saved evidence states itself: the keys used for the 11 good signatures came from the signature repository of the project and not from an independent source, so the result shows consistency and does not establish trust in the keys. A careful user obtains the keys of people they have reason to trust by a different path from the one that delivered the file, and then insists on a threshold. A matching checksum alone, from the same web page as the file, would prove only that the page is consistent with itself. The check also says nothing about whether the software has bugs, only that it is the software the builders produced.

nodes.definition: A downloaded release can be checked against the SHA-256 checksums the project publishes and the signatures on them, which shows that the file matches the published record and not that the signers' keys are trustworthy.

nodes.label: Checksum
nodes.body: A checksum is a short value computed from the whole content of a file, which can be compared with a value computed elsewhere to decide whether the two files are the same. The checksums used for Bitcoin Core's releases are the SHA-256 hash function that chapter 2 explained, applied to the bytes of the file. The standard that defines it describes the output as a message digest, and says that the algorithms are secure because it is computationally infeasible to find a message that corresponds to a given digest or two different messages that produce the same digest (Eastlake and Hansen, 2011). For SHA-256 the digest has 32 bytes, which is shown as 64 hexadecimal digits.

paras.text: A checksum is a short value computed from the whole content of a file, which can be compared with a value computed elsewhere to decide whether the two files are the same. The checksums used for Bitcoin Core's releases are the SHA-256 hash function that chapter 2 explained, applied to the bytes of the file. The standard that defines it describes the output as a message digest, and says that the algorithms are secure because it is computationally infeasible to find a message that corresponds to a given digest or two different messages that produce the same digest (Eastlake and Hansen, 2011). For SHA-256 the digest has 32 bytes, which is shown as 64 hexadecimal digits.

A checksum makes comparison cheap. Two files of ninety million bytes cannot be compared by looking at them, and sending one to a person who holds the other would be as costly as downloading it again, but their two digests of 64 characters can be compared in a moment, in a message or on a page. The same standard states the property that makes this useful: any change to a message in transit will, with very high probability, result in a different message digest (Eastlake and Hansen, 2011). A flipped bit in a bad download is therefore detected as surely as a deliberate change.

The file SHA256SUMS of release 31.1 has one line for each of its 28 files, with the checksum, a gap and the name of the file, and the saved run of this chapter computed the checksum of the Linux archive with the program sha256sum (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The archive has the checksum b80d9c3e04da78fb6f0569685673418cf686fadba9042d926d13fb87ff503f9e, which was computed again for this chapter. The standard's own test vector is the message abc, whose digest begins ba7816bf8f01cfea, and the worked example computes it with the python hashing module and compares it to the standard's text.

The way a checksum behaves is best seen on a small change. The digest of abc begins ba7816bf8f01cfea, whereas that of abd, which differs in one character, begins a52d159f262b2c6d, and 58 of the 64 hexadecimal digits of the two digests differ, close to the 60 that would be expected to differ between two unrelated values, since each digit differs with probability 15 in 16. There is no way to predict which digits will change, and no way to make a file with a chosen digest, which is what the words computationally infeasible in the standard mean.

A checksum detects change; it does not say who made the file. If an attacker can replace the file, the attacker can replace the line of checksums that sits on the same server, and the check will pass. That is why the project signs the list of checksums, and why the signature, not the checksum, is what ties the list to people. The second thing to watch is the comparison: a checksum is compared as text, and a copy that changed a letter or lost a character will fail, while a glance at the first few characters is not a check at all, since the standard's guarantee holds for the whole value.

nodes.definition: A checksum is a short fixed-size value computed from a file by a hash function, so that any change to the file makes the value change.

nodes.label: OpenPGP signature
nodes.body: OpenPGP is a standard for the message formats used in secure messages and signed files. Its specification says that OpenPGP provides encryption with public key or symmetric cryptographic algorithms, digital signatures, compression and key management (Wouters et al., 2024). An OpenPGP signature is the digital signature of chapter 2 in this format: the signer uses a secret key to produce a value from the content that anybody holding the matching public key can check. In this chapter the content is the list of checksums of a release, and the signers are the builders who built the release.

paras.text: OpenPGP is a standard for the message formats used in secure messages and signed files. Its specification says that OpenPGP provides encryption with public key or symmetric cryptographic algorithms, digital signatures, compression and key management (Wouters et al., 2024). An OpenPGP signature is the digital signature of chapter 2 in this format: the signer uses a secret key to produce a value from the content that anybody holding the matching public key can check. In this chapter the content is the list of checksums of a release, and the signers are the builders who built the release.

The signature gives the checksum list an author. Without it the list is an assertion by whoever controls the web server, and with it the list is an assertion by a key, which the user can decide to trust or not. Several signatures on the same list add something more: a list that is signed by several independent builders is accepted only if each of them produced the same files, so that an attacker would have to compromise many of them. The documentation of the project describes this as a check based upon a plurality of signatures (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

The file SHA256SUMS.asc of release 31.1 contains 11 signature blocks, each starting with a line of the form BEGIN PGP SIGNATURE and ending with a matching END line, and the saved run reported 11 good signatures after the 38 builder keys of the signature repository were imported (Bitcoin Core, 2026). These are detached signatures: the specification explains that some applications use so-called detached signatures, where a file travels with a second file that holds one or more signature packets stored separately from the data for which they are a signature (Wouters et al., 2024). The file of checksums is the data and the file with the ending asc is the signatures.

The saved run counted, for the signatures on the list, the checks that reported a good signature, and the count was 11. A good signature is a mathematical statement, that the holder of the secret key signed exactly these bytes, and it is checked in the way chapter 2 described for transactions: the public key confirms that the value was produced from this content. It says nothing yet about who the holder is. The step from key to person is the trust decision, which in this design is made by each user for themselves, as the documentation of the project's script says when it tells the user to decide which keys to trust (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

A good signature from a key that was imported from the same place as the file proves little about authenticity, and the saved check of this chapter states this limit in its own output. Keys also expire or are revoked, and the specification of the format has fields and packets for both, so a signature by a revoked key should not be counted (Wouters et al., 2024). The third thing to watch is the difference between this signature and the one in a bitcoin transaction: both use public-key cryptography and both are called signatures, but the OpenPGP one follows a general file format, whereas the transaction signature is a part of the rules of the network and is checked by every node.

nodes.definition: An OpenPGP signature is a digital signature in the format of the OpenPGP standard, made with a person's secret key over a file and checked with the matching public key.

nodes.label: Reproducible build
nodes.body: A reproducible build is a way of compiling a program such that everybody who follows the same steps on the same source gets exactly the same files, byte for byte. The build files of Bitcoin Core are described by the project as bootstrappable builds that allow the user to audit and reproduce the toolchain instead of blindly trusting binary downloads, and they achieve this by using Guix, which the documentation calls a functional package manager (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The toolchain, the compiler and its libraries, is itself part of what is reproduced, so that the result does not depend on the machine of the builder.

paras.text: A reproducible build is a way of compiling a program such that everybody who follows the same steps on the same source gets exactly the same files, byte for byte. The build files of Bitcoin Core are described by the project as bootstrappable builds that allow the user to audit and reproduce the toolchain instead of blindly trusting binary downloads, and they achieve this by using Guix, which the documentation calls a functional package manager (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The toolchain, the compiler and its libraries, is itself part of what is reproduced, so that the result does not depend on the machine of the builder.

Reproducibility turns a download into something that can be verified from the source. If the release files could depend on the builder's machine, nobody could say whether a file differed from the source because of the machine or because of an attack. If they cannot, then a builder who rebuilds the release and obtains the same checksums as the project has confirmed that the published files correspond to the published source, and the more builders do it, the harder it is for any single one of them to be tricked or bribed.

The documentation describes the steps the builders follow. After a successful build the checksums of the outputs are gathered into files named SHA256SUMS in the output directories; each builder then attests to the outputs, which means that the signed lists go into the signature repository, and other builders can check them against their own with a verification command (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The release process documents the same sequence, including the cloning of the signature repository and the commit of each builder's signed list to it (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The signature repository is thus both the store of the attestations and the place where the keys of the builders sit.

The reproducibility rests on removing every source of difference between builds. The documentation mentions, among the options of the build, an override of the reference timestamp used for bit-for-bit reproducibility, which fixes the one value that would otherwise change with every run of the build (Bitcoin Core, 2026). Each builder then signs the checksums of what they obtained, and the project's verification script counts the signatures of a list: a list with many good signatures from different builders is a list that many people obtained independently from the same source.

Reproducibility is evidence about the build and not about the source: the builders confirm that the binary matches the source, and they do not read the source for bugs. The check also depends on the keys: if the keys of the builders are not independent of the project, the attestations are weaker than they appear. Finally, a reproducible build is expensive to do, and most users will not do it; they rely on the signatures of the few that do, which is a delegation of trust, though one that can be checked by any user who is willing to spend the time.

nodes.definition: A reproducible build produces bit-for-bit identical files from the same source, so that several builders can independently attest to the same checksums.

nodes.label: Package registry
nodes.body: A package registry is a public service where the authors of a programming language's libraries publish them, so that others can install them by name and version. The queries of this chapter used six: npm for the JavaScript toolkits, PyPI for the Python ones, the module proxy of the Go language for btcd, the crates.io registry for the Rust crate, Maven Central for the two projects of the Java and Scala headings, and NuGet for NBitcoin (Package registries, 2026). The registry records the versions of a library and, in most cases, the dates at which they were published.

paras.text: A package registry is a public service where the authors of a programming language's libraries publish them, so that others can install them by name and version. The queries of this chapter used six: npm for the JavaScript toolkits, PyPI for the Python ones, the module proxy of the Go language for btcd, the crates.io registry for the Rust crate, Maven Central for the two projects of the Java and Scala headings, and NuGet for NBitcoin (Package registries, 2026). The registry records the versions of a library and, in most cases, the dates at which they were published.

The registry is the place to look when choosing a library, because it holds the facts that a list in a book cannot keep up to date. The book's list was written at one moment, and the registry shows what has happened since: whether the library still publishes releases, how recent the latest one is, and which version a new project would get by default. A query to a registry is a computation on public data, which can be repeated by anybody, and it replaces an impression such as the library seems abandoned with a date.

The saved query of this chapter was made on 2 October 2026 and covers ten entries, one for each project of the book's list except Bitcoin Core itself. For python-bitcoinlib the latest version is 0.12.2, from 3 June 2023, and the package index shows the same date as the one in the project's metadata read earlier (Package registries, 2026) (Todd, 2023). The Rust crate named bitcoin has the version 0.32.102 dated 22 July 2026, and the Python package pycoin has the version 0.92718.20260405, whose number contains its date. The worked example lists the registry and latest version for two of the registries.

Each registry has an interface that answers a request with a document, usually in the JSON format, listing a library's versions and times, and the script of the chapter's evidence reads the latest version and its date from it. The names of the fields differ between registries: npm lists the latest version under a tag, PyPI lists the files of the release with an upload time, the Go proxy returns a version with a time, and Maven Central returns a timestamp for the newest artifact (Package registries, 2026). The script therefore has one small function for each registry, and it records an error rather than guessing when a registry does not answer.

The date of a registry entry is the date of the registry's record and may differ from the date of the work: the NuGet listing used here gives only the list of versions, so the entry for NBitcoin has the latest version 10.0.14 and no date, and the chapter makes no claim about its age. A recent release also does not mean that a library is correct, secure or maintained for the use the reader has in mind. The registries themselves are trusted intermediaries, and an install from a registry is an act of trust of the same kind as the download of a release, though without the signatures the Bitcoin Core project provides.

nodes.definition: A package registry is a public index of the software libraries published for a programming language, with each library's versions and release dates.

nodes.label: Alternative toolkit
nodes.body: An alternative toolkit is a library, a client or even a full-node implementation, other than Bitcoin Core, that lets a programmer work with Bitcoin in a language of their choice. The last section of the chapter lists them by language: Bitcoin Core for C and C++, bcoin, Bitcore and BitcoinJS for JavaScript, bitcoinj for Java, python-bitcoinlib and pycoin for Python, btcd for Go, rust-bitcoin for Rust, bitcoin-s for Scala and NBitcoin for C#, which makes eleven projects under eight language headings (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The book adds that many more libraries exist and more are created all the time (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: An alternative toolkit is a library, a client or even a full-node implementation, other than Bitcoin Core, that lets a programmer work with Bitcoin in a language of their choice. The last section of the chapter lists them by language: Bitcoin Core for C and C++, bcoin, Bitcore and BitcoinJS for JavaScript, bitcoinj for Java, python-bitcoinlib and pycoin for Python, btcd for Go, rust-bitcoin for Rust, bitcoin-s for Scala and NBitcoin for C#, which makes eleven projects under eight language headings (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The book adds that many more libraries exist and more are created all the time (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

A toolkit saves the programmer from writing the serialization, the hashing and the signing again. The wrapper library of the interface branch is one kind; the others on the list do more, such as building and signing transactions without a node. The choice among them matters because a bug in the code that serializes a transaction or computes a hash is a bug in the money handling of the program, and because a toolkit that no longer follows the rules of the network will fail at some upgrade.

The registries show that the upkeep of the listed toolkits varies. On the day of the query, the latest release of bitcoinjs-lib was dated 7 September 2026, of btcd 24 July 2026, of the Rust bitcoin crate 22 July 2026 and of pycoin 5 April 2026, all within a year; the latest releases of the Bitcore library, bitcoinj and bitcoin-s were between January and July 2025; python-bitcoinlib's latest was from June 2023, and the latest npm release of bcoin was from 13 July 2018 (Package registries, 2026). The worked example turns three of the dates into ages in days.

To judge a toolkit with data, one reads from the registry the latest version and the date, from the project's documentation what version of Bitcoin Core it supports, and from its repository how recently it changed. The saved metadata of python-bitcoinlib states that its RPC interface should work with Bitcoin Core v24.0 or later, and the run of release 31.1 in this chapter confirms that for the calls tried (Todd, 2023) (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The age of the latest release is therefore a starting point for a question and not a verdict, since a small, stable library may need few releases.

Three limits apply to the figures. The registry shows the packages that carry a name, and the book's names of the projects do not always match the package names: BitcoinJS appears here as bitcoinjs-lib and Bitcore as bitcore-lib, and the choice of the package is the author's. The data are from one day, and the figures for age will be different when the query is repeated. And the book's list is a list of existing libraries and not a recommendation; the book itself says only that it lists some of the best libraries, clients and toolkits (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

nodes.definition: Libraries, toolkits and full nodes in many languages give native access to Bitcoin, and their upkeep varies, so a listed toolkit's latest release is worth checking.

nodes.label: Semantics
nodes.body: The semantics branch connects the chapter to the course's wider theme, the meaning of data. A node answers every request in the JSON text format, a structure of names and values, which a program can read but whose names carry no meaning of their own; the field called height in a block's answer means what the documentation says it means, and nothing in the text states it. The technologies of the semantic web were designed for this gap, and the branch uses the chapter's data to show two of their ideas, that data can be given an identity that others can refer to, and that the origin of a piece of data can be described.

paras.text: The semantics branch connects the chapter to the course's wider theme, the meaning of data. A node answers every request in the JSON text format, a structure of names and values, which a program can read but whose names carry no meaning of their own; the field called height in a block's answer means what the documentation says it means, and nothing in the text states it. The technologies of the semantic web were designed for this gap, and the branch uses the chapter's data to show two of their ideas, that data can be given an identity that others can refer to, and that the origin of a piece of data can be described.

A reader who has run a node knows why the node's answer is worth trusting: it is the answer of a program that verified the data itself. Chapter 2 introduced the provenance graph for describing where data came from, and the node is the clearest case of a source whose provenance can be stated in a sentence. The branch states it, and also shows how the JSON that the node returns can be turned into linked data by adding a context, which is a small step that makes the same text interpretable by programs that know nothing about Bitcoin.

The branch is met in the examples of this chapter, where the node's answers to the block and transaction commands are JSON texts whose keys the reader has to interpret. The standards involved are the JSON-LD 1.1 recommendation of the World Wide Web Consortium for the format and the same consortium's PROV ontology for provenance, and both were read for this chapter (World Wide Web Consortium, 2020) (Lebo et al., 2013).

The branch has one group, linked data, with three concepts. Verified data is the idea that makes a node's answer authoritative, and is described in the vocabulary of provenance. The context of a JSON-LD document is the mechanism that maps the names of a JSON text to identifiers. The identifier itself, the IRI, is the third concept, since linking data means that two documents use the same identifiers for the same things.

nodes.label: Linked data
nodes.body: Linked data is a way of publishing data so that its parts can be referred to from other data. Each thing that is described, and each kind of property it can have, is given a global identifier, and statements are made by connecting identifiers; the JSON-LD specification describes the idea as being all about describing the relationships between different resources, which may be defined in different documents on the web or within the same document (World Wide Web Consortium, 2020). In this chapter the things are blocks, transactions and nodes, and the statements are the fields that the node returns.

paras.text: Linked data is a way of publishing data so that its parts can be referred to from other data. Each thing that is described, and each kind of property it can have, is given a global identifier, and statements are made by connecting identifiers; the JSON-LD specification describes the idea as being all about describing the relationships between different resources, which may be defined in different documents on the web or within the same document (World Wide Web Consortium, 2020). In this chapter the things are blocks, transactions and nodes, and the statements are the fields that the node returns.

Shared identifiers are what lets data from different sources be combined without guessing. The specification of JSON-LD explains the problem with plain names: tokens such as name and homepage are ambiguous, and the solution is to use IRIs for unambiguous identification, so that developers do not accidentally step on each other's terms (World Wide Web Consortium, 2020). The same argument applies to the Bitcoin data: the word hash in one program's output may mean the hash of a block and in another's the hash of a transaction including its witness, as the chapter's own transaction decoding showed.

The concepts of this group are met in the way the node's output could be published as a dataset. A block, with its height, hash, time and the identifiers of its transactions, is a natural description of a resource; a context can be added to it while the result can still be read by every program that reads JSON, since the format was designed to integrate easily into deployed systems that already use JSON (World Wide Web Consortium, 2020).

Linked data does not make data true. It makes data interpretable, and what a statement says about the world is still up to the source of the statement. For Bitcoin, the truth of a statement about a block comes from the verification the node performed, not from the identifiers used to publish it, and that is why the verified data concept is placed in this group beside the technical ones.

nodes.label: Verified data
nodes.body: Verified data is data that the party using it has checked against the rules instead of taking on someone's word. A full node downloads the blocks, checks each against the consensus rules and keeps only those that pass, so every answer it gives about the chain is the answer of a program that checked the chain; that is the property that the book relies on when it has the reader ask the node, and not a block explorer, about block 123456. The block explorer of chapter 2 shows the same data and can be right, but the reader cannot check it.

paras.text: Verified data is data that the party using it has checked against the rules instead of taking on someone's word. A full node downloads the blocks, checks each against the consensus rules and keeps only those that pass, so every answer it gives about the chain is the answer of a program that checked the chain; that is the property that the book relies on when it has the reader ask the node, and not a block explorer, about block 123456. The block explorer of chapter 2 shows the same data and can be right, but the reader cannot check it.

The property can be described in the vocabulary of provenance. The PROV ontology of the World Wide Web Consortium provides classes for representing and exchanging information about how data was produced (Lebo et al., 2013). It describes an entity as a thing, physical, digital or conceptual, an activity as something that occurs over a period of time and acts upon or with entities, and an agent as something that bears some form of responsibility for an activity taking place (Lebo et al., 2013). In these terms the answer of a node is an entity that was generated by an activity, the verification, and attributed to an agent, the node that the reader runs.

The worked example shows verification in miniature. The header of block 123456 is a set of six fields: the version, the hash of the previous block, the Merkle root, the time, the bits and the nonce. Packed into 80 bytes and hashed twice with SHA-256, the header gives a value which, written backwards, equals the hash that the node printed as the identifier of the block; the example computes this and prints True. A reader who does this has not trusted the node's printed identifier but recomputed it from the fields.

The chain of verification has a precise shape. The identifier of a block is the hash of its header, the header contains the Merkle root, which commits to every transaction of the block, and the header also contains the hash of the previous block, so that checking one header ties it to all the earlier ones. A node does all of this for every block from the first one, and adds the check of the proof of work and of each transaction's signatures; when it then says that a block has a given height or a transaction a given identifier, the statement rests on the checks that it made.

Verified data is authoritative only for the party who verified it, and only to the extent of the node's software and its keeping of the data. A node that was altered, as the assurance group warned, would verify nothing. Verified data also does not travel: if the reader copies the node's answer into a document, the document's readers see only a number, and the provenance has to be added deliberately, for example with the vocabulary above, to tell them where the number came from.

nodes.definition: Data from your own node is authoritative because the node verified it itself, which is the kind of fact a provenance record states about any dataset.

nodes.label: JSON-LD context
nodes.body: A JSON-LD context is the part of a JSON document that says what its keys mean. The specification of JSON-LD 1.1 defines the format as a JSON-based format to serialize linked data, whose syntax is designed to easily integrate into deployed systems that already use JSON, and explains that a context is introduced using an entry with the key @context (World Wide Web Consortium, 2020). In its own words, a context is used to map terms to IRIs (World Wide Web Consortium, 2020). The terms are the keys of the JSON text, such as height and hash, and the IRIs are global identifiers of the concepts they stand for.

paras.text: A JSON-LD context is the part of a JSON document that says what its keys mean. The specification of JSON-LD 1.1 defines the format as a JSON-based format to serialize linked data, whose syntax is designed to easily integrate into deployed systems that already use JSON, and explains that a context is introduced using an entry with the key @context (World Wide Web Consortium, 2020). In its own words, a context is used to map terms to IRIs (World Wide Web Consortium, 2020). The terms are the keys of the JSON text, such as height and hash, and the IRIs are global identifiers of the concepts they stand for.

A context lets the same document be read by a person as ordinary JSON and by a program as linked data. The specification gives the reason in a short phrase: the terms should expand to IRIs so that developers do not accidentally step on each other's terms (World Wide Web Consortium, 2020). For the data of a Bitcoin node this solves the ambiguity of names. The field hash of a block and the field hash of a decoded transaction are both called hash, and a context for each document can map the same key to different identifiers, so that a program combining the two sees that they are different properties.

The worked example is a small model of the mechanism and not an implementation of JSON-LD. It takes two fields of the answer for block 123456, the height and the hash, and a context that maps each key to an identifier in a vocabulary that was made up for the exercise, and prints the pairs of identifier and value. A real processor does much more, such as handling nested objects, types and relative identifiers, and the specification describes all that, but the mapping from term to identifier is the part that matters here.

In the specification the context sits under the key @context, either at the top of the document or inside an object, and its entries map a term to an IRI or to a map, which the specification calls an expanded term definition and which can add a type or other details (World Wide Web Consortium, 2020). The processing of a document replaces each term by the IRI that the context assigns, and the result is a set of statements about identified things. The document needs no change in its shape: a program that reads the JSON as before sees one extra key, @context, and a program that understands linked data uses it.

Adding a context does not check anything. A context that maps height to an identifier for a different meaning would still be a valid context, so the quality of the vocabulary behind the identifiers is what matters, and a vocabulary of Bitcoin terms that the community has agreed on is not something this chapter relies on. The identifiers in the worked example are invented for the example and point to nothing. A context is also written against a particular set of keys, so it has to be revisited if the keys of the answer are renamed.

nodes.example: a context that maps JSON keys to IRIs
nodes.definition: A JSON-LD context maps the keys of a JSON text to IRIs, so that the same JSON becomes linked data without changing its shape.

nodes.label: IRI
nodes.body: An IRI, short for internationalized resource identifier, is a global name written like a web address. The JSON-LD specification defines the absolute form of an IRI as one that contains a scheme along with a path and optional query and fragment segments, and says that Linked Data, and the Web in general, uses IRIs for unambiguous identification (World Wide Web Consortium, 2020). Chapter 2 introduced the uniform resource identifier, with which the payment links of that chapter are written; the IRI is the identifier used by the web standards on which JSON-LD builds.

paras.text: An IRI, short for internationalized resource identifier, is a global name written like a web address. The JSON-LD specification defines the absolute form of an IRI as one that contains a scheme along with a path and optional query and fragment segments, and says that Linked Data, and the Web in general, uses IRIs for unambiguous identification (World Wide Web Consortium, 2020). Chapter 2 introduced the uniform resource identifier, with which the payment links of that chapter are written; the IRI is the identifier used by the web standards on which JSON-LD builds.

Identity is the foundation of linking: two documents can only be about the same thing if they use the same name for it. The specification says that IRIs are a fundamental concept of Linked Data, and that for nodes to be truly linked, dereferencing the identifier should result in a representation of that node (World Wide Web Consortium, 2020). Dereferencing means using the identifier to fetch something, so an IRI can serve at once as a name and as the address of a page that tells what the name means.

IRIs appear in the context of a JSON-LD document, where each term is mapped to one, and as the identifiers of nodes marked by the keyword @id (World Wide Web Consortium, 2020). They appear in the vocabularies that data is described with, such as the PROV ontology, whose terms all have a common namespace beginning http://www.w3.org/ns/prov# (Lebo et al., 2013). In the worked example the IRI is split at the symbol # into the address of a vocabulary and the name of a term in it.

An IRI is made of parts, in the form of a scheme such as https, a path, and optionally a query and a fragment, which is the part after the symbol #. In a vocabulary, the part before the fragment names the vocabulary and the fragment names the term, so that many terms share one address. The specification calls an IRI whose parts are all given absolute, and it turns a relative reference into one by using a base IRI (World Wide Web Consortium, 2020).

An IRI looks like a web address but need not lead anywhere, and the worked example's identifiers do not. Two IRIs that differ in one character name different things, so the capitalization and the final slash or fragment have to be exactly the same in every document that uses the identifier. A well-formed IRI is also not a promise that the thing is well defined: the quality of the definition is a matter of the people who maintain the vocabulary.

nodes.example: a term expanded to an IRI
nodes.definition: An IRI is an internationalized resource identifier, a global name for a thing or a concept, which linked data uses in place of ambiguous words.

nodes.label: Computing foundations
nodes.body: The computing foundations branch collects the everyday vocabulary of programs and computers that the other branches use without stopping to explain it: bytes and bit shifts, times and random numbers, files and processes, libraries and databases, protocols and tests. A student of this course is expected to know Bitcoin's own ideas from the first two chapters, and the first two chapters introduced hashes, hexadecimal notation and public-key cryptography, but they did not need the plain machinery on which Bitcoin Core runs. Chapter 3 is the first chapter in which the reader works with the software itself, so the machinery has to be named.

paras.text: The computing foundations branch collects the everyday vocabulary of programs and computers that the other branches use without stopping to explain it: bytes and bit shifts, times and random numbers, files and processes, libraries and databases, protocols and tests. A student of this course is expected to know Bitcoin's own ideas from the first two chapters, and the first two chapters introduced hashes, hexadecimal notation and public-key cryptography, but they did not need the plain machinery on which Bitcoin Core runs. Chapter 3 is the first chapter in which the reader works with the software itself, so the machinery has to be named.

Without this vocabulary the commands and logs of the chapter are noise: a log that says the signature cache has 16 MiB and the server was started with worker threads means nothing to a reader for whom a mebibyte, a cache and a thread are undefined. With it, each line of the output becomes a small fact that can be checked, and the reader can see why the project chose, say, a fixed number of bytes for a cookie or a database for the set of unspent outputs. The branch is deliberately plain, and each concept is tied to a line or a file of the chapter's own evidence.

The concepts are met in the start-up log, in the data directory, in the documentation of the build and in the source code that the chapter asks the reader to read. The branch has two groups. The first, representation, explains how information is written down: as bytes, as shifted bits, as a time, as a random value and in the Base64 text form. The second, systems, explains the places where programs run and meet each other: files and directories, processes, libraries, databases, platforms, network protocols and software tests.

Every concept of the branch has a worked example that runs on the python standard library alone and prints a value that the text then uses. Where the concept was introduced by a document, the document is quoted and the quotation is checked against the saved copy of the document, so that the foundations rest on the same kind of evidence as the Bitcoin concepts that depend on them.

nodes.label: Representation
nodes.body: Representation is the group of concepts about how a program writes information down. Bitcoin Core's data is numbers and text, but on a computer both are sequences of bytes, and the same number can be written as bytes in two orders, as hexadecimal text or as Base64 text. A time is a number of seconds, a secret is a number that nobody can predict, and an amount is an integer that the program halves by moving its bits. The five concepts of the group are the byte, the bit shift, Unix time, the random number and Base64.

paras.text: Representation is the group of concepts about how a program writes information down. Bitcoin Core's data is numbers and text, but on a computer both are sequences of bytes, and the same number can be written as bytes in two orders, as hexadecimal text or as Base64 text. A time is a number of seconds, a secret is a number that nobody can predict, and an amount is an integer that the program halves by moving its bits. The five concepts of the group are the byte, the bit shift, Unix time, the random number and Base64.

Many apparent puzzles in the chapter are only questions of representation. Why does the hash of a block, printed by the node, look reversed compared with the bytes that were hashed? Why is the halving of the subsidy a shift and not a division? Why does the cookie file hold 64 characters when the cookie is 32 bytes? In each case the answer is that the same information has two representations, and that a program converts between them at a known point. A reader who sees this stops being confused by the conversions and can check them.

The group is met in the serialized transaction, in the fields of the block header, in the files of the data directory and in the headers of the HTTP requests of the interface branch. The saved evidence of the chapter contains each of these: the 80 bytes of a header, the 4-byte time, the 32 random bytes of the cookie, and the Basic scheme of the web request, all of which are used by the concepts below.

A representation is not the information. The text 1a6a93b3 and the four bytes it stands for are the same value, but a program that compares text with bytes will find them different, and a number written with its bytes in the other order is a different number. The concepts of the group therefore state, next to each representation, the rule for converting it and a computation that shows the conversion.

nodes.label: Bit and byte
nodes.body: A bit is a single binary digit, which is either 0 or 1. A byte is a group of eight bits, so it can take 256 different values, and a computer stores and sends information as a sequence of bytes. Chapter 2 introduced hexadecimal notation, in which each digit stands for 4 bits, and the connection is that one byte is exactly two hexadecimal digits: sixteen times sixteen is 256, which is two to the power eight. The worked example reads the text 0a0b as two bytes and the text ff as the byte with the value 255.

paras.text: A bit is a single binary digit, which is either 0 or 1. A byte is a group of eight bits, so it can take 256 different values, and a computer stores and sends information as a sequence of bytes. Chapter 2 introduced hexadecimal notation, in which each digit stands for 4 bits, and the connection is that one byte is exactly two hexadecimal digits: sixteen times sixteen is 256, which is two to the power eight. The worked example reads the text 0a0b as two bytes and the text ff as the byte with the value 255.

Sizes in Bitcoin are given in bytes, and the chapter's figures only make sense when the unit is clear. A block header is 80 bytes, a hash is 32 bytes, which is 64 hexadecimal digits, a cookie is 32 random bytes, and the chapter's examples talk about caches of 16 MiB and a pruning target of 550 MiB. The size of a transaction in bytes decides how much of a block it takes, and the cost of running a node is counted in the bytes it stores and transfers, so a reader needs to move between the units easily.

The units appear in the start-up log, where the book prints that 16 MiB out of 16 MiB were requested for the signature cache, and in the output of the clone command, which reports 217.74 MiB received at 13.05 MiB per second (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The source of Bitcoin Core defines the unit in a small file of conversions, where a mebibyte is written with a shift of 20 bits and a gibibyte with a shift of 30 (Bitcoin Core, 2026). A mebibyte is therefore 1,048,576 bytes, the 550 MiB of the pruning minimum are 576,716,800 bytes, and the 217.74 MiB of the clone are about 228 million bytes.

The prefix mebi means a power of two, 2 to the power 20, and differs by about five percent from the million bytes of the prefix mega, which is why the file with the conversions uses its own names. Several bytes can also be read as one number, and then the order matters. The block header stores the bits field as the four bytes b3 93 6a 1a, which read with the last byte first, called little-endian, give the number 0x1a6a93b3, whereas the same four bytes read with the first byte first would give a different number. The worked example prints the 4-byte form of the number 1 in both orders, and the documentation of SQLite notes the same distinction for its files, which can be copied between architectures that differ in it (SQLite, 2026).

Two confusions are frequent. A bit and a byte are different units, and a link speed given in bits per second must be divided by eight to give bytes. And a mebibyte is not a megabyte, so a figure in one unit must not be compared with a limit in the other without converting it; the download page of Bitcoin Core speaks of gigabytes, and the log speaks of mebibytes, so the reader should not expect the figures to match exactly.

nodes.definition: A bit is a binary digit, a byte is eight bits and holds one of 256 values, so it is written with two hexadecimal digits.

nodes.label: Bit shift
nodes.body: A bit shift moves all the bits of an integer by a number of places. Shifting to the left by one place doubles the number and shifting to the right by one place halves it, with the bit that falls off the right end lost. Shifting by n places multiplies or divides by two to the power n. The operation is written with the signs << and >> in the C++ of Bitcoin Core and in python, and the worked example applies it to the initial subsidy of 5,000,000,000 satoshis, which gives the amounts of the successive eras: 5,000,000,000, 2,500,000,000, 1,250,000,000 and 625,000,000.

paras.text: A bit shift moves all the bits of an integer by a number of places. Shifting to the left by one place doubles the number and shifting to the right by one place halves it, with the bit that falls off the right end lost. Shifting by n places multiplies or divides by two to the power n. The operation is written with the signs << and >> in the C++ of Bitcoin Core and in python, and the worked example applies it to the initial subsidy of 5,000,000,000 satoshis, which gives the amounts of the successive eras: 5,000,000,000, 2,500,000,000, 1,250,000,000 and 625,000,000.

Bitcoin's rules use shifts where one would otherwise write a division or a power. The function that computes the block subsidy starts from 50 coins and shifts the amount right by the number of halvings, and it first returns zero if the number of halvings is 64 or more, because the shift would then be undefined (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The compact form of the target in a block header multiplies a three-byte number by a power of 256, which is a shift left by a whole number of bytes. BIP 9 shifts a block's version right by 29 bits to see whether its top three bits are 001 (Wuille et al., 2015).

In the source, the halving is the line nSubsidy >>= halvings in the function GetBlockSubsidy (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The target of block 123456 is the number 0x6a93b3 shifted to the left by 23 bytes, as the worked example of the compact target does, and the version check of BIP 9 turns the value 0x20000002 into 1 with a right shift of 29 bits, as the soft fork concept shows. Shifting by 8 places moves a number by one byte, so that 0x6a93b3 shifted by 8 is 0x6a93b300, two hexadecimal digits longer.

The shift is exact as long as no non-zero bit falls off. The amount 5,000,000,000 is divisible by 2 to the power 9, so nine shifts to the right are exact and give 9,765,625; this number is odd, so the tenth shift does not divide exactly, and it gives 4,882,812, which drops half a satoshi. The consensus rules accept this rounding because the rule is the code: the subsidy of every era is whatever the shift gives, and every node computes the same value.

Shifts on integers of limited size have limits. The comment in the source says that the explicit check, which returns zero for 64 or more halvings, exists to force the block reward to zero when the right shift is undefined (Bitcoin Core, 2026). A shift whose result is undefined is a hazard of fixed-size integers, and the authors guard against it with a check. The python integers of the worked examples have no fixed size, so the examples of this chapter do not meet that limit, and the reader should not assume that every language behaves in the same way.

nodes.definition: A bit shift moves the bits of an integer to the left or to the right, which multiplies it by a power of two or divides it by one, dropping what falls off.

nodes.label: Unix time
nodes.body: Unix time is a way of writing a moment as a single number, the count of seconds since the start of 1 January 1970 in universal time. The book's table of the block header describes the time field as the approximate creation time of the block in Unix epoch time (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The worked example shows that the value 0 is that start and that the largest value of a 4-byte unsigned number, 4,294,967,295, is a moment in February 2106, which is the date at which the header's time field runs out.

paras.text: Unix time is a way of writing a moment as a single number, the count of seconds since the start of 1 January 1970 in universal time. The book's table of the block header describes the time field as the approximate creation time of the block in Unix epoch time (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The worked example shows that the value 0 is that start and that the largest value of a 4-byte unsigned number, 4,294,967,295, is a moment in February 2106, which is the date at which the header's time field runs out.

A single number is easy to store, compare and calculate with. The consensus rules compare times of blocks with other times, such as the median time past of the previous blocks, and BIP 9 measures the start and the timeout of a deployment in the same unit (Wuille et al., 2015). A time in the header takes only four bytes, which is the reason the format was chosen, and the node can use ordinary integer comparison to enforce the rules about it.

The times of the chapter are Unix times. The first block carries the time 1231006505, which the worked example of the founder concept converts to 3 January 2009 18:15:05, and block 123456 carries 1305200806, with a median time past of 1305197900 (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The release process of Bitcoin Core uses the same notion when it fixes a reference UNIX timestamp so that builds are reproducible (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The nodes also reject blocks whose time is too far ahead of their own clock, and the limit in the source is 2 hours, 7,200 seconds (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

Unix time counts seconds from one fixed moment, so the number is the same everywhere and a program turns it into a local date only when it prints it; the worked example prints its dates in universal time. Because a block's time is a number, a rule about time is a comparison of numbers: the node compares the time of a block with a limit of 2 hours, 7,200 seconds, beyond its own current time, and with the median time past of the previous blocks.

The time of a block is a claim by the miner and not a measurement. The header of block 123456 has a time that is 2,906 seconds later than the median time past of its predecessors, and both numbers are correct for their purposes. A student who reads the time of a block as the exact moment of its creation will be wrong by minutes, and a student who forgets that a 4-byte unsigned number ends in February 2106 will misjudge how long the field can serve.

nodes.definition: Unix time counts the seconds since 1 January 1970 at 00:00 UTC, and Bitcoin uses it for the times in block headers.

nodes.label: Random number
nodes.body: A random number, in the sense that security needs, is a value that an attacker cannot predict. It is not enough that the value looks irregular; the value must come from a source whose output cannot be guessed, such as the sources of randomness that the operating system and the processor provide. Bitcoin Core uses such values for the cookie that protects its interface and for the salt of stored credentials, and the helper script for credentials draws them from the secrets module of python.

paras.text: A random number, in the sense that security needs, is a value that an attacker cannot predict. It is not enough that the value looks irregular; the value must come from a source whose output cannot be guessed, such as the sources of randomness that the operating system and the processor provide. Bitcoin Core uses such values for the cookie that protects its interface and for the salt of stored credentials, and the helper script for credentials draws them from the secrets module of python.

Every secret in the chapter is a random number whose strength is its length. The cookie is 32 random bytes, which is 256 bits, and the salt of a stored credential is 16 random bytes. If the source were predictable, the attacker could compute the secret instead of guessing it, and the interface, which has the power to spend from a wallet, would be open. Randomness is therefore a security matter, and the log of the node reports where it gets it.

The log of release 31.1 contains the lines that say the node uses RdSeed and RdRand as additional entropy sources (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The source of the authentication cookie declares the size of 32 bytes and fills it with the function that draws random bytes (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The comment in the header of the random number code states that the node maintains a single global 256-bit state for all high-quality randomness, and describes a second generator that is seeded once with secure random data but is then completely deterministic, for the cases where speed matters more than secrecy (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The script rpcauth.py asks for 16 bytes of salt and 32 bytes of password from the secrets module (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

A source of randomness collects unpredictable events and mixes them into a state from which it produces output. The worked example calls the same function twice, and gets two different 32-character values, each the hexadecimal text of 16 random bytes. The test that the two differ cannot prove randomness, but a failure would prove a fault, and the chance that two truly random 128-bit values agree is negligible.

A value that merely looks random, such as the output of a deterministic generator started from a known number, is not secure. The cookie or the salt must come from the secure source, and reusing the same value for two purposes would defeat it. Another trap is the length: a short random value is easy to guess even if the source is perfect, which is why the project chose 32 bytes for the cookie.

nodes.definition: A random number is a value that nobody can predict, which Bitcoin Core draws from the computer's secure sources of randomness for cookies and salts.

nodes.label: Base64
nodes.body: Base64 is an encoding that writes any sequence of bytes using only 64 printable characters. The standard that defines it describes the commonly used base 64, base 32 and base 16 encoding schemes, of which base 16 is the hexadecimal text of chapter 2 (Josefsson, 2006). The worked example encodes the text user:pass into dXNlcjpwYXNz and decodes it back to the original, so nothing is lost and nothing is hidden.

paras.text: Base64 is an encoding that writes any sequence of bytes using only 64 printable characters. The standard that defines it describes the commonly used base 64, base 32 and base 16 encoding schemes, of which base 16 is the hexadecimal text of chapter 2 (Josefsson, 2006). The worked example encodes the text user:pass into dXNlcjpwYXNz and decodes it back to the original, so nothing is lost and nothing is hidden.

Many carriers of data, such as the headers of a web request, can hold only text. Base64 lets a program put arbitrary bytes into such a carrier. The Basic authentication scheme of HTTP, which Bitcoin Core accepts for its interface, transmits credentials as a user and a password separated by a colon, encoded using Base64 (Reschke, 2015).

The book's calls to the interface and the helper libraries use the form: the Authorization header holds the word Basic and the Base64 text of the user and the password (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Todd, 2023). The helper script rpcauth.py creates a password with the function token_urlsafe(32), whose comment in the source says that it creates a 32-byte password in Base64 form (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The encoded text is longer than the data: 30 bytes become 40 characters, and 31 bytes become 44, because the output is written in groups of four characters, three bytes at a time.

The standard describes the process: the encoding represents 24-bit groups of input bits as output strings of 4 encoded characters, formed by concatenating three 8-bit input groups and treating the 24 bits as four 6-bit groups, each of which is used as an index into an array of 64 printable characters, and special processing, the padding, is performed if fewer than 24 bits are available at the end (Josefsson, 2006). Decoding reverses the steps. The process uses no key and no secret, which is why the encoding is reversible by anybody, and why it is called an encoding and not an encryption.

The most common mistake is to treat the encoded text as protected. The standard of the Basic scheme itself warns that it is not secure on its own and should be used with a secure system, since the user and the password are passed over the network as cleartext (Reschke, 2015). For Bitcoin Core this is the reason the project advises against exposing the interface over the public Internet, and the reason a cookie or a hashed credential is kept in a file with restricted access.

nodes.definition: Base64 is a way of writing bytes as text with 64 characters, so that binary data can travel in a text header, and it is not encryption.

nodes.label: Systems
nodes.body: Systems is the group of concepts about where programs run and how they meet. A program lives in files in a directory, runs as a process with threads, uses libraries written by others, keeps data in a database, is built for a platform, talks to other programs through a protocol, and is checked by tests. All of these appear in the chapter, from the data directory and the daemon to the libraries and the unit tests of the source.

paras.text: Systems is the group of concepts about where programs run and how they meet. A program lives in files in a directory, runs as a process with threads, uses libraries written by others, keeps data in a database, is built for a platform, talks to other programs through a protocol, and is checked by tests. All of these appear in the chapter, from the data directory and the daemon to the libraries and the unit tests of the source.

Bitcoin Core is a large program, and the chapter shows a reader how to build it, run it and talk to it. Each of those activities touches one of the concepts of this group, and a reader who can name them can read the documentation of the project, for example the file that lists what the data directory contains or the notes on what each platform needs. The group also helps with the final part of the chapter, where the choice of a library or a node implementation depends on the language and the platform.

The concepts are met in the chapter's evidence. The 28 files of release 31.1 are named for the platform that they were built for. The data directory holds the databases of the chain state and the index. The log records the threads of the server. The README of the project describes the tests that every change must pass, and the build notes name the package managers of the supported systems.

These are general concepts, and the explanations here only go as far as the chapter needs. A reader who wants more about operating systems or databases will find that each concept is the subject of a large field; the aim here is to be precise about the facts the chapter rests on.

nodes.label: File and directory
nodes.body: A file is a named piece of stored data, and a directory is a place that holds files and other directories, so that names form a tree. A path is the list of names from the top of the tree to a file. The example from the book's log is the path /lotsofspace/bitcoin/.cookie, which the worked example splits into the top, the directories lotsofspace and bitcoin, and the file name .cookie. Directories are also called folders, and the release archive of the chapter has a folder bin and a folder libexec.

paras.text: A file is a named piece of stored data, and a directory is a place that holds files and other directories, so that names form a tree. A path is the list of names from the top of the tree to a file. The example from the book's log is the path /lotsofspace/bitcoin/.cookie, which the worked example splits into the top, the directories lotsofspace and bitcoin, and the file name .cookie. Directories are also called folders, and the release archive of the chapter has a folder bin and a folder libexec.

Almost everything that Bitcoin Core keeps is a file in a directory, and the documentation of the project describes the layout. The data directory of the node holds the blocks, the chain state, the log, the configuration file and the cookie, and the reader must know which of them can be deleted, which must be backed up and which must be protected from other users. A path is also how the node is told where to put its data, with an option that names a directory.

The project's file documentation lists the entries of the data directory in a table, with the block index in blocks/index/, the chain state in chainstate/ and the optional transaction index in indexes/txindex/, each marked as a LevelDB database (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The evidence of the chapter lists the entries that a fresh node created, from banlist.json and bitcoin.conf to peers.dat and settings.json, and the book's log names the cookie file by its full path (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The directory tree is resolved from the top: to find the cookie, the system reads the top directory to find lotsofspace, reads that to find bitcoin, and reads that to find .cookie. Each file has attributes, among them who may read and write it. The cookie is created with permissions that depend on a mask applied at creation time, and the project sets the mask so that, by default, only the owner can read the file.

A path is relative or absolute, and a relative path depends on the directory the program was started in, which is a common cause of a program not finding its configuration. The project's documentation gives a different default location of the data directory for each of the three common systems, so a path that works on one machine is not a path that works on another.

nodes.example: the path of the cookie file
nodes.definition: A file holds data under a name, a directory holds files and other directories, and a path names a place in that hierarchy.

nodes.label: Process and thread
nodes.body: A process is a program in execution: the computer loads the program, gives it an area of memory of its own and runs it. A thread is a sequence of steps inside a process, and a process can have several threads, which share its memory and can run at the same time on different processor cores. The worked example divides the numbers below 1000 into four quarters, as four threads would share the work, adds up each quarter and combines the four partial sums into the total 499,500; the browser that runs the example cannot start threads, so the quarters are added one after another, which gives the same sums.

paras.text: A process is a program in execution: the computer loads the program, gives it an area of memory of its own and runs it. A thread is a sequence of steps inside a process, and a process can have several threads, which share its memory and can run at the same time on different processor cores. The worked example divides the numbers below 1000 into four quarters, as four threads would share the work, adds up each quarter and combines the four partial sums into the total 499,500; the browser that runs the example cannot start threads, so the quarters are added one after another, which gives the same sums.

The distinction explains several facts about a running node. The daemon of the chapter is a single process that runs for days. Within it, the log of the book says that script verification uses 3 additional threads and that the interface started 4 worker threads, while the current log reports 16 worker threads, so that the node can check signatures and answer requests in parallel (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The project's documentation presents the split of the program into several processes as a gain in isolation (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

The documentation of the multiprocess build describes the future division of the program in these terms: the node, the wallet and the graphical interface would run in separate address spaces for better isolation, with the node starting the wallet as another process and communicating with it over a socket pair (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The command that starts an external program, the one that the alert notification uses, runs in a thread of its own so that a slow script cannot hold up the node, as the source of the notification shows.

The operating system schedules processes and threads onto the processor cores, and gives each process its memory, so that the memory use of a node is the sum of what its parts request. That is why the guide to reducing memory speaks of the sizes of the caches and of the number of connections, and why the build notes of the project warn that a compilation needs at least 1.5 GB of memory. Threads share data and must coordinate their access; processes share nothing unless they ask, through a channel such as a socket.

A thread does not make a program faster in every case, and more threads use more memory. For a reader the practical rule is that the number of threads, like the cache sizes, is a setting with a default, and the default of one release is not the default of another, as the two logs, with 4 and 16 worker threads, show.

nodes.definition: A process is a running program with its own memory, and a thread is a flow of execution inside a process that shares its memory with the others.
