nodes.label: Software library
nodes.body: A software library is a collection of ready-made code that other programs call. The program does not copy the code into its own text; it names the library and uses its functions. The worked example calls the hashing library of python to compute the SHA-256 digest of the text abc, and prints the first eight characters, ba7816bf. The same word is used for the libraries a build needs, the shared library of the project itself, and the libraries for other languages in the last section of the chapter.

paras.text: A software library is a collection of ready-made code that other programs call. The program does not copy the code into its own text; it names the library and uses its functions. The worked example calls the hashing library of python to compute the SHA-256 digest of the text abc, and prints the first eight characters, ba7816bf. The same word is used for the libraries a build needs, the shared library of the project itself, and the libraries for other languages in the last section of the chapter.

Libraries make large programs possible and are also a source of risk. The build notes of Bitcoin Core list the libraries that must be installed before a build, such as the Boost libraries for general C++ code, SQLite for the wallet, ZeroMQ for messaging and Cap'n Proto for communication between processes (Bitcoin Core, 2026). Each of them is code that the project did not write and that guards money all the same, which is why the project documents its dependencies and offers a way to build them from source.

The reference implementation is itself a library as well as a program. The file documentation of the project lists a shared library, libbitcoinkernel, which contains the core consensus and validation code, so that other programs can reuse the rules without taking the rest of the node (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The book glossary describes LevelDB, the database in which the chain state is kept, as a light-weight, single-purpose library for persistence (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The wrapper library of the interface branch and the toolkits of the ecosystem branch are libraries for programmers who talk to a node.

A library is used in one of two ways. It can be linked into the program when it is built, so that the finished program contains it, or it can be a shared file that the program loads when it starts, which is the form of libbitcoinkernel.so and which lets several programs use one copy. In both cases the program needs the library's version to be compatible, which is the reason the build documentation names the packages for each system.

A library is trusted by the program that uses it. A flaw in a library affects every program that includes it, and a library that is no longer maintained, like the toolkits that the registry data of the ecosystem branch shows to be old, can fail when the rules of the network change. The reader should therefore ask of a library, as of a program, where it comes from and who looks after it.

nodes.example: a shared library of consensus code
nodes.definition: A library is a collection of code written to be used by other programs, which saves them from writing it again and which they load or compile in.

io.code: __import__('hashlib').sha256(b'abc').hexdigest()[:8]

nodes.label: Database
nodes.body: A database is a store of data organised so that a program can find and change particular items quickly and safely. Two kinds appear in the chapter. A key-value store keeps one value under each key, and the book glossary describes LevelDB as an open source on-disk key-value store (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). A relational database keeps tables of rows and is queried with SQL, and the SQLite project describes its product as an in-process library that implements a self-contained, serverless, zero-configuration, transactional SQL database engine (SQLite, 2026).

paras.text: A database is a store of data organised so that a program can find and change particular items quickly and safely. Two kinds appear in the chapter. A key-value store keeps one value under each key, and the book glossary describes LevelDB as an open source on-disk key-value store (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). A relational database keeps tables of rows and is queried with SQL, and the SQLite project describes its product as an in-process library that implements a self-contained, serverless, zero-configuration, transactional SQL database engine (SQLite, 2026).

A node must look up the unspent output that a new transaction spends, without reading the whole chain, and must do so for every input of every transaction. A database makes this lookup quick and, as SQLite's own summary of its features puts it, offers ACID transactions, even after power loss (SQLite, 2026). The same need arises for a wallet, which keeps keys, descriptors and transactions that it must never lose.

The project's file documentation names the databases of the data directory: the block index in blocks/index/, the chain state in chainstate/, and the optional transaction index in indexes/txindex/ are all LevelDB databases (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The wallet of the current release is a single SQLite file, as the descriptor wallet concept explains, and SQLite's own description says that it reads and writes directly to ordinary disk files and has no separate server process (SQLite, 2026). The older wallet format used a third database, BerkeleyDB, which the book's log of the wallet check names with its version (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The worked example holds the two outputs of Alice's transaction in a python dictionary, which is a small key-value store kept in memory, sums them to 95,000 satoshis, and looks one up by its key; a dictionary does what a key-value store does, but without a file and without the guarantees against power loss.

A key-value store is searched by exact key, as the lookup by outpoint in the example, and is very fast for it; it cannot answer a question about all values at once without reading them. A SQL database can sum, sort and join with a single query, where the example needs a line of its own for the sum. The cost of that flexibility is a more complex engine. Both kinds write changes so that, after a crash, the data is either in the state before the change or the state after it, which is what the word transactional means for SQLite, and which is a different use of the word from a Bitcoin transaction.

A database is not the chain. The chain state is derived from the blocks, and the help text of the node describes the option -reindex-chainstate as wiping the chain state and rebuilding it from the block files on disk (Bitcoin Core, 2026). Also, the word transaction means two different things in this chapter, a transfer of bitcoin and an atomic change of a database, and the two must not be mixed up.

nodes.definition: A database stores data so that it can be searched and updated reliably, and Bitcoin Core uses a key-value database for the chain and an SQL database for the wallet.

nodes.label: Platform
nodes.body: A platform is the kind of computer a program is built for. It is described by the processor family, which decides the machine instructions, and by the operating system, which is the program that starts other programs and gives them access to memory, files and the network. A program compiled for one platform does not run on another. The names of the files in the release of Bitcoin Core show it: the list of checksums of release 31.1 has archives for eight platforms, among them aarch64-linux-gnu, x86_64-linux-gnu, arm64-apple-darwin, x86_64-apple-darwin and win64.

paras.text: A platform is the kind of computer a program is built for. It is described by the processor family, which decides the machine instructions, and by the operating system, which is the program that starts other programs and gives them access to memory, files and the network. A program compiled for one platform does not run on another. The names of the files in the release of Bitcoin Core show it: the list of checksums of release 31.1 has archives for eight platforms, among them aarch64-linux-gnu, x86_64-linux-gnu, arm64-apple-darwin, x86_64-apple-darwin and win64.

The user has to choose the right file, and the builder has to build one for each. The names combine, by their form, the processor family at the start with the operating system after it: x86_64-linux-gnu names the x86_64 family with Linux, arm64-apple-darwin the arm64 family with the system of Apple's computers, whose name in the book is macOS, and win64 names Windows on a 64-bit processor. The download for the wrong platform will not run, and the checksum list is organised by these names so that a user can find the line for the file they have.

The chapter itself names the platforms in two places. The build instructions are separate for each: the book names Android, FreeBSD, NetBSD, OpenBSD, macOS, Unix and Windows, and the current tree has a file of build notes for each of the systems (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The release evidence of this chapter lists 28 files of release 31.1, of which the Linux archive for the 64-bit processors was downloaded, checked and run. The continuous integration of the project, as its README says, makes sure that every pull request is tested on Windows, Linux and macOS (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

The worked example extracts the platform name from each file name of the checksum list and finds eight. The same platform can appear in several files: the checksum list has, besides the ordinary archives, debug archives, archives whose names contain unsigned or codesigning, and the source archive, which belongs to no platform. The platform also decides the defaults of the program, for example the location of the data directory, which the project's documentation gives separately for each system.

The word platform is used loosely. In the first chapter it was used for kinds of wallet, such as desktop and mobile, and here it means the processor and the operating system. A program built for a platform may depend on features of the operating system, such as the way it handles files or the network, which is one more reason to test on each of them.

nodes.definition: A platform is the combination of processor family and operating system for which a program is built, and a release has one archive for each.

nodes.label: Network protocol
nodes.body: A network protocol is an agreement between programs about what messages look like and in what order they are sent. HTTP, for example, is described by its standard as a stateless request and response protocol for exchanging messages across a connection, in which a client sends requests to a server and the server answers (Fielding et al., 2022). A client and a server are roles, not kinds of machine: the program that asks is the client and the program that answers is the server, and a single program, like a node, can be a server for one party and a client of another.

paras.text: A network protocol is an agreement between programs about what messages look like and in what order they are sent. HTTP, for example, is described by its standard as a stateless request and response protocol for exchanging messages across a connection, in which a client sends requests to a server and the server answers (Fielding et al., 2022). A client and a server are roles, not kinds of machine: the program that asks is the client and the program that answers is the server, and a single program, like a node, can be a server for one party and a client of another.

The protocols decide who can talk to the node and how. The interface of the chapter uses JSON-RPC messages carried by HTTP, and the specification of JSON-RPC says that it is independent of the transport, so that the same messages may travel within a process, over sockets or over HTTP (JSON-RPC Working Group, 2013). The network of nodes uses its own protocol, whose spreading of data chapter 2 described as gossiping, and the network information of a node reports a protocol version, 70016 in the book's example (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

A network address has two parts: the machine and the port. The worked example splits the address http://127.0.0.1:8332/ into the scheme http, the host 127.0.0.1, the port 8332 and the path, which are the parts of the address in the book's curl call. The port number selects the service on the machine, and the source gives a different default for each network, so that a main-network node and a test-network node can run on one computer. The start-up log of the chapter records that the interface was bound to the address 127.0.0.1 and the port 8332 (Bitcoin Core, 2026). It also shows that the node first tried the address ::1 on the same port, which failed with a warning: the first is an address of the fourth version of the internet protocol and the second of the sixth, the two versions that the network information of a node lists as reachable (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

A connection starts with the client opening a channel to the address and the port, over which the two sides exchange the messages of the protocol. Because the protocol fixes the format, any program that speaks it can take part: the book's example uses curl, a general program for HTTP, to talk to the node, and the specification notes that the carrier does not matter. The release notes of version 30.0 add that a node started through the new command can listen on a Unix socket for client connections (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

A protocol says nothing about trust. HTTP in the form used here sends the credentials as cleartext, so the interface should not be reached over an open network, and the evidence node bound the interface to 127.0.0.1, which is why the chapter treats opening the port to the network as the largest risk. Two programs that speak the same protocol may also differ in the version they support, as the protocol version in the network information shows.

nodes.definition: A network protocol is an agreed format and order of messages between programs, such as HTTP between a client and a server, and a port number names the service on a machine.

nodes.label: Software testing
nodes.body: A software test is a small program that runs another program, or a part of it, on chosen inputs and checks that the result is the expected one. The README of Bitcoin Core describes two kinds: unit tests for the C++ code, which developers are strongly encouraged to write for new code, and regression and integration tests, which are written in python and exercise the whole node (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The worked example is a test in miniature: it computes the subsidy at the blocks around each halving and prints the values that a correct program must give.

paras.text: A software test is a small program that runs another program, or a part of it, on chosen inputs and checks that the result is the expected one. The README of Bitcoin Core describes two kinds: unit tests for the C++ code, which developers are strongly encouraged to write for new code, and regression and integration tests, which are written in python and exercise the whole node (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The worked example is a test in miniature: it computes the subsidy at the blocks around each halving and prints the values that a correct program must give.

The README itself gives the reason: testing and code review is the bottleneck for development, and this is a security-critical project where any mistake might cost people lots of money (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The software holds no money itself, but it decides which transactions are valid, and a bug in the rules could split the network or let a transaction through that should be refused. For a reader, the tests are also a source of runnable examples of the behaviour that the chapter describes.

The tests are met in the project and in the release. The README says that the CI systems make sure that every pull request is tested on Windows, Linux and macOS (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The release of version 30.0 installs the unit-test executable in the folder libexec and makes it available through the new command as bitcoin test (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The worked example shows that the subsidy at block 775,072 is 625,000,000 satoshis, which is 6.25 bitcoin: this differs from the 25 BTC reward that the book's output states for that block, which is a discrepancy that a test of the rule exposes (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

A test has three parts: the input, the expected output and the comparison. Tests are most useful at the edges of a rule, so the example has the blocks 209,999 and 210,000, on either side of the first halving. A failing test shows that either the code or the expectation is wrong, and finding which is the work of the developer. The tests are run automatically on every change, and the order of the project's process, with review by someone other than the author, adds a second kind of check.

Passing tests do not prove that a program is correct; they show that it behaves as expected on the cases that someone thought of. The project's own statement that review is the bottleneck acknowledges that tests and review complement each other. A reader who relies on a release should also remember that the release was tested on the platforms of the project's continuous integration, and not necessarily on the reader's own.

nodes.definition: A software test runs a program on chosen inputs and compares the result with the expected one, and Bitcoin Core requires its tests to pass before a change is merged.

nodes.label: Programming language
nodes.body: A programming language is a formal notation in which a person writes the instructions of a program, together with the rules that give each form of writing its meaning. The text of a program in such a notation is its source code, and the worked example shows the point on a single number: in python the hexadecimal literal 0xff, the text 'ff' read in base 16 and the text '11111111' read in base 2 all give the value 255, and the literal 0b11111111 equals 0xff. The language decides which notations exist and what they mean.

paras.text: A programming language is a formal notation in which a person writes the instructions of a program, together with the rules that give each form of writing its meaning. The text of a program in such a notation is its source code, and the worked example shows the point on a single number: in python the hexadecimal literal 0xff, the text 'ff' read in base 16 and the text '11111111' read in base 2 all give the value 255, and the literal 0b11111111 equals 0xff. The language decides which notations exist and what they mean.

The choice of language shapes what a program can do and what its authors have to take care of. The files of Bitcoin Core's source tree that the chapter reads have the ending cpp or h, such as validation.cpp and pow.cpp, which is the C++ in which the node is written, and the build notes warn that C++ compilers are memory-hungry (Bitcoin Core, 2026). Python appears where convenience matters more than speed: the project's README says that its regression and integration tests are written in Python, and the helper script for credentials, rpcauth.py, is a python program (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

A reader meets the languages at three places in the chapter. The node and its tools are built from C++ source with the compilation step of the build branch. The tests and helper scripts are run directly by the python interpreter, and every worked example of this chapter is a python expression, which the chapter's builder executes so that the printed values are the real ones. The last section of the chapter lists the toolkits by language, under eight headings from C and C++ to JavaScript, Java, Python, Go, Rust, Scala and C#, so that a programmer can talk to Bitcoin in the language they already use (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

A program in a compiled language, such as C++, is translated before it runs into machine instructions for one platform, which is why a release has an archive for each platform. A program in an interpreted language, such as python, is read and carried out by another program, the interpreter, at the time it runs. The difference explains why a python script runs unchanged on the platforms that have an interpreter, whereas a C++ program has to be built again for each of them, and why the compiled node is the part that must be fast.

A language is not a library and not a platform, although the three are often mentioned together. Knowing the language of a toolkit does not tell the reader whether the toolkit is maintained or correct, which is a question for the package registry and the project, as the ecosystem branch shows. And the same idea looks different in each language: the shift, the byte and the hash of the earlier concepts exist in all of them, but their spelling and limits differ, so a result computed in python is a statement about the rule and not about how another language would write it.

nodes.definition: A programming language is a notation for instructing a computer, and the chapter meets C++ for the node, Python for tests, helpers and examples, and the languages of the toolkits.

findings: Background

Chapter 3 presents Bitcoin Core as the reference implementation and leads a reader from its source to a running full node: selecting a release tag, building bitcoind with autogen.sh, configure and make, running and configuring the node, exploring status, transactions and blocks with bitcoin-cli, and calling the JSON-RPC interface from Python with python-bitcoinlib, before listing alternative libraries.
Comparative analysis

The chapter's examples reproduce on the real 31.1 release: decoding Alice's serialized transaction gives the book's txid, hash, size 194, vsize 143 and weight 569, both outputs and, on a mainnet node, the same two addresses and descriptor checksums; Python over the same hex gives the same txid and wtxid; block 123456's 13 transaction identifiers hash to the Merkle root the book shows, its header hashes to the block hash the book prints and its difficulty follows from its bits; and python-bitcoinlib 0.12.2 on Python 3.14.4 runs the book's rpc_example.py against 31.1 unchanged.
Comparative analysis

One printed result does not match its script: rpc_block.py reads block 775072, where Core's schedule gives a subsidy of 6.25 bitcoins, yet the text reports 10,322.07722534 BTC including a 25 BTC reward and 0.0909 BTC of fees; the explorer's data for that block's 1,966 transactions sum to 5,863.00566521 BTC, with a coinbase of 6.33799108 that is the 6.25 subsidy plus 0.08799108 in fees, so the printed figure belongs to another block. The chapter's own suggestion to compare with a block explorer would expose it.
Comparative analysis

Resource figures differ by source and year: the chapter says over 500 GB at first and about 400 MB a day in 2023, which is about 12 GB a month; the download page now says about 600 GB plus 5 to 10 GB a month and pruning to as little as 10 GB; the bitcoin.org page the owner's notes link lists about 740 GB for the first start and about 20 GB a month, so the figures are orders of magnitude to be re-read where the software is downloaded.
Comparative analysis

The chapter's toolkit list has aged unevenly: the registries queried on 2026-10-02 show releases within the previous year for bitcoinjs-lib, btcd, the Rust bitcoin crate and pycoin, while bitcoinj's latest on Maven Central is dated 2025-02-21 (the earlier query of 2026-09-28 had read it as 2026, which this query does not reproduce); python-bitcoinlib's latest release 0.12.2 dates from June 2023 and its documentation says its RPC interface should work with Bitcoin Core 24.0 or later, which the run above confirms for 31.1; the bcoin package's latest release on npm is from July 2018.
Comparative analysis

A download of the current release can be checked before it is run: the Linux tarball's SHA-256 equals the value in the release's SHA256SUMS, and that file carries 11 good PGP signatures from builder keys held in the guix.sigs repository; recomputed on 2026-10-02 the archive has the size 90293352 bytes and the same SHA-256, the signature file holds 11 signature blocks and the check reports 11 good signatures with 38 builder keys imported; this shows the download matches the published record, and it does not establish trust in the keys, which the check took from the same repository.
Comparative analysis

The book's printed outputs for the status commands differ from release 31.1 in ways that the explanations now state: getnetworkinfo printed relayfee 0.00001000, which is 1 satoshi per virtual byte, whereas 31.1 returns 1e-06, which is 0.1 satoshi per virtual byte; the local services printed as 0x409 (NETWORK, WITNESS, NETWORK_LIMITED) are 0xc09 in 31.1 because the version 2 transport P2P_V2 is added; the start-up log line of 125 automatic connections is reproduced by 31.1 although the newest source defines a default of 200 connections; getblockchaininfo returns its warnings as an array. Each figure is read from the saved output and recomputed by a claim.
Comparative analysis

The source of the reward figure and of the block header are re-derived without a node: block 123456's header hashes to its printed identifier and block 1000's header, saved from a block explorer's API, hashes to its identifier; a transaction parser written with the python standard library reproduces the txid, the wtxid, the size 194, the 125 bytes without witness and the weight 569 of Alice's transaction; the Merkle root of block 123456 follows from its 13 transaction identifiers; and the difficulty of block 123456, 157416.40184364893, follows from its bits 1a6a93b3.
Conclusion

For the course theme, a full node's answers are authoritative because the node verified them, the property that provenance records try to describe, and the JSON that Bitcoin Core returns can be given a meaning as linked data: JSON-LD 1.1 is the W3C's JSON-based format to serialize Linked Data, designed to integrate with systems that already use JSON.
Contemporary developments

The build steps the chapter prints have been replaced: Bitcoin Core 29.0 migrated the build from Autotools to CMake, so a current build is cmake -B build, cmake --build build and cmake --install build; the book's --disable-wallet corresponds to -DENABLE_WALLET=OFF, and the graphical client is now opt-in for a source build with -DBUILD_GUI=ON; since 30.0 a bitcoin command starts the node and tools and with -m runs the multiprocess binaries bitcoin-node and bitcoin-gui; the newest release is 31.1.
Contemporary developments

Several defaults and outputs the chapter prints have moved: the database cache default rose from 450 to 1024 MiB in 31.0 on machines with at least 4096 MiB of memory; legacy BerkeleyDB wallets can no longer be created or loaded since 30.0, and starting the 31.1 release logs SQLite where the book's log shows Berkeley DB 4.8.30; the 31.1 help gives 300 megabytes as the default mempool limit where the chapter's constrained example sets 150; automatic pruning needs a target of at least 550 MiB and cannot be combined with txindex; the warnings field is an array, not the string the book prints.
Course notes

The owner's course notes for this chapter (2021, after the 2nd edition; mostly slide titles over screenshots of the book) add three topics beyond the book's flow, each checked here: the wallet in Bitcoin Core, which the 3rd edition defers to chapter 5 and which the current release keeps in SQLite as a descriptor wallet; the graphical client and the Windows instructions, which the 31.1 release still ships as bitcoin-qt and a win64 installer; and the minimum-requirements page, whose figures now differ from the book's (see the resource finding).
Known limit

Known limit of the chapter page. The quality gate that governs this chapter's ontology is a SHACL shape file, sen0401_ch03_domain_shacl_v1_1_1.ttl, which states 3 node shapes: that every individual carries a label, that anything defined cites its source, and that a worked example carries exactly one input and one output. The chapter builder applies those shapes to the TBox and the ABox before it writes them, and the build fails if they are violated, so the gate does run; what it does not do is reach the student. The interactive page embeds the chapter's TBox, ABox, document and this research record as Turtle, and the shape file is not among them, so a reader who opens the page can read the ontology it teaches from but cannot read, query or re-run the gate that admitted it, and the page's own list of the triples in each corpus file never mentions the shapes. The limit is recorded here rather than repaired here because the list of files the page embeds is set by the page build chain, which this chapter does not own; repairing it means adding the shape file to that chain's corpus list, after which this finding should be revised to say that the gate is shipped.
Methodology

An audit of the vocabulary of the explanations against the concepts of this chapter and of chapters 1 and 2 found terms used without a concept of their own, which are now concepts: Checksum, OpenPgpSignature, ReproducibleBuild, PackageRegistry, Iri, Byte, BitShift, UnixTime, RandomNumber, Base64, FileAndDirectory, Process, Library, Database, Platform, NetworkProtocol, SoftwareTesting, PackageManager, Salt, Hmac, Fork, OutputType, ProgrammingLanguage. The audit compared every term of a list of computing and Bitcoin terms with the text of all explanations and with the concept labels, and the added concepts were checked in turn for further gaps until none of the listed terms remained undefined.

stories.title: The project that outlives its keyholders
stories.who: Satoshi Nakamoto to Gavin Andresen (2011); Andresen to Wladimir van der Laan (2014)
stories.story: Bitcoin Core is the program Satoshi published in January 2009, still developed in public. In 2011 Satoshi handed the project to Gavin Andresen - the faucet builder of chapter 2 - and withdrew. In April 2014 Andresen passed the lead-maintainer role to Wladimir van der Laan to focus on protocol work. Hundreds of contributors and several maintainers later, the repository, its tags and its releases carry on; no single person has been indispensable since.
stories.lesson: The reference implementation is an institution, not a person
stories.source: Repository history of bitcoin/bitcoin (the chapter's pinned checkout is commit 05bc2f53); maintainer handoffs of 2011 and April 2014 as recorded in the project history and summarized at en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bitcoin_Core.

imgs.credit: Bitcoin-Qt 0.5.2, the 2011-era GUI the maintainers inherited - the software's own MIT licence, via Wikimedia Commons

stories.title: Version 0.1, set in stone
stories.who: Satoshi Nakamoto, announcing on the metzdowd.com cryptography mailing list
stories.story: Six days after the genesis block, Satoshi announced Bitcoin version 0.1 - a Windows program on SourceForge. A year and a half later he wrote the sentence this course keeps returning to: once version 0.1 was released, the core design was set in stone for the rest of its lifetime. Everything this chapter builds, configures and queries descends from that one program, which is why Bitcoin Core is called the reference implementation.
stories.lesson: The software came first; the specification IS the software
stories.source: Announcement of 2009-01-09 on the metzdowd.com cryptography list ('Bitcoin v0.1 released'); the 'set in stone' sentence is Satoshi's forum post of 2010-06-17; project history summarized at en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bitcoin_Core.

stories.title: Dozens of builders, one identical binary
stories.who: independent Bitcoin Core builders publishing signed attestations
stories.story: A downloaded binary asks for trust; Bitcoin Core answers with arithmetic. Every release is built reproducibly - first under Gitian, since release 22.0 under Guix - so that anyone compiling the tagged source gets a byte-identical result. Independent builders publish signed hashes of what they produced, side by side, in a public repository. If one build differed, its hash would betray it instantly - the same trick the chapter's Merkle root plays on transactions.
stories.lesson: Verify, don't trust - the project applies its own rule to itself
stories.source: bitcoin-core/guix.sigs on GitHub: per-release folders of builder attestations; Guix build documentation in the pinned source tree, contrib/guix/README.md.
